channel.description: Keeping DFIR Intelligence on your Radar. The latest DFIR research from hundreds of sources, ranked by relevance for practitioners.

item.title: [0day-rubbish] ProSoft Technology RLX-IFH24E v2.2.44 unsigned firmware upgrade package to root command execution and full account-database overwrite (7.2)
item.description:
ProSoft Technology RLX-IFH24E industrial wireless radio accepts unsigned firmware packages, giving an authenticated admin a direct path to root command execution and full account-database overwrite. CVSS 3.1 score: 7.2 High.
- The root cause is CWE-494 (unsigned code installation) with CWE-345 and CWE-347 as co-equal findings. The upgrade handler at /cgi-bin/tool_reprogramming.cgi accepts a multipart/form-data POST, uses the client-supplied filename unmodified to move the file into /upgrade/upgrade/, then passes that same filename to /sbin/upgrade running as root. No extension whitelist, no digest check, no signature verification exists anywhere in the path. The "authenticity" check is a string equality between DEVICE_PRODUCT_NAME from /etc/MHX_CONFIG and PKG_LOCK_NAME from inside the attacker-supplied package itself: both values are attacker-controlled, and the expected value PRODUCT_NAME=IPx21PROSOFT is a compile-time constant readable from the shipped firmware.
- The installer dispatches on file extension. A .pkg payload executes an attacker-authored pre script as uid=0 before the rootfs write, extracts an inner archive with tar -xf extract/upgradepkg.tar -C / (no path restrictions, no allowlist), runs a post script as uid=0 after the write, then reboots, making the change persistent and destroying runtime evidence. A .passwd upload independently overwrites both /etc/passwd and /etc/passwd_original, so the device's own recovery path restores the modified account database. A .factory upload rewrites /etc/db1, the configuration store controlling interface transports and radio behaviour.
- The 0day Rubbish Research Team executed the unmodified /sbin/upgrade inside a chroot sandbox against the real firmware filesystem. The load-bearing evidence is a marker file written at runtime containing PRE-RAN-AS-UID=0, confirmed by a negative control that failed with "This unit doesn't support the image." when given a wrong product string. The upload hop was not executed against hardware: the staging file was placed by hand, and the web server access controls were neither proved nor disproved from the available artefacts. Published CVSS 7.2 reflects PR:H (administrative session required); an unauthenticated path to 9.8 is structurally possible if boa applies no access control, but was not demonstrated.
- Detection is weak by design. A successful install prints the same two lines as a legitimate upgrade. Post-hoc filesystem indicators the report names: a package whose LOCK_NAME and VERSION pair matches no operator-obtained release, a file remaining under /upgrade/upgrade/, and a uid=0 account whose login shell is a general shell (such as /bin/sh) rather than the vendor-shipped restricted interface /bin/txtUI. The factory account model ships an upgrade account at uid=500 with /bin/sh and a home directory of /upgrade/upgrade/, the exact staging path, sharing the same password hash as admin.
- The vendor has no security.txt, no vulnerability-disclosure page, and no CVE assignment is noted in the report. The firmware is listed under a Legacy Products directory on the vendor's support site. The OEM platform (MicroHard Systems IPx21 on MHX-910) is a shared component, and the report flags that other devices built on it plausibly share the root cause, though no other products were tested or scored.
For operators: place /etc/passwd, /etc/passwd_original, and /etc/db1 under file-integrity monitoring and alert on any uid=0 account whose shell is not /bin/txtUI. Isolate the management listener behind an authenticating proxy, confirm factory credentials have been rotated on both the admin and upgrade accounts, and treat every firmware install as a supply-chain event with digests recorded before and after. The full technical analysis, sandbox transcript, and Python 3 proof-of-concept (build-only mode is network-free) are published at the report's linked URL.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2114644033582555514

item.title: Malicious File in Downloads Folder Tries to Trick AI Coding Agent Into Installing Malware
item.description:
A planted AGENTS[.]md in ~/Downloads tricked OpenAI's Codex into installing MALFEX-linked npm package function-color in over 90% of test runs. Check ~/.codex/config.toml for unexpected server blocks and rotate any exposed session tokens.

item.title: Brotli2Shell: Beyond Node(2Shell) and HTTP(2Shell)
item.description:
CVE-2026-111497 in Google's Brotli decoder extends far beyond Node.js and HTTP: JFrog reproduces instruction-pointer control via FFmpeg JPEG XL files and confirms .NET and Apache Arrow are also in scope. Version-only scanners miss large portions of the attack surface.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-111497 is an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder's block-switch error handling. An invalid block switch is treated as a need-for-more-input condition, allowing the decoder to continue with invalid state and write beyond the intended buffer. Affected upstream ranges are Brotli 1.0.3 before 1.0.10, 1.1.0 before 1.1.1, and 1.2.0 before 1.2.1. The upstream fix is in Google Brotli commit 0ed4268 (included in 1.2.1). Node.js fixed it in versions 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. Downstream projects such as ClickHouse (fix merged in PR 127419, no patched release yet) and Apache Arrow (tracked in issue 55166, open at time of writing) may still be shipping vulnerable builds even when a source-level fix exists.
- JFrog confirmed three additional exploitation paths beyond HTTP. First: a crafted JPEG XL file reaches BrotliDecoderDecompressStream() through the chain FFmpeg to libjxl to a brob metadata box, achieving instruction-pointer control at 0x414141414141 via the malformed byte sequence 200010414141fcffff07002228f00b60f7f41f000000 embedded in the brob box. No HTTP connection is required. Second: a two-stage crafted Brotli stream passed to .NET's System[.]IO.Compression.Brotli APIs (BrotliStream and related) triggers a native SIGSEGV, terminating the managed process. Microsoft announced updates rolling out October 25, 2026. Third: a 534-byte input causes an infinite decode loop in Apache Arrow's pyarrow, consuming CPU indefinitely when processing Brotli-compressed Parquet data pages.
- ClickHouse is vulnerable through a different HTTP path than Node.js. A single HTTP request with Content-Encoding: br and a crafted 23 MB body crashes the server. The malformed Brotli stream corrupts decoder state, and the process terminates with a segmentation fault when BrotliReadBuffer is destroyed and the decoder state is freed, interrupting all in-flight queries on that server.
- Version-only scanners miss the real exposure because Brotli is introduced as a bundled source copy, a transitive native dependency, or through high-level APIs that decompress automatically. An application that never calls BrotliDecoderDecompress directly may still reach the vulnerable code through an HTTP client automatic response decompression, request-body middleware, or a native media library. The key questions are: is a vulnerable decoder present, and can attacker-controlled input reach it? These must be answered independently.
Practitioner takeaway: scope your exposure beyond package manifests. Hunt for BrotliDecoderDecompress and BrotliDecoderDecompressStream symbols in ELF binaries using nm or strings, and trace call paths from HTTP response handlers, file parsers, and middleware into those symbols. JFrog's open-source scanner (github[.]com/jfrog/vulnerability_scanners/tree/main/brotli2shell_cve_2026_111497) covers JavaScript fetch() and body-parser patterns, Python clients including Requests, HTTPX, aiohttp, and urllib3, native ELF decoder references, and Brotli CLI decompression invocations. Cross-reference scanner findings against whether your deployed build includes commit 0ed4268, not just the upstream version number, since downstream projects may still be shipping pre-fix releases.

item.title: HTTP2Shell: Sweet Security Confirms Brotli Vulnerability Also Affects Native Go Implementations | Sweet blog
item.description:
CVE-2026-111497, a Brotli decoder out-of-bounds write, confirmed in Go Brotli v1.2.6, affecting Traefik, Fiber, and fasthttp. Upgrade to v1.2.7 and audit services decompressing untrusted Brotli payloads.

item.title: Gheist: Attempted Scaled Abuse of Stolen GitHub Tokens Stumbles
item.description:
Gheist campaign plants secret-dumping GitHub Actions workflows across 850+ compromised accounts, exfiltrating CI/CD secrets and cloud credentials through GitHub's own API with no attacker-controlled C2.
Key details:
- Active since September 15, 2026, Gheist uses stolen GitHub tokens (sourced from infostealer logs and earlier supply-chain compromises, including the Trivy compromise in March) to push a workflow named sync-check.yml to a branch matching ^ci-sync-[0-9a-z]{6}$ with commit message "ci: sync config". The workflow base32-encodes secrets before printing them, bypassing GitHub's verbatim masking, then the tool retrieves the log via the GitHub API and deletes the run within seconds. No attacker domain is involved: secrets exit entirely through GitHub's own infrastructure, making network-layer blocking ineffective.
- Two tool variants run in parallel. Tool A uses a hexadecimal branch suffix. Tool B (base36 suffix) evolved rapidly: it added an environment matrix to capture deployment-scoped production secrets, then on October 19 pushed a second job, sync-host, targeting self-hosted runners. That job writes .gdmp_pat, .gdmp_patg, and .gdmp_sweep to the runner, reads /proc/*/environ, mounts the host root filesystem through the Docker socket, and searches for 31 token formats covering AWS, GCP, Azure, Kubernetes service account tokens, Terraform state, shell history, and AI provider keys for Anthropic, Hugging Face, Groq, and NVIDIA.
- GitHub's approval hold (in place since July 28, 2026) has successfully blocked all public repository runs: every public Gheist workflow sits at action_required. Private repositories and GitHub Enterprise Server have no equivalent control. GitHub audit logs show ci-sync-* workflow runs completing and being deleted by the gheist user agent. CloudTrail confirms the organizations' own workflows ran on attacker branches and assumed AWS roles, providing a detection path that does not depend on GitHub logs at all: look for OIDC role assumptions or token exchanges whose subject includes a ci-sync- branch.
- The compromised account pool overlaps with multiple concurrent campaigns. On October 6, 391 accounts renamed roughly 1,461 repositories to cracked-software lures. On October 18, 25 Gheist accounts created "Windows RDP Runner" repositories within nine minutes to abuse Actions for cryptomining. Three victims show signs of PolinRider, the DPRK-linked malware that hides JavaScript in build configs with backdated force-pushed commits. 57 accounts from Gheist's first phase were also Megalodon victims in May, illustrating how stolen credentials circulate across threat actor ecosystems.
- Wiz's report names detection rules including "New Workflow Completed And Deleted In Short Time Span", "Workflow Pushed With Secret Dump", and "Commit Created With Known Malicious Commit Message", and the Threat Center advisory includes an Event Explorer query covering planted commits, Gheist activity in GitHub audit logs, and cloud role assumptions from attacker branches.
Hunt in CloudTrail and equivalent cloud audit logs for OIDC token exchanges or role assumptions whose subject claim contains ci-sync-: this fires even with zero GitHub log retention and confirms Actions executed on an attacker branch. On self-hosted runners, look for .gdmp_pat, .gdmp_patg, .gdmp_sweep, and the string gdmp-pivot in job logs. If any ci-sync- branch ran on a self-hosted runner, treat the host and its instance role as fully compromised. Rotate every secret in scope for affected repositories: deleting the branch or the run does not undo the exposure. IOCs and detection content are in the report.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2114432451623956769

item.title: AI coding agents hijacked using AGENTS.md file in Downloads folder

item.title: Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497): Detecting the Node.js Brotli RCE
item.description:
CVE-2026-111497 (Node2Shell): Critical 9.2 CVSS Brotli out-of-bounds write in Node.js demonstrated achieving RCE on arm64 in one day from patch to public PoC, with crashes reproducible across multiple versions.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-111497 is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) combined with an unchecked return value (CWE-252) in the Brotli decoder bundled inside Node.js, rooted in Google's Brotli library versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0. The decoder confuses incomplete input with invalid input, processes a malformed block-type switch without erroring out, and writes past the end of its buffer. Fixed releases are Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. Node.js 20 and older receive no fix. Bun 1.4.3 and earlier are also affected; Bun 1.4.4 includes the fix. Debian packages for both nodejs and brotli remained unfixed as of October 23. Critically, on distros that link Node.js against the system Brotli library (Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, RHEL, Alpine), the Node.js version number alone does not tell you whether the instance is patched.
- Exploitation is not universal. An app is only reachable when its code, or a dependency, decompresses Brotli data the attacker controls. That covers two directions: inbound compressed request bodies (body-parser with Brotli enabled, or framework-level decompression middleware) and outbound fetches from attacker-controlled servers whose responses are Brotli-encoded. Express 5 with default JSON parsing is called out as placing a large class of services in the exposed group.
- Demonstrated impact as of October 23: Imperva achieved code execution against the official Node.js 24.22.0 image on Linux arm64 after repeated attempts, confirmed by a marker file, and the patched 24.22.1 rejected the same input with a format error. Crashes are easily reproducible across Node.js 20.19.5, 22.23.3, 24.22.0, and 26.12.0. One team reported local command execution in three of three runs but required a system Brotli build and a predictable memory layout. Blind remote execution with ASLR enabled did not work in that test. Memory disclosure on unpatched 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x has also been reported. No confirmed in-the-wild exploitation exists, and the CVE is not in CISA KEV, but 11 public GitHub repositories tracking exploitation appeared within about a day of the fix shipping.
- Post-exploitation behavior is the detection backstop. A runtime sensor cannot observe the heap overflow itself, but a successful exploit lands attacker code running as the Node.js process user. The post-exploitation chain looks like: crash or partial crash, then in-place program execution from the same workload, followed by shell spawns, outbound network connections, credential or cloud token access, or a malware download. The Sysdig report describes a managed detection rule named "Node.js Process Crash Followed by In-Place Program Execution" that correlates the crash with subsequent suspicious execution in the same workload as the exploitation pattern.
- Mitigation while patching proceeds: disable Brotli decompression in body-parser with express.json({ inflate: false }), which returns a 415 but also drops gzip, so test clients first. Reject Content-Encoding: br at the proxy or load balancer for paths where clients do not send it, noting this does not cover outbound fetch responses. Audit all direct calls to createBrotliDecompress() and fetch calls to untrusted servers. Run Node.js services as unprivileged users and keep secrets out of the process environment, because code execution inherits the process's permissions.
Practitioner takeaway: Start with inventory, not patching. Map every Node.js runtime across containers, CI runners, serverless functions, and build tools, then identify which services decode Brotli from attacker-influenced sources. Those are your first patch targets. For distro packages, check the system Brotli library version, not just the Node.js version number, since the fix may need to come from the distribution's brotli package. On any workload that cannot be patched immediately, hunt for Node.js process crashes followed by child process execution or unexpected outbound connections from the same host. The report describes IOCs and managed detection rules tied to the Node2Shell exploitation chain.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2114085602018644017

item.title: Detecting and mitigating ZDI-CAN-33367 and five other Linux flaws
item.description:
A public root exploit for ZDI-CAN-33367, a pre-CVE Linux kernel LPE, targets Ubuntu, Debian, and AlmaLinux with no merged fix yet. Five more Linux flaws disclosed simultaneously, two rated CVSS 9.0, widen the exposure window for defenders this week.
Key findings:
- ZDI-CAN-33367 is the seventh path to drop the Dirty Frag flag first introduced by CVE-2026-43284. skb_zerocopy() moves shared page-cache pages into a new socket buffer without carrying the shared-frag marker, so ESP decrypts in place and writes attacker-controlled bytes into the page cache. The code path dates to kernel 3.14. A patch ("net: skbuff: propagate shared-frag marker in skb_zerocopy()") is on netdev but unmerged. TuxCare confirmed a root shell on AlmaLinux 8-10, CloudLinux 9-10, Debian 12-13, and Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04. A kernel carrying only the CVE-2026-90049 fix is not protected.
- The exploit runs entirely as an ordinary unprivileged user process through a fixed syscall sequence: unshare into new user and network namespaces, write sysctls, bring up an nlmon interface, install XFRM state over netlink, add an nftables NFQUEUE rule, attach a tc pedit action with a redirect, then splice() into a socket on 127.0.0[.]1. No KASLR leak required. Modules needed: nlmon, nft_queue, nfnetlink_queue, cls_u32, act_pedit, act_mirred, and esp4.
- ZDI-CAN-33774 and ZDI-CAN-33549 are both CVSS 9.0 ksmbd bugs. 33774 is a pre-auth dispatch race that leaks 28 bytes of kernel heap per attempt and can crash the kernel. 33549 is an integer underflow in the SMB Direct RDMA transport leading to a heap overflow of up to 8 KB. Neither affects Samba (smbd). A fix for 33774 is in ksmbd-for-next but unreleased. Exposure check: look for the ksmbd kernel module, the ksmbd.mountd daemon, and a kernel-owned listener on TCP 445.
- ZDI-CAN-34068 is a CVSS 8.8 out-of-bounds write in vmwgfx, the VMware virtual GPU kernel driver, exploitable only on VMware guests (vSphere, Workstation, VMware-based VDI). No patch exists. The trigger is DRM ioctl() calls on the vmwgfx device node by a local process. Sysdig TRT confirmed it does not reproduce on Lima or EC2 instances. Disabling 3D acceleration or blocking the vmwgfx module removes exposure on guests that do not need it.
- None of the six bugs has a CVE ID assigned and no in-the-wild exploitation has been reported as of publication, but reproduction details were sent to public mailing lists before fixes merged, meaning attackers had the same disclosure window defenders did.
DFIR takeaway: ZDI-CAN-33367 is the priority. The syscall sequence is distinctive enough to catch in motion: no legitimate unprivileged process unshares into both user and network namespaces, installs XFRM state, configures nftables NFQUEUE, attaches tc pedit, and then calls splice() to loopback. Instrument your runtime sensor for that chain. For ksmbd, runtime detection is a backstop only since the race and overflow happen inside kernel worker threads with no attacker process visible. Run inventory now: grep loaded modules and netstat output for ksmbd and TCP 445 across your estate. For Kubernetes, enforce seccomp RuntimeDefault cluster-wide via the kubelet --seccomp-default flag. Restrict unprivileged user namespaces (user.max_user_namespaces=0, or kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=0 on Debian) on hosts that do not need rootless containers. Track these by ZDI ID until CVEs are assigned; your scanner will not find them yet.

item.title: PHP2Shell Exploit Attempts Hit Millions as Attackers Try to Deploy Mirai Malware
item.description:
CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (CVSS 9.2) in PHP2Shell enable unauthenticated RCE across tens of millions of exposed hosts. Exploitation attempts hit millions within hours of disclosure, though no confirmed successful RCE has been observed yet.
Key findings:
- The two critical flaws, both CVSS 9.2, affect the PHP engine itself, not any specific application, meaning WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla sites with clean code are still exposed if the underlying PHP version is unpatched. Vulnerable code traces back to PHP 5.4 (2012). Patches exist for PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. Older branches (7.4, 8.0, 8.1) receive no fix. Censys counts over 34.4 million PHP services still assessed as vulnerable as of October 23, 2026.
- The Mirai botnet variant Potassium, first flagged in March 2026, is the payload threat actors attempted to deliver via these flaws. It uses ChaCha20 for its static config table, a single static byte (0xED) for wire traffic, a named reverse-shell protocol (SHELL/SHOUT) on the same channel as attack commands, and a DNS misdirection scheme that swaps the two 16-bit halves of every resolved A record before connecting. C2 resolves through the hostname thunder.godofthunder[.]st to 134.199.154[.]64 over TCP port 50792. Attack sources were 85.11.167[.]243, 217.60.242[.]76, and 45.198.224[.]169, which retrieved a loader from 92.118.112[.]100. The botnet supports 24 DDoS commands across ICMP, TCP, UDP, and OpenVPN. Both ARM and x86 builds include inactive ENS-based C2 resolution, a capability that, if activated, would reduce dependence on traditional DNS and registrar-based disruption.
- Attacker tooling found on an exposed server at 206.188.197[.]105:9999 included aslr_exploit.py, a Python "one-click" exploit for PHP 8.4.26 under Apache mod_php that chains the two CVEs, leaks memory addresses through the session cookie to defeat ASLR, then abuses PHP session upload progress handling to execute shell commands entirely over ordinary HTTP. Companion scripts php2shell_fp.py, deep_probe.py, and wp_attack.py performed fingerprinting, error-page and session-injection checks, and WordPress user and plugin enumeration across roughly 20 public sites spanning Canada 🇨🇦, China 🇨🇳, Finland 🇫🇮, France 🇫🇷, Poland 🇵🇱, the U.K. 🇬🇧, and the U.S.. Ten additional open directories hosting PHP2Shell tooling have been identified; the full IP list is in the report.
- VulnCheck independently confirmed a working ASLR-bypass chain on x86-64 systems using PHP's recommended production configuration, the first public confirmation that this barrier can be overcome without special error-display settings. Successful exploitation runs code with web-application-process permissions, exposing API keys, database credentials, and internal services reachable from that context. A China-based IP was observed attempting to drop a web shell via a server-side session file.
- Current exploitation status: scanning and fingerprinting dominate observed activity. Previdian, Wordfence, Cisco Talos, and Beelzebub all report no confirmed successful RCE or dropped web shells as of the report's writing. The first recorded exploit attempt at CVE-2026-109618 was October 21, 2026 at 13:05 UTC. Cloudflare observed tens of thousands of attempts within 45 minutes of public disclosure, scaling to millions within two days. Wordfence attribution IOCs including 87.121.84[.]174, 181.215.186[.]252, 185.196.220[.]132, and others are in the report.
Takeaway for responders: The ASLR bypass operates entirely over standard HTTP using PHP session upload progress handling, so look for unusual session file creation in the PHP session temp directory and repeated HTTP requests that recycle PHP workers or trigger session cookie reflection. Hunt web server logs for the three-stage request pattern described in aslr_exploit.py: a worker-recycling request, a memory-leak request reading the session cookie, and a follow-on session-upload-progress request carrying a shell command. On Linux hosts, monitor for unexpected ELF binary downloads where the response begins with magic bytes 7F 45 4C 46, outbound TCP to port 50792, and DNS queries for thunder.godofthunder[.]st. IOCs and additional context are in the Sophos, SOCRadar, Arctic Wolf, and Hunt[.]io reports.

item.title: Russia-Linked Hackers Used New Mesh Network Backdoor in Destructive Ukraine Attack
item.description:
Russian 🇷🇺 UAC-0099 handed access to Sandworm after deploying a novel Yggdrasil mesh-network backdoor against a Ukrainian 🇺🇦 logistics company, ending in a destructive wipe more than two months later.
Key details:
- The intrusion began July 16, 2025, with a spear-phishing email delivering a malicious attachment. This triggered the MATCHBOIL downloader, which deployed the MATCHWOK backdoor. One day later, UAC-0099 (also tracked as Earth Sirrush) deployed MythicRatatoskr, a previously undocumented implant that routes C2 traffic through the Yggdrasil peer-to-peer mesh network, making traditional infrastructure blocking largely ineffective against it. ESET notes this is the first documented case of a state-aligned actor abusing Yggdrasil this way.
- MythicRatatoskr's capabilities include victim metadata exfiltration, command polling, screenshot capture, file upload and download, directory enumeration, shell execution via cmd.exe, C2 URL rotation, and spawning a reverse SOCKS5 proxy. A 10-minute startup delay is built in, likely to avoid immediate Yggdrasil network connections that might trigger behavioral detection. Source code references to "crond" suggest a Linux variant may exist alongside the confirmed Windows build.
- Access was handed off to Sandworm, which struck on September 17, 2025, more than 60 days after initial compromise. Sandworm deployed the SDelete utility via Active Directory Group Policy to carry out the data-wiping attack. This is consistent with prior Sandworm tradecraft: NikoWiper is itself derived from SDelete, and using GPO for lateral tool delivery is a documented Sandworm pattern in Ukrainian 🇺🇦 operations.
- ESET's APT Activity Report Q2-Q3 2025 identifies this as part of a broader brokered-access pattern where UAC-0099 conducts initial access operations against government, energy, logistics, and grain sector targets in Ukraine 🇺🇦, then transfers validated footholds to Sandworm for destructive post-exploitation. Collaboration between Russia-aligned groups is escalating: Gamaredon and Turla have been observed co-compromising Ukrainian 🇺🇦 entities, with Gamaredon's PteroGraphin delivering Turla's Kazuar backdoor.
Practitioner takeaway: the 60-plus day dwell time before the wipe underscores why full-scope investigation matters even when the initial phishing is caught late. For responders working Ukrainian 🇺🇦 critical sector incidents, hunt for SDelete execution originating from GPO (look for processes spawned under Group Policy client context) and review Active Directory for recently modified or newly created GPOs pushing executables or scripts. Yggdrasil-routed C2 will not resolve to a conventional domain or IP, so netflow anomaly detection on unusual encrypted peer traffic is the more viable signal than blocklists. Check for cmd.exe child processes with no interactive parent, screenshot-capable processes running without user session context, and any SOCKS5 listener activity on non-standard ports. The report is from ESET but contains no public IOC table.

item.title: Malware Reverse Engineering: 7 Step Quick Guide
item.description:
A vendor guide lays out a seven-step malware reverse engineering loop covering static triage, behavioral detonation, disassembly, and unpacking, with DarkGate cited as a real-world illustration of why the workflow cycles rather than runs straight through.
Key details:
- Static triage (Step 3) centers on seven indicators before a sample runs: file hash and reputation, PE headers and entry points, imported API calls flagged for networking or injection, readable strings (URLs, registry paths, commands), entropy in PE sections, embedded resources, and obfuscation markers. High entropy alongside few readable strings is the early signal that the sample is packed and Step 6 will be required.
- Behavioral detonation (Step 4) captures six signal classes during execution: process creation and injection targets, registry modifications tied to persistence, file-system drops, network connections and C2 communication, dropped payloads written to disk, and injected or decrypted code visible in memory. Wireshark alongside sandbox capture is the recommended pairing so C2 traffic is caught as it leaves the guest. The guide flags that modern malware checks for VM artifacts and debugger presence before revealing real behavior, pointing to DarkGate as a case where an obfuscated AutoIt script only exposes its shellcode after deobfuscation, making sandbox evasion-resistance a prerequisite for a useful result.
- Disassembly and debugging (Step 5) start from a suspicious string or flagged import rather than reading the binary top to bottom. IDA Free and Ghidra are named for disassembly and decompilation. The guide recommends setting breakpoints on specific API calls such as InternetConnectA to inspect live parameters, and patching out IsDebuggerPresent checks so the sample runs to completion rather than self-terminating mid-analysis.
- Unpacking (Step 6) feeds confirmed packed samples through Detect It Easy or PeStudio to name the packer, then dumps the unpacked code from memory at runtime and rebuilds the Import Address Table with Scylla. Script-based obfuscation in JavaScript, PowerShell, or AutoIt is handled by loading the file in its native interpreter and breaking on execution rather than decoding manually. After unpacking, the workflow loops back to Step 5, not forward.
- Output (Step 7) converts findings into YARA rules on distinctive strings or byte sequences, IOC lists covering hashes, domains, and registry keys, documented C2 infrastructure and communication patterns, extracted malware configurations (campaign IDs, encryption keys, mutexes), MITRE ATT&CK behavior mappings, and threat intelligence shared through platforms such as MISP.
Practitioner takeaway: the loop structure is the actionable part. If your current RE workflow runs linearly, triage to dynamic to code review, you are probably missing packer layers that only appear after disassembly and send you back to dynamic capture. Build your case notes and lab snapshots around the loop: scope a specific question in Step 1, triage against it in Step 3, and when unpacking in Step 6 surfaces new code, restate the question before returning to Step 5. DarkGate's AutoIt layer is a concrete reminder that a "clean" behavioral report on a packed sample is a data-collection failure, not a verdict. The guide contains no IOC table or detection rules.

item.title: BlackX UEFI bootkit exploits Baton Drop flaw to bypass Secure Boot
item.description:
Chinese 🇨🇳 APT41 deployed the BlackX UEFI bootkit against Central Asian diplomatic agencies in early 2026, exploiting the Baton Drop flaw (CVE-2022-21894) on fully patched Windows systems because admins never triggered the mandatory manual revocation step.
Key findings:
- CVE-2022-21894 (Baton Drop) is the entry point. BlackX's exploit is "remarkably similar" to BlackLotus, enrolling custom Machine Owner Keys (MOKs) to load arbitrary EFI files and bypass Secure Boot. Victims ran fully patched Windows, but the patch only revokes the "Windows Production PCA 2011" certificate when manually triggered, a step almost no admin takes. The October 19, 2026 expiration of that certificate does not block the vulnerable binaries either unless the certificate is explicitly added to a blocklist. APT41 (also tracked as Brass Typhoon, Wicked Panda, Barium) is attributed with medium confidence and targeted diplomatic agencies in Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan.
- The malicious kernel driver is signed with a now-revoked certificate issued to "Wenjiang District Mingyu Network Technology Service Studio." Once loaded, it disables security-related processes and registry callbacks, tampers with ETW providers to obstruct monitoring, and conditionally targets Kaspersky and Avast processes specifically. It also intercepts user requests to open bootkit files and launches Windows Calculator as a decoy, a file-protection trick worth knowing when you wonder why calc.exe is spawning unexpectedly on a compromised host.
- The espionage payload chain is layered. A RAT uses Google Drive, OneDrive, or Yandex.Disk for C2 to execute .NET payloads and move files. OxiDLLRunner, an OLLVM-obfuscated DLL, is sideloaded by googleupdate.exe. It decrypts v8_context_snapshot.bin to launch shellcode and a Rust payload that retrieves DLL plugins from archivetj[.]com and executes their "create_plugin" functions in separate threads. The use of legitimate cloud storage as C2 makes network-layer detection harder without endpoint context.
- Attribution hinges partly on code lineage. BlackLotus source code leaked in July 2023, but that release was incomplete. Kaspersky found code in BlackX that was absent from the public repo but present in older BlackLotus samples, meaning the BlackX operator either reverse-engineered BlackLotus or purchased its full source code. This distinction matters for understanding the barrier to entry for UEFI-level threats.
Practitioner takeaway: The immediate action is not a new patch, it is finishing the old one. Confirm whether the "Windows Production PCA 2011" certificate has been revoked on every endpoint in your fleet and add it to the UEFI Secure Boot blocklist if not. On the hunt side, watch for googleupdate.exe loading unexpected DLLs, the presence of v8_context_snapshot.bin in non-Chrome paths, outbound traffic to cloud storage providers from non-user processes, and calc.exe spawning from system-level parent processes. ETW tampering at the kernel level will suppress a lot of telemetry, so cross-reference Secure Boot status logs and firmware integrity measurements where available. Microsoft's full remediation instructions for CVE-2022-21894 are linked in Kaspersky's report.

item.title: Machine speed attacks require machine speed detection and response
item.description:
Attackers enumerate and exfiltrate data within 15 minutes of initial access across three recurring patterns: stolen developer tokens, ClickFix AI-tool lures, and help desk vishing. Native IdP and platform controls consistently fail to stop them.
Key findings:
- Stolen OAuth tokens are a persistent blind spot. In one case, a gho_ prefixed GitHub OAuth token sat dormant for 95 days after a developer installed GitHub Desktop, then pulled 76 repositories through residential proxies across two dozen European cities in roughly 15 seconds. GitHub issued no alert. The attacker reached 472 of 638 repositories before containment. GitHub does not natively monitor token usage behavior, gho_ tokens do not expire on their own for a year, and disabling the developer in the identity provider does not revoke the token without SCIM. These tokens are only visible through the CLI, not the SSO dashboard.
- ClickFix lures are bypassing email and download controls by weaponizing AI tool install trust. In one incident, a victim searching for Claude Code instructions landed on a shared Claude conversation containing a one-line install command that loaded a macOS stealer. The stealer faked a System Preferences password prompt, then copied the macOS keychain, browser cookies, saved passwords, and cloud credentials. Because the victim executed the command themselves, traditional perimeter controls did not apply. Scope assessment should cover all tokens and credentials minted by the affected user across every connected application.
- Help desk vishing leads to full session hijack in under 10 minutes. Attackers following a script consistent with Scattered Spider register their own MFA device and start bulk download activity 2.5 to 7 minutes after the victim approves a real push notification. One case resulted in 140,000 files exfiltrated and a ransom demand. AiTM kits like one hosted on oskeysetup[.]com are written from scratch, making signature-based detections for Evilginx and similar public kits ineffective. Microsoft flagged one session as risky, then cleared the risk after MFA passed. The stolen token was replayed from two countries within one second. In vishing cases, data exfiltration continued 44 minutes to 3 hours after the IdP session was revoked, and in one case attacker-planted inbox rules survived a password reset.
- Revoking the IdP session is not containment. Okta's Universal Logout reaches Google Workspace and Slack but not GitHub, Snowflake, or AI model providers. AWS and Snowflake sessions started through SSO keep running independently. The report recommends pre-building per-application revocation playbooks with a dedicated service account that already holds the required permissions before an incident starts, because a 403 mid-response is a documented failure mode they observed.
Practitioner takeaway: The earliest strong signal in identity attacks is a new MFA method registered from a device and network the user has never touched. Stack that with first-seen country, first-seen ISP, and OS or user-agent mismatches against the account's history. For GitHub token compromise specifically, hunt for gho_ token activity crossing the user's baseline geography, OS, and request rate simultaneously, since no single signal is enough on its own. Build and permission your revocation API calls for each critical service (the report provides the specific API endpoints and required permission scopes for Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, Google Workspace, GitHub Enterprise Cloud, Snowflake, AWS, and Anthropic) before you need them. The defanged IOC contoso.add-passkey[.]com and the AiTM kit domain oskeysetup[.]com are named in the report.

item.title: Leaked LiteLLM Master Key Let Attackers Steal GitHub Tokens and Hijack Release Pipeline
item.description:
Leaked LiteLLM master key sat unrevoked for months before an attacker used it to hijack the PyPI release pipeline and push a backdoored Python package that activates on Python startup, even without importing the library.
Key findings:
- The attack chain began May 27, 2026, when a config file containing the LiteLLM Agent Platform master key was committed to the public LiteLLM-Labs/lite-harness repo. The key was identified quickly and the commit force-pushed over, but revocation never happened. On October 10, an attacker operating from 69.48.229[.]143 used that still-valid key to authenticate to the Agent Platform and extract a GitHub CLI OAuth token tied to an org owner account, granting full write access across all repositories.
- The attacker then ran two short-lived malicious workflows via throwaway branches named ci-tmp-a351cc and ci-tmp-4d8517, each pushing .github/workflows/cache.yml with the benign-looking commit message "ci: bump cache config." The branches were created, triggered, and deleted within minutes. This is why the activity leaves almost no trace in ordinary repository history. Both workflows exfiltrated secrets to webhook[.]site/65a42464-3cfa-4b02-a18c-17a6d7b86f37 and webhook[.]site/4da03473-a3e7-4dc2-a087-9c564b4208e1. Harvested material included GitHub tokens, a GitHub App private key and signing key, Linear workspace session state, OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS Bedrock, Tavily, Together AI, GitGuardian, PostgreSQL credentials, Redis credentials, and Playwright serialized browser storage state. The GitGuardian key is notable: it gave the attacker control over the secret-scanning platform that would otherwise surface this activity.
- On October 21, the attacker overrode branch protections and repointed the release pipeline source from BerriAI/litellm to the lookalike Berri-AI/litellm. Using one stolen engineer token to trigger and a second to approve, LiteLLM version 1.107.0 was published to PyPI at 11:39 a.m. UTC, with Docker Hub and GHCR images following at 11:46 a.m. Run records were deleted by 11:54 a.m. PyPI quarantined 1.107.0 at 1:23 p.m., about 77 minutes after a researcher reported the supply chain compromise.
- The malicious package installs components outside the LiteLLM application directory so they survive application removal and execute automatically at Python startup regardless of whether LiteLLM is imported. It runs two paths: a credential harvester targeting SSH files, Git and GitLab tokens, environment variables, npm, PyPI, pip, Yarn, Maven, Gradle, Composer, RubyGems, and Cargo tokens, plus cloud and browser credentials, exfiltrating compressed data via HTTP POST to litellm[.]dev/healthcheck (domain registered October 13, 2026). A second path launches a Unix backdoor as a background process that fetches and runs attacker-supplied code every hour.
DFIR takeaway: If LiteLLM 1.107.0 touched any environment, do not stop at removing the package. Inspect Python startup paths and site-packages directories outside the application install for malicious files dropped by the installer, because Microsoft's analysis confirms the startup components persist after the application is removed. Hunt outbound POST requests to litellm[.]dev/healthcheck and connections to webhook[.]site in network logs around October 10 and October 21. Audit GitHub Actions logs for workflow runs on branches matching ci-tmp- patterns that no longer exist, then cross-reference the repository activity log, which retains records even after branch deletion. Treat every secret that existed in the affected environment as compromised: rotate GitHub tokens, cloud API keys, database credentials, and any serialized session state. The IOCs and workflow analysis are in Socket's published report.

Inspect Python startup paths and site-packages directories outside the application install for malicious files dropped by the installer, because Microsoft's analysis confirms the startup components persist after the application is removed. Hunt outbound POST requests to litellm[.]dev/healthcheck and connections to webhook[.]site in network logs around October 10 and October 21. Audit GitHub Actions logs for workflow runs on branches matching ci-tmp- patterns that no longer exist, then cross-reference the repository activity log, which retains records even after branch deletion. Treat every secret that existed in the affected environment as compromised: rotate GitHub tokens, cloud API keys, database credentials, and any serialized session state. The IOCs and workflow analysis are in Socket's published report.

item.title: Inside an Exposed ARTEX Workspace
item.description:
An exposed working directory on an ARTEX AI pentest operator's host handed researchers 29 files reconstructing a full JNDI injection test chain, revealing the platform labeled 78 findings "confirmed" while its own logs show zero code execution.
Key findings:
- ThreatMon recovered 29 files (27 distinct SHA-256 values) from an open directory listing on 64.176.34[.]176, the same host running the ARTEX console and callback services. The workspace included round1_calib.py, round2_matrix.py, round3_positions.py, Exploit[.]java, Exploit.class, a hand-written LDAP server (ldap_srv.py), an RMI reference server (RmiRefServer[.]java), and operator notes in SUMMARY[.]md. The Chinese-language web console ran on Next.js, and both godliketrenchan[.]com and www.godliketrenchan[.]com resolved to the same IP. The TLS listener on TCP/443 served a self-issued certificate with common name bf4119-beacon regardless of SNI, fingerprint 07654e9c10b01c9274639a45a2ad1d163edad8405add3dc264b0f52bbaab57e3, a stable pivot for internet-wide certificate searches.
- The operator built a four-service JNDI injection chain: an LDAP server on TCP/11389, an RMI registry on TCP/11099, an HTTP server on TCP/8000 serving Exploit.class (SHA-256: 24724c1acd5fcfe1feccde612e09c283676a19b5e227efcad9e4ab382f6b2f45), and a TCP callback listener on TCP/18080. Exploit.class carried a CLASSLOADED execution marker: if the static initializer ran on the target, it would beacon home. The operator also used DNS-based out-of-band logging via dnsutil[.]py and dns.raw.jsonl, confirmed external reachability through a SOCKS5 exit, and compiled the payload with javac -release 8 for older JDK compatibility. The local LDAP/RMI stack validated successfully, but the local test explicitly enabled com.sun.jndi.ldap.object.trustURLCodebase, a setting disabled by default in current JDKs, which makes local success irrelevant to the external target.
- No CLASSLOADED marker appears in cb.log, ldap.log, or http.stdout. HTTP 500 responses were returned both by test payloads and by a deliberate negative control for the nonexistent class com.example.NotExistFoo4316, so the error code carries no execution signal. LDAP search requests and DNS resolution activity were logged externally but cannot be tied to the target's Java process. MITRE ATT&CK mapping covers T1595.002 (scanning), T1583.001 (domain acquisition), T1587.004 (exploit development), T1608.001 (staging Exploit.class over HTTP), and T1190 (attempted exploitation of a public-facing application, execution not observed).
- The platform produced 78 findings each labeled "confirmed": 5 critical, 33 high, 31 medium, 9 low. All 78 also carry traffic_count = 0, a field the platform does not document. None of these findings relate to the JNDI retest; none was independently validated. The "confirmed" label reflects platform output, not a traceable request-response-execution chain on the target.
- OPSEC failures made the entire workspace recoverable: the directory sat open on the same host as the console, and the certificate's common name bf4119-beacon is a durable fingerprint across internet scan datasets.
Hunt action: Search proxy, firewall, and NetFlow logs for connections to 64.176.34[.]176 on TCP/8000, 11389, 11099, and 18080. Hunt application and request logs for jndi:ldap:// and jndi:rmi:// strings. On any legacy Java runtime in your environment, verify com.sun.jndi.ldap.object.trustURLCodebase and com.sun.jndi.rmi.object.trustURLCodebase are not set to true. The IOC table and file hashes are in the ThreatMon report. For any AI or automated pentest output your team receives, the bar is a traceable request, response, and execution signal tied to the target: "confirmed" from the platform is the start of validation, not the end.

item.title: Famous Chollima APT Group: Major Activities, TTPs, and Simulation
item.description:
North Korean 🇰🇵 Famous Chollima weaponizes the developer hiring pipeline across GitHub, npm, and VS Code to deliver BeaverTail, OtterCookie, and PylangGhost, while fraudulent IT workers maintain insider access at Western employers using US 🇺🇸 laptop farms.
Key details:
- The attack chain starts with fake recruiters on LinkedIn, Fiverr, and Discord (T1566.003) pushing trojanized coding assessments hosted on GitHub, Bitbucket, or GitLab. Repositories average 20,000 to 30,000 lines of legitimate code with a single malicious line buried after hundreds of blank lines or spaces (T1027), and payloads are disguised as font files under /public/fontawesome/ or embedded in .svg assets (T1036.008). Execution triggers include npm lifecycle scripts mapping "prepare" to "npm start" so the payload fires on install (T1204.005), VS Code tasks.json with "runOn": "folderOpen" that run git config core.hooksPath .githooks followed by git checkout master to fire a post-checkout hook delivering platform-specific second stages via curl or wget (T1204.002), and more than 2,500 malicious npm packages, including private ones requiring auth tokens to inspect, linked as dependencies (T1195.001). Staging URLs are Base64-encoded and fetched from legitimate SaaS mock-API services like jsonkeeper[.]com and api.mocki[.]io rather than attacker infrastructure.
- The ClickFix lure (T1204.004) targets crypto job seekers with a fake camera-driver error, instructing Win+X then A to open an elevated PowerShell prompt and paste a command that pulls a ZIP to %TEMP%\vdriverWin[.]zip, expands it, and launches update.vbs, which extracts a bundled Python runtime and starts PylangGhost. PylangGhost's auto[.]py steals browser credentials and session cookies from over 80 extensions including 1Password, NordPass, MetaMask, and Phantom, and communicates over plain HTTP with RC4 encryption prefixed by a 16-byte MD5 checksum and a 128-byte key in the clear.
- OtterCookie checks /proc/cpuinfo on Linux for hypervisor, vmware, virtualbox, qemu, kvm, xen, parallels, and bochs strings (T1497.001) and tags its C2 beacon with "(VM)" or "(Local)" so operators filter sandbox runs. Its remote shell uses socket.io-client upgrading HTTP to WebSocket, receiving "command" events and passing msg.message to child_process.exec with windowsHide: true (T1071.001). A keylogging variant installs node-global-key-listener and screenshot-desktop, writing keystrokes to 1.tmp in a Windows cache folder under the temp directory every second and screenshots as 2.jpeg every four seconds (T1056.001). BeaverTail previously dropped a helper module from the C2 path /node/ and saved it as %USERPROFILE%\store.node to decrypt Chrome credentials (T1555.003).
- The parallel IT worker operation (T1684.001) uses US 🇺🇸 laptop farms where facilitators receive employer-issued hardware, then operatives connect remotely from overseas through residential US 🇺🇸 IPs. Operators redirect shipments by filing false theft reports, claiming last-minute relocations, or routing through staffing firms. In August 2025, US 🇺🇸 sanctions exposed nearly $600K in crypto-to-cash transfers; in October 2026, over 40 laptop farms were shut down and 14 people charged, but operations continue. Infrastructure includes hiring-themed domains like coinbase.talenthiringtool[.]com and krakenhire[.]com, and payload hosts like api.quickcamfix[.]online and api.nvidia-release[.]org. Account creation flows through Astrill VPN with residential proxy egress, and the same exit IPs appear in other North Korean 🇰🇵 operations.
- The PolinRider campaign (March 2026) implanted obfuscated JavaScript in hundreds of GitHub repositories to spread a BeaverTail variant, extending supply chain reach beyond individual job applicants. BeaverTail C2 URLs are reassembled at runtime from a 40-character scrambled Base64 string sliced into four 10-character chunks, one of which decodes to "hxxp://" and the remainder to the host, e.g. 195.201.172[.]170:1224. Python modules from BeaverTail and InvisibleFerret use an XOR-over-Base64 scheme where the first 8 characters are the key and the rest is ciphertext passed to exec().
Hunt developers' endpoints for node processes spawning curl, wget, or cmd as children; look for .githooks directories in cloned repositories alongside .vscode/tasks.json containing "runOn": "folderOpen" and git config core.hooksPath; inspect package.json for "prepare" mapped to "start"; and check %TEMP% for vdriverWin[.]zip, update.vbs, and 1.tmp. On the insider-access side, correlate employer-issued device geolocation with VoIP numbers and identity documents flagged for multiple employer-address changes. IOC tables and MITRE ATT&CK mappings are in the report.

item.title: [remote] Exasol Database 7.1.30 - command execution
item.description:
Exasol Database 7.1.30 ships a hardcoded SYS credential (sys / exasol) that grants full DBA access and OS command execution via a built-in Python UDF, scoring 8.8 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:A/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H).
- The credential pair sys / exasol is printed in the vendor's own docker-db README under "Connecting to the Database" and appears in two internal CI test scripts at /usr/opt/EXASuite-7/EXAClusterOS-7.1.30/docker/test/. Nothing in the container's init path rotates it, sets a must-change flag, or refuses service until it is changed. The ConfD AuthenticationToken and BucketFS WritePasswd are generated as per-deployment randoms; the most privileged credential is not. CWE-1392 is primary; CWE-94, CWE-798, CWE-78, CWE-1188, and CWE-250 are co-recorded.
- The two-step exploit chain requires no memory corruption or protocol bypass. Leg one: authenticate to the binary SQL service on port 8563 over TLS using the shipped constant. Leg two: issue four SQL statements (CREATE SCHEMA, OPEN SCHEMA, CREATE OR REPLACE PYTHON3 SCALAR SCRIPT with an os.popen body, SELECT) and read stdout back through the ordinary result set. No exfiltration channel is needed because the return value crosses the trust boundary in-band. The executing identity observed was uid=500(exadefusr) gid=500(exausers) groups=500(exausers),0(root); that supplementary root group under the vendor-required privileged container mode is a recognised escalation position, though escalation to uid=0 was not attempted or claimed.
- SYS authority over the SQL layer is the larger half of the impact: every schema, table, view, user, and privilege in the analytical warehouse is readable and writable without touching the script engine at all. An attacker can create additional accounts with chosen privileges, giving a durable second entry point that survives rotation of the factory credential. Availability follows the same authority. A separate smaller finding (not scored here): the BucketFS default bucket has Public=True, allowing unauthenticated read listing; write attempts returned 403 because the bucket WritePasswd is a per-deployment random.
- Detection is weak by design. Every step is legitimate product activity: a TLS handshake, a SYS login, a CREATE SCRIPT, and a SELECT. No [28000] authentication-failed sequence will precede a successful hit with the shipped constant. The highest-value detection signal is script-object creation logged with the creating user and source address; the report notes the default deployment does not surface this. A SYS session originating from an unexpected address is the next-best indicator, but operators who never rotated the credential have no baseline to compare against.
- The docker-db 7 deployment form is end-of-life on CentOS 7 and the vendor states no fix is planned for it. The CVE is pending. A conditional 9.8 Critical reading (AV:N) applies to multi-node --network=host deployments and any deployment where port 8563 is published without a loopback restriction. The full proof-of-concept (Python 3, standard library only, --allow-remote gated) and IOCs are in the report at 0day-rubbish[.]com/blog/exasol-database-default-credential-python-udf-os-popen-rce.
Hunt: enumerate all SCRIPT objects in Exasol system tables (EXA_ALL_SCRIPTS) for PYTHON3 bodies referencing os.popen, os.system, or subprocess. Cross-reference script creation timestamps against known administrator sessions. Rotate the SYS credential immediately; with the factory credential changed and no non-admin account holding script-creation rights, the report states this finding does not arise.

item.title: Widespread Token-Spraying Attacks Target Microsoft 365 Accounts For Email Compromise
item.description:
A global token-spraying BEC campaign hit Microsoft 365 environments across 79 organizations, making 200,000+ login attempts and achieving 497 confirmed account takeovers between July and September 2026, all without ever needing a victim's password.
Key findings:
- The attack chain combined AiTM phishing (fake sign-in pages and device-code phishing lures) with session token theft. Because tokens are issued after a legitimate login and MFA verification, whoever holds the token can replay it against Microsoft 365 services with no MFA challenge. The threat actor automated this replay at scale, and in several cases was inside a compromised environment within minutes of token theft.
- Post-compromise persistence was methodical and multi-layered. Attackers wiped existing MFA registrations and enrolled their own authenticator devices, registered attacker-controlled hardware in Entra ID to enable future token requests, and planted hidden inbox rules to silently divert emails from specific contacts, all classic BEC staging moves designed to survive a password reset.
- The monetization pivot was observed: a compromised mailbox was used to send a payroll-redirect phishing email to an internal target. The legitimacy of the sending address is precisely what makes BEC effective. In this instance the payment does not appear to have been completed, but the infrastructure was ready.
- The Huntress report covers 79 customer organizations and at least 200,000 login attempts. The campaign's global reach and automation suggest the operators had significant token inventory and tooling to manage replay sessions at volume, consistent with a financially motivated, organized BEC group rather than opportunistic activity.
For responders investigating a suspected token replay compromise: start in the Entra ID sign-in logs and look for token replay indicators such as sign-ins from unfamiliar IP addresses or ASNs, "Interrupted" or "Success" sign-in results with no corresponding MFA challenge, and sign-ins arriving in rapid succession from geographically inconsistent locations. Then audit registered MFA methods and Entra-joined devices for entries the legitimate user did not add. Pull every inbox rule for affected mailboxes and flag any rule created during or after the suspicious sign-in window. Revoke all active sessions and reset credentials before restoring MFA to prevent re-entry. The Huntress report recommends Conditional Access Policies scoped to All Users, All Cloud Apps, and All Client App types as the structural control to restrict where replayed tokens can be used.

item.title: 2026-10-09: Pcap of infection from Macfinger Clickfix activity
item.description:
A pcap from a Macfinger ClickFix infection chain is now publicly available for analysis, giving DFIR practitioners a full traffic capture to dissect the delivery and post-infection behavior.
Key details:
- The released file is 2026-10-09-Macfinger-ClickFix-and-infection-traffic.pcap[.]zip, weighing in at 20.7 MB (20,689,369 bytes), captured on Friday, October 9, 2026. The naming convention ties it directly to a Macfinger campaign using a ClickFix lure, the social-engineering technique that tricks users into manually executing malicious commands by presenting fake CAPTCHA or browser-fix prompts.
- ClickFix infections typically generate distinctive early-stage traffic: DNS lookups and outbound connections initiated by user-spawned processes like cmd.exe, PowerShell, or mshta shortly after the lure page is visited. The pcap covers both the ClickFix delivery phase and the downstream infection traffic, making it useful for building a full timeline from lure to payload.
- The zip is password-protected under Malware Traffic Analysis's updated password scheme. The password is no longer the legacy format: check the site's "about" page directly before attempting to extract. Failing to do so wastes time and risks confusion about file integrity.
- For network defenders and threat hunters, pcaps like this are ground truth. You can reconstruct the full URI paths, user-agent strings, JA3/JA4 fingerprints, certificate subject fields, and payload delivery hosts directly from the capture without relying on third-party reporting. Wireshark's Protocol Hierarchy and Export Objects features are the fastest first pass.
Practitioner takeaway: load the pcap and filter on HTTP and DNS activity in the first 60 seconds of the capture to isolate the ClickFix delivery stage, then pivot to any non-browser process making outbound connections to identify the post-execution C2 or payload retrieval. Cross-reference resolved domains and IP destinations against passive DNS and threat intel feeds. IOCs will be embedded in the traffic itself.

item.title: PHP2Shell: One Upload, Full Server
item.description:
PHP2Shell: Two critical CVEs in the PHP runtime itself enable unauthenticated memory disclosure and remote code execution beneath every CMS and framework, affecting all PHP versions back to 5.4 across roughly 70% of the web.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are rated critical and sit in the PHP core engine, firing before any application code executes. PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php (highest risk), php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed are all affected across every PHP version from 5.4 onward. RCE was demonstrated against current WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla container images. A clean, fully patched CMS on a vulnerable PHP runtime is still exposed.
- The attack chain starts with a crafted multipart/form-data upload timed to exhaust memory_limit during session upload-progress handling, a pre-application-code phase. The resulting out-of-memory fatal error skips worker cleanup, leaving three engine-global pointers stale: PS(id) for session ID, BG(unserialize) for unserializer state, and EG(last_fatal_error_backtrace) for error tracking. The worker survives and is reused, still holding freed allocations the attacker can reclaim.
- Bug 1 reads leaked worker memory out of the reclaimed PS(id) allocation and encodes it into the PHPSESSID response cookie, defeating ASLR. Bug 2 abuses the stale BG(unserialize) pointer as a memory-corruption primitive and, chained with Bug 1, achieves unauthenticated RCE. Bug 3 abuses EG(last_fatal_error_backtrace) into a second path toward corruption and RCE. A fourth bug, CVE-2026-109619, is an OPcache type confusion in shared memory caused by a race between process-local and shared allocation trackers, exploitable across workers. The researchers note AI tooling compressed exploit development from months to days.
- App-layer logging may capture nothing because exploitation begins in the multipart parsing phase before application code runs. The report's detection signals: malformed or oversized multipart upload requests paired with memory-limit errors or bursts of HTTP 500s; an oversized or malformed PHPSESSID cookie in a response indicating memory leakage; and a PHP worker spawning a child process during upload parsing before application code executes, which the report calls a high-confidence signal. If a server was running vulnerable PHP before the October 21 patch, assume credentials, tokens, and API keys resident in worker memory are compromised.
- Patched releases are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35, shipped October 21. PHP 8.1 and older have no official fix. Varonis states it found no evidence of compromise in its own portfolio and says customers need no additional action for Varonis products specifically.
Practitioner takeaway: inventory every PHP instance, not just public CMS deployments but bundled appliances and internal tools, because the flaw predates your application stack. On web and proxy logs, hunt for multipart upload requests to the same worker IP or process that are followed immediately by HTTP 500 responses or Set-Cookie headers carrying an unusually long or binary-looking PHPSESSID value. Flag any PHP worker process that spawns a child during upload handling. Rotate secrets on any server that ran PHP before October 21. Patch to the relevant fixed branch as the closing step, not the only one.

item.title: Investigating PHP2Shell after patching
item.description:
Two critical PHP RCE vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both CVSS 9.2) disclosed 21 October 2026 enable unauthenticated code execution. Patching closes the door but does not evict an attacker already inside.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are memory-safety flaws in the PHP runtime. The first exploits a race between memory exhaustion and request cleanup against an incomplete internal state. The second lets a worker reuse freed memory from a prior request. Both allow pre-auth code execution at the web worker's permission level. Apache mod_php is the highest-priority target: demonstrated exploitation fires before application code runs, bypassing login controls entirely. PHP-FPM and other deployments also need review depending on the specific vulnerability and application conditions. Fixed releases are PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12.
- The real DFIR concern is the window before the patch. The report draws directly on a prior Exchange investigation where an org patched within days of disclosure, believed the server decommissioned after migrating to Office 365, and then suffered a ransomware attempt nearly a year later. The attacker had planted a webshell during that brief pre-patch window and returned through it long after the underlying flaw was remediated. The same scenario is live for every PHP server exposed before today's patch.
- Hunt web roots, upload directories, and other application-writable paths for unexpected scripts. Compare against trusted release baselines. Attackers disguise file extensions and alter timestamps, so scope the search broadly. Correlate suspicious file paths against web server request logs, PHP error logs, process execution records, and outbound connection logs. Useful signals called out in the report include large form submissions, memory-exhaustion errors, and unexpected shells spawned by web worker processes. Successful webshell execution may return HTTP 200 with no crash, so absence of errors does not mean absence of compromise.
- The companion download from Binalyze includes two draft hunting rules: php_web_worker_shell.yml, a Sigma rule for Linux web workers directly spawning shells, and php_webshell_candidates.yar, a YARA rule matching PHP files that contain both request-input references and code or command execution functions. The report notes these are hunting rules, not definitive PHP2Shell signatures. Legitimate applications can match, obfuscated shells and indirect execution can be missed, and local validation and tuning are required before operational use.
- Do not stop at webshells. If an attacker had execution, also examine associated accounts for credential theft, scheduled tasks and cron jobs, new or modified services, and any secrets accessible to the web worker. Include systems believed retired: verify they are actually offline, not just assumed to be. Preserve evidence before removing suspected shells.
Takeaway: Run YARA against collected PHP files from exposed hosts using php_webshell_candidates.yar, and run the Sigma rule php_web_worker_shell.yml against process telemetry for the exposure window. Pull web server access logs and look for POST requests to paths outside normal application routes, especially those returning HTTP 200 without corresponding application session activity. Patch closes CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Finding surviving access requires the investigation.

item.title: PHP2Shell: What This Week Tells Us About the Web We Built
item.description:
PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) achieves unauthenticated RCE and memory disclosure across every PHP version since 5.4, with mass exploitation confirmed in the wild before patches shipped. 54.9 million web properties are in scope.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-109618 abuses how PHP handles an out-of-memory condition while request data is half-initialised. CVE-2026-109619 abuses global state that continues pointing at freed request memory. Both are CVSS v4 9.2, both are pre-auth, and both can read live process memory where database credentials, API keys, and session secrets are stored. Every PHP execution model is affected: PHP-FPM, mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. The OOM weakness was first noticed in 2020 and re-discovered in 2024 but never fixed because exploitation looked impractical. In August 2026, AI-assisted research by Calif and OpenAI collapsed that assumption and produced a working exploit chain.
- The embargo failed on multiple fronts. Amazon's MadPot honeypots recorded exploitation attempts on 17 October, four days before coordinated disclosure. CVE IDs leaked publicly on 20 October. A researcher's proof-of-concept video was published by mistake that evening. Chainguard shipped patched container images more than six hours before the embargo lifted, enabling binary diff analysis of the patch. By 21 October at 02:00 UTC, public exploits were circulating. Exploitation "at scale" against the session upload-progress path was reported that afternoon, and European government sites went dark rather than stay online unpatched.
- Patch availability is uneven and that unevenness is where the real incident risk lives. PHP 8.2 through 8.5 have clean updates (8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, 8.5.12). PHP 7.4 through 8.1 have source backports only, requiring a local build and test cycle. PHP 5.4 through 7.3 have no fix at all. Any internet-facing host still on end-of-life PHP is currently unpatched with no vendor-supported remediation path, and Censys counts roughly 2.58 million internet-facing hosts running PHP.
- The natural attacker outcome is a web shell dropped inside a legitimate, SSL-certified site, giving persistent access that blends with normal traffic. From that foothold the attacker can read process memory for credentials, pivot to cloud accounts linked to the host, phish customers from a trusted domain, and serve malware from a URL that reputation systems score clean. For responders: assume compromise on any internet-facing PHP host that was unpatched and reachable after 17 October, the date Amazon first recorded exploitation.
Practitioner takeaway: The immediate hunt priorities are web shells in document roots, new or modified admin accounts, altered core PHP application files, and unexpected outbound connections from PHP worker processes. Rotate every secret that could reside in PHP process memory on an exposed host: database credentials, API keys, cloud access keys, and signing secrets. For hosts on PHP 7.3 and older where no patch exists, isolate from the internet or enforce WAF rules for the known PHP2Shell vectors before treating the asset as a long-term rebuild. Inventory is the forcing function: the organisations that answered "where do we run PHP" in minutes were patched within hours; those still discovering their estate are discovering it in the same order attackers are. The Orca report includes detection details and host-reachability context; the PHP Foundation advisory and Calif's writeup cover the full technical chain.

item.title: How to Identify Compromised eMudhra Certificates With Qualys (CVE-2026-111943 and CVE-2026-111944)
item.description:
CVE-2026-111943 and CVE-2026-111944: Eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates carry fatally weak P-384 keys, enabling private-key recovery and fraudulent cert issuance. Chrome, Mozilla, Apple, and Microsoft have blocked them; your environment may still trust them.
Key findings:
- The root cause is a flaw in a key generation ceremony held April 30, 2025, for 24 subordinate CAs. A wrap/unwrap step produced a second set of weak P-384 keys, reducing effective entropy to an estimated 3 to 8 bits, making private-key recovery trivial to compute. Six of the eight affected intermediates are TLS CAs; two are code-signing CAs. Google removed emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from the Chrome Root Store entirely. eMudhra states its root CA private keys and other intermediates are not affected, and that no leaf certificates were issued to websites or end users under the compromised intermediates.
- The eight affected intermediates span eMudhra BV (G3B) and eMudhra Inc (G3C) and cover EV/OV/DV TLS and OV code-signing roles. Reliable identifiers for each are their SHA-256 fingerprints and serial numbers, all listed in the report. Example: EM EV TLS CA - G3B carries serial c7c41efe92d825f05eae841a4a82c1 and fingerprint E7568FE6E12331F4FD7DE61DA4C7559D0F8EB192A218D4741A3BA75184333838.
- Go runtimes are a distinct exposure path. Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 block chains containing the compromised keys under CVE-2026-111943. Older Go versions will still accept those chains. The report notes that unmanaged endpoints and custom trust stores that do not receive automatic distrust updates remain at risk regardless of browser-level blocks.
- Revocation is not a complete control. eMudhra has revoked all eight intermediates, but clients that skip revocation checks can still accept a chain containing them. Confirming that CRL and OCSP checks are functioning correctly is a required response step, not optional hygiene.
Hunt. The issuer-organization query is certificate:(issuer.organization:eMudhra BV or issuer.organization:eMudhra Inc) and the serial-number query targets all eight compromised intermediates individually. For Go runtime exposure, the report ties QID 5019897 to affected Go versions. For certificate chain enumeration on hosts, QID 48395 (eMudhra Intermediate CA Certificates Enumeration) covers assets presenting or using chains containing the compromised intermediates. Any leaf certificate whose chain includes one of the eight should be reissued by a different trusted CA and redeployed before trusting revocation status alone to protect users. The eight SHA-256 fingerprints and serial numbers are in the report.

item.title: BlackX UEFI Bootkit Bypasses Secure Boot on Patched Windows Systems Missing Revocations
item.description:
APT41-linked BlackX UEFI bootkit targets Central Asian-linked espionage campaign, exploiting a 2022 Secure Boot flaw still viable on patched systems that skipped manual revocation steps.
Key findings:
- BlackX is an evolved version of BlackLotus, exploiting CVE-2022-21894 (CVSS 4.4), the "Baton Drop" Secure Boot bypass. The critical gap: Windows updates alone do not block exploitation. Organizations must manually add the "Windows Production PCA 2011" certificate to the UEFI Forbidden List (DBX). Kaspersky confirms the certificate expired October 19, 2026, but expired does not mean blocklisted. Vulnerable binaries still load on systems missing the DBX update, and APT41 appears to have specifically targeted this gap in enterprise patching awareness.
- Infection begins post-compromise with administrator access. The installer drops inst.exe and an encrypted extensionless file PVMDIJGKAX2 to C:\ProgramData\Intel\, launched via command line with an RC4 decryption key as the argument. The binary then writes files to both system and UEFI partitions, installs Machine Owner Keys (MOK), and loads arbitrary EFI files, bypassing Secure Boot entirely. The source code of BlackLotus was never public, meaning APT41 either reverse-engineered or purchased the original to build BlackX, a rare crimeware-to-APT technology transfer.
- Post-exploitation is layered. A kernel driver signed by "Wenjiang District Mingyu Network Technology Service Studio" (certificate now revoked) is injected via the UEFI payload. The driver attempts to tamper with endpoint security, with specific routines targeting Kaspersky and Avast, though Kaspersky's analysis found these ineffective. A RAT using Google Drive, OneDrive, and Yandex.Disk for C2 exfiltrates files and harvests system info. A malicious DLL, OxiDLLRunner, is sideloaded by a delivered googleupdate.exe, decrypting a Rust payload that beacons to archivetj[.]com for additional DLL plugins.
- Attribution to APT41, specifically the FishMonger cluster (also tracked as Aquatic Panda and Earth Lusca), rests on two overlapping indicators: the string "xdd" appearing in both BlackX and a FishMonger kernel implant documented in an ESET June 2026 report, and the DLL sideloading pattern characteristic of Chinese 🇨🇳 threat actors. Diplomatic targets in Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan align with documented APT41 espionage priorities against high-value government networks.
- DFIR takeaway: On any host where BlackX is suspected, recovery cannot stop at the OS layer. UEFI partition forensics are required. Look for unauthorized MOK entries and unexpected EFI binaries. Verify DBX state against Microsoft's published revocation list. Hunt for inst.exe and PVMDIJGKAX2 under C:\ProgramData\Intel\, googleupdate.exe outside its expected install path, and unsigned or revoked kernel drivers loaded at boot. item.content:encoded:
APT41-linked BlackX UEFI bootkit targets Central Asian-linked espionage campaign, exploiting a 2022 Secure Boot flaw still viable on patched systems that skipped manual revocation steps.

Key findings:

- BlackX is an evolved version of BlackLotus, exploiting CVE-2022-21894 (CVSS 4.4), the "Baton Drop" Secure Boot bypass. The critical gap: Windows updates alone do not block exploitation. Organizations must manually add the "Windows Production PCA 2011" certificate to the UEFI Forbidden List (DBX). Kaspersky confirms the certificate expired October 19, 2026, but expired does not mean blocklisted. Vulnerable binaries still load on systems missing the DBX update, and APT41 appears to have specifically targeted this gap in enterprise patching awareness.

- Infection begins post-compromise with administrator access. The installer drops inst.exe and an encrypted extensionless file PVMDIJGKAX2 to C:\ProgramData\Intel\, launched via command line with an RC4 decryption key as the argument. The binary then writes files to both system and UEFI partitions, installs Machine Owner Keys (MOK), and loads arbitrary EFI files, bypassing Secure Boot entirely. The source code of BlackLotus was never public, meaning APT41 either reverse-engineered or purchased the original to build BlackX, a rare crimeware-to-APT technology transfer.

- Post-exploitation is layered. A kernel driver signed by "Wenjiang District Mingyu Network Technology Service Studio" (certificate now revoked) is injected via the UEFI payload. The driver attempts to tamper with endpoint security, with specific routines targeting Kaspersky and Avast, though Kaspersky's analysis found these ineffective. A RAT using Google Drive, OneDrive, and Yandex.Disk for C2 exfiltrates files and harvests system info. A malicious DLL, OxiDLLRunner, is sideloaded by a delivered googleupdate.exe, decrypting a Rust payload that beacons to archivetj[.]com for additional DLL plugins.

- Attribution to APT41, specifically the FishMonger cluster (also tracked as Aquatic Panda and Earth Lusca), rests on two overlapping indicators: the string "xdd" appearing in both BlackX and a FishMonger kernel implant documented in an ESET June 2026 report, and the DLL sideloading pattern characteristic of Chinese 🇨🇳 threat actors. Diplomatic targets in Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan align with documented APT41 espionage priorities against high-value government networks.

- DFIR takeaway: On any host where BlackX is suspected, recovery cannot stop at the OS layer. UEFI partition forensics are required. Look for unauthorized MOK entries and unexpected EFI binaries. Verify DBX state against Microsoft's published revocation list. Hunt for inst.exe and PVMDIJGKAX2 under C:\ProgramData\Intel\, googleupdate.exe outside its expected install path, and unsigned or revoked kernel drivers loaded at boot. Network-side, flag cloud storage C2 patterns and outbound connections to archivetj[.]com. The Kaspersky report contains IOCs.
