item.title: Obstacles to Weaponizing PHP2Shell Likely Constrain Immediate Widespread Exploitation
item.description:
PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) discloses two critical RCE flaws in PHP affecting versions before 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12. No confirmed exploitation in the wild yet, but weaponization attempts are already underway.
Key findings:
- Three distinct memory-corruption flaws underpin PHP2Shell. CVE-2026-109618 is a partial HashTable insertion bug: if a memory allocation fails mid-parse of HTTP request variables, PHP may update its entry count before the corresponding bucket is fully initialized, then attempt to access or release that invalid data at request shutdown, enabling memory corruption or arbitrary code execution. CVE-2026-109619 covers two separate use-after-free conditions tied to cross-request worker state: a serialization-context UAF triggered when zend_bailout() interrupts serialize() or unserialize() and leaves a stale pointer alive into the next request, and a session upload-progress UAF where a fatal error during multipart processing skips session cleanup, again leaving live pointers in a persistent worker.
- The worker reuse model is the forensic thread to pull. Both mod_php and PHP-FPM reuse long-running worker processes across requests. Exploitation of the UAF flaws depends on a subsequent request hitting the same corrupted worker. That means exploitation evidence may appear across two separate HTTP requests in access logs, not a single obvious payload, and worker crashes (PHP-FPM pool restarts, Apache worker segfaults) are a key indicator to correlate with inbound request patterns.
- CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations reproduced RCE but has not observed successful wild exploitation or a fully weaponized public exploit. What has been observed is testing, probing, and failed exploitation attempts. POC code circulating now is largely crash-only. Converting crash POCs to reliable RCE requires knowing the exact PHP version, libc, SAPI, and application stack, including specific Docker image releases. This is a meaningful barrier to mass exploitation but not to targeted attacks against known deployment profiles.
- Older and end-of-life PHP versions are also impacted. PHP powers roughly 70% of all websites, including WordPress deployments, making the potential scope enormous if a reliable public exploit emerges. The report notes AI-assisted vulnerability research is accelerating the discovery-to-exploit timeline, and the media attention around PHP2Shell will likely drive additional PHP vulnerability research in the near term.
- Disabling session.upload_progress.enabled in php.ini blocks the upload-progress paths for the two UAF conditions in CVE-2026-109619 but does not address the HashTable flaw in CVE-2026-109618. Restricting request body size, parameter-name length, nesting depth, and form field count at the reverse proxy or WAF layer before requests reach PHP reduces the attack surface for the HashTable parsing bug. After patching, rebuild container images and restart all Apache and PHP-FPM workers to eliminate any stale in-memory state.
Hunt priority: pull PHP-FPM pool error logs and Apache error logs for segfaults and worker restarts, then cross-reference timestamps with access logs for requests containing abnormally long parameter names, deeply nested form fields, or multipart bodies triggering upload-progress handling. IOCs and CrowdStrike's analysis context are in the report.

item.title: PHP2Shell: How to Stay Ahead of a Zero-Day, from Asset Discovery to Threat Hunting
item.description:
PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) are unauthenticated RCE zero-days in PHP itself, affecting every release back to 5.4, with exploitation confirmed four days before the October 21st patch shipped.
Key findings:
- Both CVEs sit in the PHP runtime, not in any application layer. CVE-2026-109618 is an out-of-memory condition during request setup that can produce code execution or leak server memory back in the response. CVE-2026-109619 is a stale-reference-after-free bug where subsequent worker requests can access freed memory, with PHP's session upload progress feature confirmed as one exploitation path. Every PHP deployment mode is affected: PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. Updating WordPress or Drupal does nothing; the runtime itself must be patched to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35.
- Exploitation was observed in honeypot infrastructure by Amazon on October 17th, four days before a patch existed. Cloudflare reported thousands of attempts in the 10 hours before public announcement, jumping to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes after. Government and commercial services across Japan 🇯🇵, the United States 🇺🇸, the United Kingdom 🇬🇧, the Netherlands 🇳🇱, Finland 🇫🇮, France 🇫🇷, Denmark 🇩🇰, Germany 🇩🇪, and Brazil 🇧🇷 went offline as a precaution, with payroll and national identity services among those disrupted.
- Application logs and WAFs frequently miss these exploits because the flaws trigger before application code runs. The ExtraHop report highlights a critical detection finding: the most dangerous CVE-2026-109618 requests were not readable as well-formed HTTP, making transaction-level rules blind to them. Connection-level analysis, comparing total bytes a client sent against what was parseable as HTTP, caught them. In lab replay across 263 attack connections, the server's share of traffic was under 0.06%, because PHP sends nothing until it has read the full flood. Attack packet sizes ran 74-117 bytes; normal large uploads ran about 1,430. Status codes also mislead: the same crash returns either a 500 or a 200 depending on PHP error settings.
- The report lays out concrete network-observable signatures defenders can hunt in stored traffic covering the pre-patch window. Look for: client connections to web servers that sent more than 1 MB in small packets and received almost nothing back; bursts of multipart requests carrying the PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS field from a single client; Set-Cookie PHPSESSID values longer than 256 characters or containing characters outside any valid PHP session ID format; request URIs or query strings containing sess_ paths or ../ traversal toward session directories. A Session File Include detection that returns a 200 response is the strongest network-level indicator that code actually executed.
- Post-exploitation pivots are where the real damage lands. Once a web shell is planted, attackers move to back-end databases and identity infrastructure. The report flags watching for new outbound connections from web servers, anomalous base64-encoded commands in headers, and non-standard SSH, RDP, or SMB credential-dumping activity originating from web servers that match the patterns above. Kerberos, NTLM, and LDAP traffic from a compromised web server to domain controllers is a high-priority escalation signal.
Practitioner takeaway: Do not limit your retrospective to post-patch dates. Exploitation predated the patch by at least four days. If you have packet capture or NDR flow data, search the pre-October-21st window using the hunt patterns above: oversized multipart floods with near-zero server response, session upload progress bursts from a single client, and malformed PHPSESSID values in Set-Cookie headers. For any web server that matches, immediately check PHP version, preserve packets, isolate if warranted, and trace east-west connections from that host to databases and domain controllers. The web server is the entry point, not the target.

item.title: Exposed Infrastructure Reveals How Ransomware Affiliates Used AI Agents to Execute Intrusions
item.description:
Russian-speaking ransomware affiliates ran a partially AI-executed intrusion operation across 62 organizations, with INC and The Gentlemen groups benefiting. Exposed infrastructure at 45.227.254[.]43 revealed the full kill chain, toolkit, and victim tracking system.
Key findings:
- The core framework, Phantom, is an AI-powered offensive platform deployed via OpenCode using OpenRouter-hosted commercial models. It supports 18 skill modules covering reconnaissance, EDR fingerprinting, exploit research, and steganography. When AI models declined a prompt, the operator reworded the request as an authorized red team assessment rather than switching models. Logged activity shows 8,257 messages across 133 sessions. The operation uses an "AI-executed, human-approved" structure: the human provides a victim prompt and approves each step, but execution is automated.
- CVEs actively exploited in the campaign include CVE-2024-57727 (SimpleHelp path traversal) and CVE-2026-35616 (Fortinet FortiClient authentication bypass) and CVE-2026-41940 (cPanel/WHM authentication bypass). CVE-2026-15409 (SonicWall SMA 1000 SSRF) was staged for targeting with no confirmed compromise. CVE-2026-63030 (WordPress wp2shell), CVE-2026-42208 (LiteLLM SQL injection), and CVE-2026-9082 (Drupal SQL injection) were developed or referenced in operator records.
- Post-access tradecraft followed a consistent lifecycle: domain enumeration, escalation to domain admin, credential harvesting with stealer tooling, and prioritized collection of finance, HR, legal, and executive files over reverse-SOCKS tunnels using RevSocks. In one documented case, a single reused password unlocked VPN, servers, RMM, backup, and security management platforms simultaneously. Security products were impaired using a BYOVD attack abusing the Zemana driver (zam64.sys) via a Quick Heal/Seqrite EDR killer. Operator logs record mixed results against enterprise EDRs.
- The toolkit also includes WormGPT-MCP (32 MCP servers spanning reconnaissance through extortion), Ghost C2 (three generations of polymorphic implants communicating over Cloudflare, Telegram, or DNS), a Cloudflare-fronted Mythic agent called QuickLine, and exfiltration tools rks3 and BackupAgent. AI-authored extortion records show the actors analyzed stolen financials to calibrate ransom demands below insurance or banking thresholds, then applied pressure through vishing calls and regulatory notification threats with 24-72 hour deadlines.
- Scope: 62 organizations targeted, four confirmed on INC and The Gentlemen leak sites. The US 🇺🇸 accounts for more than 50% of targets. Industrial, manufacturing, and energy sectors were hit hardest, followed by healthcare and pharmaceutical organizations.
Practitioner takeaway: the exposed directory at 45.227.254[.]43 is the starting point for infrastructure pivoting. Hunt your perimeter logs for exploitation attempts against FortiClient EMS gateways, SimpleHelp RMM servers, and cPanel endpoints tied to these CVEs. Internally, look for zam64.sys loaded by unexpected processes as a BYOVD indicator, reverse-SOCKS tunnel activity, and lateral movement patterns where a single credential authenticates across VPN, RMM, and backup platforms in short succession. The SOCRadar report is the primary source for operator TTPs documented from the exposed infrastructure.

item.title: PHP2Shell Operational Guidance
item.description:
Two critical PHP RCE flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (both CVSS v4.0 9.2), dubbed PHP2Shell, are under active exploitation attempts across internet-facing PHP deployments worldwide, with no confirmed successful compromise yet.
Key details:
- CVE-2026-109618 triggers RCE via out-of-memory corruption; CVE-2026-109619 via stale global state. Both allow unauthenticated RCE across PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. Apache mod_php is the highest-priority target: unauthenticated exploitation has already been demonstrated. A third flaw, CVE-2026-115560 (RCE, lower severity), was disclosed 23 October and will ship in the regular release cycle; its mitigation overlaps with CVE-2026-109619.
- Amazon's MadPot honeypot logged the first exploitation attempt on 17 October, four days before public disclosure. Amazon, Cloudflare, WatchTowr, and NVISO all confirm active exploitation attempts. Exploitation attempts began crashing servers, indicating probe-and-crash behavior from immature exploits. VulnCheck claims a working exploit for CVE-2026-109618 but this has not been independently confirmed. Over 748 GitHub repositories referencing PHP2Shell exist, some with over a thousand stars, but no publicly available exploit has been confirmed to reliably achieve stable code execution due to the need to bypass ASLR simultaneously.
- For CVE-2026-109618 where patching is delayed: set memory_limit=-1 via php_admin_value in FPM pool or Apache config (not overridable by application), set post_max_size to 8M (no uploads) or 32M (uploads required), and enforce request size, field count, multipart part count, header count, and nesting depth limits at the web server or proxy layer. Do not use RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA as substitutes; these can trigger the vulnerable allocation path. For CVE-2026-109619: set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart every worker via php.ini, FPM pool, or server config; on PHP 8.5 additionally set fatal_error_backtraces=0 and restart workers.
- Patch targets: PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, 8.2.35. PHP 8.1 and older receive no upstream fix; vendor backports or migration are required. Critically, updating a CMS like WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, or Magento does NOT update the underlying PHP runtime. Verify the actual runtime version in production after patching, including in load-balanced nodes, containers, and staging environments.
DFIR takeaway: Treat pre-patch windows as potential compromise windows. Hunt for php-fpm, php-cgi, apache2, or httpd spawning sh, bash, curl, or wget as child processes. Review HTTP access logs and reverse-proxy telemetry for unusual request patterns or spikes in 500-series errors around 17-21 October 2026, before patches were available. Audit web-accessible directories for newly created or modified PHP files indicating webshell staging. Where suspicious activity is found, preserve telemetry before remediation overwrites state. The NVISO report includes PHP-specific mitigation configuration steps in full.

item.title: AI-Assisted Cyberespionage Campaign Targets Government Systems
item.description:
Unattributed cyberespionage cluster CL-UNK-1211 hit government entities with AI-assisted payloads, custom Go RAT, and deep anti-forensics across a six-month Linux-focused campaign targeting databases and email.
Key findings:
- SysGoRAT, a Go-based RAT initially observed as sys-control-client and also masquerading as pip2.7, ea_install, and semanage, communicates over WebSocket to a hardcoded C2 at 104.194.158[.]65:443. It supports six persistence methods: systemd (installs sys-update.service), cron at five-minute intervals, registry Run keys, and scheduled tasks using OneDrive-themed identifiers on Windows. Its cross-platform design also provides TCP proxy and interactive shell capability, making it a full post-exploitation platform, not just a backdoor.
- Initial persistence was established by hijacking the auto_prepend_file directive in PHP configs under /etc/php/ and /opt/plesk/php/, forcing malicious code to execute before every legitimate PHP request. item.title: Enter 666: Unmasking Beast Ransomware
item.description:
Beast Ransomware, a RaaS operation attributed to actor Hyadina and linked to the later GodDamn variant, combines a GUI-driven affiliate interface with layered ChaCha20/Curve25519 encryption and aggressive recovery inhibition across Windows, NAS, and ESXi targets.
Key findings:
- The analyzed sample (SHA-256: 4c44ac1eea4bc7f4ea542d611b5658d7ac2729d79abe750da83f1581cd832eaf) is an 81 KB PE32 executable compiled 2024-08-09. Strings are stack-assembled and XOR-decoded in place with a single-byte key of 0x55, and the embedded config blob is ChaCha20-encrypted in the .data section, with the key and nonce stored immediately before it, making it recoverable via static analysis. A builder check for the literal strings !!!CONFIG!!! and !!!PASSWORD!!! can fingerprint unfinished or template payloads. The mutex BEAST HERE? provides a single-instance guard detectable in handle or memory telemetry early in execution.
- Beast phones home to iplogger[.]co/1v1i85.torrent twice per infection, passing the victim GUID in the User-Agent header and BEGIN or END in the Referer to bookend the encryption window. This gives the operator remote confirmation of execution without a traditional C2 channel. The ransomware also applies geographic exclusion via GetSystemDefaultUILanguage and GetLocaleInfoW, skipping a hardcoded list of CIS and associated country locales.
- Persistence lands at HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run with the victim GUID as the value name, requiring no admin rights. When the -I flag is active, Beast relocates itself to %ALLUSERSPROFILE%\{victim-GUID}\<8 random letters>.exe before writing that key, so the persisted binary lives at the relocation path, not the original drop location. The key file default.key, written beside the executable or in %TEMP%, holds the session public key and both attacker-protected copies of the session private key and persists across runs to maintain a consistent victim identifier.
- Encryption uses ChaCha20 with a Curve25519 ECDH key hierarchy: a per-machine session keypair is generated, the session private key is wrapped under two embedded attacker public keys and wiped from memory, then a fresh per-file ephemeral keypair is generated for every file. The 160-byte footer appended to each encrypted file contains everything needed for attacker-side decryption and ends with the 8-byte marker 66 6B EA 57 1A BE 16 66, which Beast uses to skip already-processed files. Encrypted files carry the extension .{victim-GUID}.moon and a ransom note of README.TXT. Intermittent encryption processes 25% of 128 KiB chunks by default, with a minimum of three chunks, capping encrypted volume at 512 MiB for files over 1 GiB.
- Recovery inhibition is layered: 73 services and 52 processes (backup agents, SQL engines, Veeam, Exchange, security products) are killed before encryption begins; Volume Shadow Copies are deleted via WMI ExecQuery and DeleteInstance against Win32_ShadowCopy; the Recycle Bin is emptied with SHEmptyRecycleBin; and the Windows Restart Manager (rstrtmgr.dll resolved at runtime) is used to unlock files held open by processes not on the kill list. Network targeting starts from the ARP cache via GetIpNetTable, probes private /24 subnets on TCP/445, and converts discovered shares to UNC paths for encryption, explicitly excluding ADMIN$.
Hunt tip: correlate three signals together, the HKCU Run key written with a GUID-format value name, an outbound HTTP request to iplogger[.]co with a GUID in User-Agent and BEGIN or END in Referer, and WMI activity against Win32_ShadowCopy. Any one of these alone is worth investigating; all three in sequence on a single host is a Beast infection in progress. The report includes the full IOC table, targeted service and process lists, and excluded filename, extension, and folder lists in the appendix.

item.title: Inside the LiteLLM 1.107.0 supply chain compromise: Credential theft through Python startup hooks
item.description:
LiteLLM 1.107.0 supply chain compromise delivered a credential-harvesting payload via Python startup hooks, activating on any Python invocation in an affected environment, not just LiteLLM gateway use.
Key findings:
- The attack began with stolen developer GitHub credentials used to redirect the LiteLLM release workflow to the lookalike repository Berri-AI/litellm instead of the legitimate BerriAI/litellm. A second stolen credential satisfied a production approval gate. The compromised wheel dropped three files: cook.pth, cook[.]py, and sitecustomize[.]py into the Python environment's site-packages library directory, outside the litellm application folder. That placement is the critical DFIR detail: removing the litellm directory alone does not remove the payload. The four SHA-256 hashes covering LF and CRLF variants of cook[.]py and sitecustomize[.]py are in the report's IOC table, alongside per-platform wheel hashes.
- Python startup processing, specifically .pth file execution and sitecustomize import during site initialization (T1546.018), ran the collector the moment any Python process started in the affected environment. No import of LiteLLM was required. cook[.]py Base64-decoded and zlib-decompressed the embedded PRIVCOLLECT program (T1027.013, T1140) before launching it in a daemon thread. A separate Unix loader in sitecustomize[.]py used /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock for single-instance enforcement, then polled a GitHub-hosted dead-drop file at hxxps://raw.githubusercontent[.]com/letters9813/pythonclient-test/main/domain.txt (T1102.001) for a mutable C2 address to retrieve and execute arbitrary Python from /codepy. Second-stage retrieval was not confirmed at analysis time, but the mechanism remained live.
- PRIVCOLLECT ran collection modules across developer and AI tool credentials, Git and package-manager config, AWS/Azure CLI/GCP credential caches, Kubernetes service-account files, Docker config, mounted secrets, AWS and GCP metadata API calls (T1552.005), Chromium and Firefox credential databases (T1555.003), SSH, GPG, and TLS key material (T1552.004), shell and database-client histories, Linux procfs process environments, and two LiteLLM proxy database tables via a Prisma child process targeting LiteLLM_CredentialsTable and LiteLLM_ProxyModelTable. Collected data was serialized to JSON, encrypted with AES-256-CBC under a per-run key, wrapped with an embedded 4096-bit RSA public key using OAEP, staged in a gzip tar with data.bin, key.bin, and hdr.json, then POSTed to hxxp://www.litellm[.]dev/healthcheck with a fixed browser-like User-Agent and an X-SHA256 body checksum. OpenSSL staging used temporary directories prefixed .pc_e_; the post-upload marker /tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb indicates a completed upload attempt.
- Affected environments include developer workstations, CI/CD agents, build and test containers, and LiteLLM proxy hosts, exactly the systems holding model-provider API keys, cloud workload identities, CI secrets, and source-control tokens. Microsoft Defender Antivirus signatures Trojan:PyPI/Stealer.SA, Trojan:PyPI/LiteLlmSupplyChain.A and .B, and Backdoor:PyPI/LiteLlmSupplyChain.C are available as of October 22. TVM-2026-0003 surfaces exposed endpoints in Defender Vulnerability Management.
Practitioner takeaway: do not invoke python, pip, or any interpreter inside a suspect environment to check for the package; startup alone can trigger collection. Scope exposure by searching installed environments, pip/uv caches, lock files, and container images for litellm-1.107.0 and verify against wheel hashes in the report. Hunt cook.pth (SHA-256 7f191632e7320705d154b85204f1ae546b543acbd7e8861229b76f5042b92bdb or 84dc8c82c0a4a4a62552ef826b49fcc86d1a5c4a5d0f2c06665723f93d129d7d) and the sitecustomize[.]py and cook[.]py hashes in your EDR file events. Check for .pc_e_ prefixed directories and /tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb as markers of staging and upload. Use the four KQL hunting queries in the report targeting DeviceNetworkEvents for www.litellm[.]dev, DeviceFileEvents for the four startup-file hashes, DeviceProcessEvents for the database child process pattern and OpenSSL .pc_e_ staging, and CloudProcessEvents for pkeyutl activity in /tmp/.pc_ paths. Rotate all credentials reachable from any affected identity from a known-clean machine, and revoke sessions rather than relying on password rotation alone.

item.title: php2shell in the Lab, and Where a SOC Catches It
item.description:
CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (php2shell): unauthenticated RCE in PHP core, CVSS v4.0 9.2 each, fixed October 21. Black Hills InfoSec lab-tested both on Linux and Windows and published two production Sigma rules.
Key findings:
- Two separate memory-corruption bugs, both pre-auth RCE as the web-server user. CVE-2026-109619 is a stale-pointer bug where request-owned data outlives the worker memory it references; a confirmed path is session upload progress, which is where the php2shell name originates. CVE-2026-109618 triggers when PHP hits an out-of-memory condition mid-request and cleanup treats half-built data as valid. Affected SAPIs include mod_php, php-fpm, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. Windows is equally affected: the same core ships in php-cgi.exe behind IIS. Fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. Actively exploitable on Linux with public PoCs; no reliable public Windows RCE exists yet, hardened by CFG and ASLR, but the bug is present.
- The successful Linux exploitation chain produced apache2 (www-data) spawning /bin/sh -c "id" spawning id. That process tree is the durable forensic signal, not the memory corruption itself, which is invisible to EDR. The giant multipart POST, the PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS field, Transfer-Encoding chunked, heap-spray bursts of near-identical form fields, and a Set-Cookie: PHPSESSID= carrying binary or %00 bytes all live in the request body and belong to WAF/proxy visibility, not endpoint telemetry. The one log line the lab did capture at crash time: "Allowed memory size ... in Unknown on line 0" in the Apache error log.
- Failed or mistuned attempts crash the worker instead of executing code. On Linux, Apache logs AH00052: child pid N exit signal Abort (6) for allocator-caught heap corruption and exit signal Segmentation fault (11) for unmapped-memory writes. On Windows the equivalent is WerFault.exe spawning and an Application Error Event ID 1000 as php-cgi.exe recycles. Treat a burst of worker crashes paired with matching web-server error log entries as an attempt-hunt signal, not a standalone alert.
- The critical detection lesson: writing the rule to watch for a web worker spawning a recon binary misses the actual chain. PHP's system() and exec() route through /bin/sh -c, making the recon binary a grandchild. The rule must key on the shell child's command line, not the binary. On Windows the same shape appears: w3wp.exe spawns php-cgi.exe spawns cmd.exe /s /c "whoami" spawns whoami.exe. Read the command off cmd.exe, exactly as you read it off sh -c on Linux. Both Sigma rules published in the report key on web-worker parent, shell child, and a delimiter-bounded recon verb on that shell's command line. Linux rule id: 67afd63c-418f-43a4-a4a9-feae3783a641. Windows rule id: 170d3f2a-5734-4941-99f2-cc8b4a99ebe3.
- One mitigation caveat worth carrying: CVE-2026-115560, a separate lower-severity upload-progress vector, is not fixed in the October 21 releases. A full fix is promised in the next regular release. Keep session.upload_progress.enabled = Off even after you apply the October 21 patches. Also: do not use RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA to cap memory as a workaround; the advisory explicitly warns those make mmap() fail, which triggers the same vulnerable path as CVE-2026-109618. On PHP-on-IIS hosts, check whether the php-cgi.exe worker runs as nt authority\iusr with SeImpersonatePrivilege; if a web shell lands there, privilege escalation toward SYSTEM is a risk to assess, not an assumption.
Takeaway: Hunt for web-worker processes (apache2, httpd, nginx, php-fpm, php-cgi, lsphp, frankenphp, w3wp.exe) spawning sh, bash, or cmd.exe/powershell.exe with a recon verb on the shell's command line. Both Sigma rules, with full parent-process lists, shell-child conditions, and delimiter-bounded recon-verb regexes for Linux and Windows, are published in the Black Hills InfoSec report. Backtest against your own fleet before enforcing; the report flags hostname as the most common benign false positive, and short network-recon verbs like ip and ss warrant the same baseline check.

On Windows the same shape appears: w3wp.exe spawns php-cgi.exe spawns cmd.exe /s /c "whoami" spawns whoami.exe. Read the command off cmd.exe, exactly as you read it off sh -c on Linux. Both Sigma rules published in the report key on web-worker parent, shell child, and a delimiter-bounded recon verb on that shell's command line. Linux rule id: 67afd63c-418f-43a4-a4a9-feae3783a641. Windows rule id: 170d3f2a-5734-4941-99f2-cc8b4a99ebe3.

- One mitigation caveat worth carrying: CVE-2026-115560, a separate lower-severity upload-progress vector, is not fixed in the October 21 releases. A full fix is promised in the next regular release. Keep session.upload_progress.enabled = Off even after you apply the October 21 patches. Also: do not use RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA to cap memory as a workaround; the advisory explicitly warns those make mmap() fail, which triggers the same vulnerable path as CVE-2026-109618. On PHP-on-IIS hosts, check whether the php-cgi.exe worker runs as nt authority\iusr with SeImpersonatePrivilege; if a web shell lands there, privilege escalation toward SYSTEM is a risk to assess, not an assumption.

Takeaway: Hunt for web-worker processes (apache2, httpd, nginx, php-fpm, php-cgi, lsphp, frankenphp, w3wp.exe) spawning sh, bash, or cmd.exe/powershell.exe with a recon verb on the shell's command line. Both Sigma rules, with full parent-process lists, shell-child conditions, and delimiter-bounded recon-verb regexes for Linux and Windows, are published in the Black Hills InfoSec report. Backtest against your own fleet before enforcing; the report flags hostname as the most common benign false positive, and short network-recon verbs like ip and ss warrant the same baseline check.

item.title: Signed, Sealed, and Relayed, NTLM-style: Bypassing LDAP Signing Through Reauthentication
item.description:
NTLM relay bypass defeated LDAP signing on every Windows Server 2016 through 2025 domain controller. Microsoft patched LDAP in October 2026 and SMB in September 2026; both fixes are now available and critical to apply.
- The core technique, called "The LDAP Switcheroo" by SpecterOps, works by establishing a signed LDAP connection to a domain controller using attacker-controlled credentials (or anonymous NTLM SASL where accepted), keeping the resulting session key. The attacker then coerces a victim machine over SMB, relays the victim's NTLM AUTHENTICATE message over that already-signed connection, and packs a malicious LDAP ModifyRequest into the same SASL record. The DC verifies the signature once using the attacker's session key, then switches authorization to the victim mid-record and executes the stacked operation with the victim's privileges. The attacker never learns the victim's session key or password.
- The SMB client's NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_SIGN flag, historically the thing that blocked SMB-to-LDAP relay, is exactly what makes this work. Without it set, the DC returns operationsError (0x4DC) and rejects the stacked operation. A WebDAV-coerced victim does not set that flag, so only SMB coercion enables this path.
- The practical impact is full domain and forest compromise from an unauthenticated or low-privilege position. In the SpecterOps walkthrough, relaying a domain controller's machine account (LYS-SRV22$) allowed writing msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity on that machine to grant an attacker-controlled account RBCD rights, leading directly to DCSync. The msDS-KeyCredentialLink attribute (shadow credentials) is a parallel primitive. Both run in a single signed SASL record.
- The root cause lives in LDAP_CONN::ProcessRequestEx. Before the patch, the function verified a SASL record once against the connection's current signing key, then processed every LDAP message inside it sequentially, including messages that arrived after LDAP_CONN::SetSecurityContextAtts had already switched the connection's identity to the victim. The fix adds an identity counter to each connection: LDAP_REQUEST::ReceivedClientData snapshots it when data arrives, LDAP_CONN::SetSecurityContextAtts increments it on a bind, and ProcessRequestEx discards the rest of the SASL record if the two values diverge. KB5126646 (October 13, 2026) carries the LDAP fix; KB5122882 (September 2026) carries the SMB fix.
- The bypass is limited to LDAP on 389/TCP. LDAPS (636/TCP) uses TLS for signing, and Windows does not permit NTLM SASL signing or sealing over an existing TLS connection, so there is no attacker-controlled SASL record to stack the operation into. Channel binding, which only applies to LDAPS, is irrelevant to this path; the tested DC had both signing and channel binding enforced and remained vulnerable over 389/TCP.
Takeaway: Apply KB5126646 to every domain controller immediately. After patching, hunt for evidence of exploitation: look for unexpected writes to msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity or msDS-KeyCredentialLink on domain controller computer objects in Active Directory audit logs, and correlate with LDAP bind events on 389/TCP where the binding account differs from the account that appears in the subsequent modify. SpecterOps is releasing the proof-of-concept tool wrapping ntlmrelayx[.]py at github[.]com/grayhatkiller/switcheroo; expect active exploitation attempts shortly. Blocking inbound 389/TCP to domain controllers where operationally feasible and enforcing both LDAP signing and channel binding together remain the layered controls that survive a missed patch.

item.title: How CVE-2026-73570 turns a Zimbra log file into remote code execution
item.description:
CVE-2026-73570 is an unauthenticated RCE in Zimbra that weaponizes a log file: one malformed SMTP address triggers shell execution as the zimbra user, giving an attacker read access to every mailbox and the ability to send as any local identity.
Key findings:
- The injection chain is: malformed RCPT TO -> /var/log/zimbra.log -> Swatchdog pattern match -> Perl dosnmp backtick -> /bin/sh. The attacker sends an SMTP message with an unclosed angle bracket in the recipient address. Postfix rejects it but logs the raw address, which the attacker has crafted to match the service status pattern "Service status change: localhost $(command) changed from stopped to running". Swatchdog tails the log, matches that pattern, and passes the SERVICE field directly into a backtick expression inside the dosnmp Perl subroutine in swatchrc[.]in. No authentication required, no prior foothold needed, just a TCP connection to port 25.
- The vulnerability lives in the perlcode block at line 26 of swatchrc[.]in, specifically the dosnmp function where $args{SERVICE} is interpolated unescaped into a backtick shell call: backtick $snmptrap $snmpsvctrap $snmpsvcname s args{SERVICE} $snmpsvcstatus i $statuses{args{STATUS}} backtick. The zimbra user (uid=997 in Elastic's lab) runs the resulting command with membership in the zimbra and postfix groups, giving full mailbox read, mail relay as any local identity, and likely LDAP and signing key access.
- Elastic Security Labs confirms active exploitation is feasible and that several public PoCs fail because they write incorrectly formatted log entries that Swatchdog never matches, so a failed PoC test can look like a patched server. Their working PoC uses an out-of-band curl callback to confirm execution without leaving additional on-disk artifacts. The 501 SMTP rejection is expected and does not indicate failure; the log write already happened.
- Patch status: Zimbra 10.1.20 (Daffodil release) is the complete fix. The Elastic Security Labs report confirms the vulnerability was reproduced on Release 10.1.16.BETA.4200001.UBUNTU24.64. If you run internet-facing Zimbra SMTP and have not reached 10.1.20, this is pre-auth RCE on port 25 with a public PoC chain confirmed to work.
- The Elastic report ships the detection rule "Zimbra Swatchdog SNMP Command Injection Execution" as a sequence query: it first looks for a shell (sh, bash, dash, ash, zsh, ksh) spawned by a perl parent whose command line matches .swatchdog_script. and contains snmptrap, zmservicename, and zmservicestatus, then correlated by process.entity_id it looks for any child of that shell where process[.]name != snmptrap. That second process is your payload. The rule is retroactive, so you can hunt pre-patch exploitation in historical EDR telemetry.
Responder action: Run the sequence rule against your Linux EDR telemetry going back to your earliest Zimbra logs. If you find hits, treat the zimbra account as fully compromised and scope for mailbox exfil, phishing relay from the server, LDAP exports, and signing key theft. The report calls out local databases and signing keys explicitly as post-exploitation targets beyond the mail store. IOCs and the detection rule are in the Elastic Security Labs report.

item.title: Infostealer riding the AI Train
item.description:
Aokigahara infostealer adds dedicated collection routines for AI tools and cloud dev environments, targeting Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, and AWS/Azure credentials alongside traditional browser and wallet theft.
Key findings:
- The aisessions handler is the standout capability. It collects authentication files and session databases from Claude Code and Desktop (%AppData%\.claude\credentials.json, %AppData%\Claude\), Codex (%AppData%\.codex\auth.json), ChatGPT Desktop (Packages\OpenAI.ChatGPT-Desktop_2p2nqsd0c76g0\LocalCache\Roaming\ChatGPT), Cursor and Windsurf (User\globalStorage\state.vscdb), GitHub Copilot (%AppData%\.copilot\hosts.json), Gemini CLI (gemini-cli-workspace-token.json), and JetBrains AI Assistant. The ide handler separately sweeps Git credential files, .ssh private keys, and AWS/Azure/Google Cloud config files, reaching deep into developer environments.
- The clipper component is deployed by dropping a separate binary under C:\Microsoft\Vault using embedded data. The clipper_drop handler plants it; the parent stealer does not itself touch the clipboard, which may help split behavioral signals across two processes and complicate triage.
- C2 communication follows a three-stage HTTP protocol: POST to /gate/handshake (raw 32-byte X25519 public key in body), /gate/chunk (AES-256-GCM encrypted ZIP per module, X-Chunk header names the module: sysinfo, browsers, aisessions, etc.), and /gate/complete (literal "COMPLETE" body). The User-Agent is Microsoft-CryptoAPI/10.0. The config lives in the .stgcfg PE section, magic bytes STGC, AES-256-CBC encrypted with a seed-derived key.
- Anti-analysis is gated by configuration flags. When enabled: PEB debugger flag inspection, debug port and debug object queries, hardware breakpoint register checks (DR0-DR3), CPUID hypervisor checks, VM guest-tool registry and process checks, SMBIOS fingerprinting, and username/computer name checks against strings like "sandbox", "malware", "WDAGUtilityAccount". Language check excludes Russian 🇷🇺, Ukrainian 🇺🇦, Belarusian 🇧🇾, and eight additional CIS locales via bitmask 0x6C0400C8601, a common CIS-exclusion pattern.
- A large IOC set is in the report: over 140 SHA1 sample hashes, a clipper hash (8d6c86e0af7807f9b5baf15e9f076bb81e012515), and C2 infrastructure including 2.26.252[.]48:8080, gate.dfwioeiofwr[.]info, dobeqnesmot[.]cc, kkeyyou[.]cc, neihite[.]cc, hjazfioe[.]surf, and somelitersofblood[.]pw. A YARA rule is provided in the report, keying on strings including "AISessions/", "aokigahara", "kamidere", "\\.\\pipe\\akg_%lx_%lx", and "X-Chunk-Index: %u".
Practitioner takeaway: on any suspected infected host, prioritize the aisessions and ide collection paths. State.vscdb files for Cursor, Windsurf, and VS Code are SQLite databases and can be queried directly for stored tokens. Check .aws\credentials and .aws\sso\cache for freshness anomalies. On the network side, hunt for POST requests to /gate/handshake, /gate/chunk, and /gate/complete with User-Agent "Microsoft-CryptoAPI/10.0" and Content-Type application/octet-stream. Flag any process writing to C:\Microsoft\Vault as a clipper deployment indicator. IOCs and the YARA rule are in the Check Point Research report.

item.title: Go With the Flow: Taking a Shadow Dependency in GCP Dataflow Cross Tenant
item.description:
Cross-tenant RCE in GCP Dataflow via bucket squatting and pickle deserialization: a victim's own pipeline stages malicious code without the attacker needing a single IAM permission on the target project.
Key findings:
- The attack chain starts with a predictable default staging bucket name. When a Dataflow pipeline using Beam's Python SDK omits --staging_location, Beam computes the bucket name as dataflow-staging-{region}-{md5(project_id)}. GCP project IDs are not secrets, they appear in IAM bindings, error messages, and support tickets. MD5 is used purely for length, not protection, so an attacker can precompute the target bucket name for any project they want to hit, create it in their own GCP project first, and grant AllUsers read/write. The Python SDK, unlike the Java SDK, never verified bucket ownership before this fix, so get_or_create_default_gcs_bucket() silently reused the attacker-controlled bucket.
- Code execution comes from --save_main_session. Pipelines that use global imports, helper functions, or module-level constants pass --save_main_session to sync that state to workers. Beam serializes it as a raw pickle stream named pickled_main_session and uploads it to the staging bucket. Python pickle deserialization is arbitrary code execution by design: any object implementing __reduce__ runs the moment it is unpickled. An attacker drops a malicious pickle whose __reduce__ calls the GCE instance metadata endpoint, retrieves the worker service account's OAuth token, and exfiltrates both token and identity to an attacker-controlled host.
- The race is the delivery mechanism. Once the victim submits a job, Dataflow creates a job-prefixed folder inside the squatted bucket and uploads the legitimate pickled_main_session. The attacker polls the bucket, detects the new folder, deletes the real file, and re-uploads the malicious pickle before workers start. Every worker, including those added later by autoscaling, downloads and unpickles the swapped file. The runtime service account, often the broadly privileged Compute Engine default service account, is what the payload runs as, enabling credential theft, lateral movement to other GCP resources, and access to data moving through the pipeline.
- The scope is scoped but real. The opening only exists for projects that have never run a default-bucket Dataflow job in that region. Once a project owns the name, it cannot be squatted. Still, that covers every project's first regional Dataflow deployment without an explicit staging location, which is a meaningful slice of new pipeline deployments and new region expansions across any organization.
- Google fixed this in three layers, all globally deployed: Beam 2.75.0 (PR apache/beam #39008) adds a client-side _validate_bucket_project() call that compares the pre-existing bucket's owning project number to the caller's via Cloud Resource Manager and raises ValueError on mismatch. The Dataflow control plane independently enforces the same ownership check server-side, rejecting jobs with FAILED_PRECONDITION even on older pinned SDK versions. Finally, SHA-256 integrity verification for staged artifacts, including pickled_main_session, is computed at staging time and verified by workers on startup, shutting down the swap race entirely.
Responder and defender takeaway: audit every active Dataflow pipeline for --staging_location. Jobs without an explicit staging bucket in regions where the project is new are the exposure window. Confirm staging bucket ownership directly: the bucket's owning project number must match the submitting project's number via the Cloud Resource Manager API. Treat write access to any staging or temp bucket exactly like write access to source code. Even after patching, --save_main_session still uses pickle, so staging bucket ACLs are a code supply chain control, not just a storage hygiene item. The full technical write-up, attack flow video, and fix details are in the Varonis report.

item.title: CVE-2026-0257: Actively Exploited PAN-OS GlobalProtect Authentication Bypass Vulnerability
item.description:
CVE-2026-0257 is an actively exploited PAN-OS GlobalProtect authentication bypass enabling ransomware groups to skip MFA and land inside corporate networks via forged VPN sessions. Qilin and Inc Ransom have been observed in the wild since October 19.
Key findings:
- The flaw lives in the authentication override cookie mechanism on GlobalProtect portal and gateway. item.title: Microsoft 365 accounts compromised at 79 organizations, no passwords needed
item.description:
AiTM "token spraying" campaign hit 79 organizations over 10 weeks without a single password: 497 successful sign-ins, rogue Entra devices, swapped MFA, and hidden inbox rules kept attackers resident long after sessions expired.
Key findings:
- The attacker used three initial access methods: adversary-in-the-middle phishing to harvest post-MFA session tokens, device-code phishing where victims entered codes on Microsoft's legitimate login page, and social engineering during ordinary logins. Because the token is issued after MFA completes, replaying it bypasses MFA entirely. Huntress calls the bulk replay "token spraying," the session-token analog to password spraying. All replay traffic came from the 193.26.115[.]0/24 range, cycling through six addresses across four phases, with Microsoft Entra ID Protection independently flagging several of those IPs. The hosting provider behind those addresses is 1337 Services GmbH, incorporated in Hamburg, Germany 🇩🇪.
- Session-to-intrusion windows were extremely short. In the July 21 incident, a hijacked session appeared from a campaign address 12 minutes after the victim hit the MFA prompt. On September 22 the gap was four minutes. Speed matters here for triage: if Entra sign-in logs show a token replay from 193.26.115[.]0/24 within minutes of a legitimate authentication, containment was already behind.
- Persistence was layered and durable. Huntress found at least 48 rogue devices registered in victim Entra directories, each named "DESKTOP-" followed by eight hex characters. In 19 organizations, existing MFA methods were wiped and a new authenticator registered within three hours of first access. In the July 21 case, an authenticator labeled "iPhone 13" was enrolled under an hour after session hijack. A registered authenticator and a registered device both survive a password reset unless an administrator explicitly audits and removes them.
- Inbox manipulation concealed the intrusion and enabled fraud. Rules with names like ".", "sss", and "iT" deleted mail, marked messages read, and shunted them to RSS Feeds or Conversation History. In one business email compromise pivot, the attacker sent a payroll-related message to an external accountant from a victim mailbox, then created a rule catching any mail mentioning payroll, direct deposit, bank, or bonus, and five minutes later added a second rule hiding all mail from that accountant. Conditional Access policies blocked the attacker 1,052 times across four organizations, stopping sign-ins the compromised tokens would otherwise have completed.
Practitioner takeaway: Start your hunt in Entra sign-in logs and audit logs. Look for successful non-interactive token sign-ins originating from the 193.26.115[.]0/24 range, then pivot to the same account's audit log for device registrations matching the "DESKTOP-[8 hex chars]" pattern and MFA method changes within three hours of that sign-in. Pull inbox rules for any account that touched that IP block and look for single-character or short-string rule names moving mail to RSS Feeds or Conversation History. Any account with a new authenticator or registered device needs those objects removed before a password reset means anything. IOCs and mitigation guidance are in the Huntress report.

item.title: Microsoft Links ConnectWise Breach to China-Linked Group Using AI Pentesting Tool ARTEX
item.description:
Chinese 🇨🇳 Storm-0940 used AI pentesting framework ARTEX to compromise 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants via a ConnectWise supply chain breach, achieving privileged cloud access in under three hours in multiple cases.
Key findings:
- Storm-0940 ran a password spray from 144.172.64[.]99 between October 10-14, logging more than 151,000 failed attempts against 327 accounts across eight organizations, peaking at 2,900 attempts per minute on October 11. Forty-eight accounts each absorbed over 1,000 attempts. None succeeded. On October 15, one day after the ConnectWise breach went public, the campaign pivoted: the AI agents dropped password spraying entirely and began authenticating directly using stolen ConnectWise cloud application credentials, skipping interactive user sign-in altogether.
- ARTEX is an open-source Go-based agentic AI penetration testing framework that coordinates multiple AI models. The campaign targeting South Korean 🇰🇷 financial institutions used DeepSeek, GLM, and Grok as coordinated agents, with GLM cross-checking DeepSeek's output. The project has since gone closed-source, but existing copies remain fully functional.
- After authenticating into customer Microsoft 365 environments, Storm-0940's agents moved into Microsoft Graph, ran directory reconnaissance, modified application credentials to establish persistence, and attempted changes to identities, groups, and privileged roles. This follow-on activity hit a subset of the 2,250 tenants reached. The sectors targeted span aerospace, defense, energy, financial services, government, and manufacturing.
- The persistence mechanism is the critical artifact for responders. Credential additions to service principals made before access was revoked remain live backdoors. Microsoft is explicit: revoking the original ConnectWise application connection does not remove attacker-added credentials on trusted applications. Those keys survive remediation unless separately identified and removed.
- ARTEX is not exclusive to Storm-0940. Microsoft's report notes threat actors across multiple regions have used the same framework, and Zscaler and Recorded Future separately documented a Chinese-speaking group deploying it against South Korean 🇰🇷 financial institutions. The agentic model, running 24/7 across multiple attack paths simultaneously, is what made 2,250-tenant scale at 2,900 attempts per minute possible.
Takeaway: Audit every service principal and application credential addition in your Microsoft 365 tenant going back to at least October 1, not October 15. Look for new credentials added to existing trusted applications, especially any with Graph API permissions to read directory objects or modify group and role membership. The OAuth app abuse and Graph reconnaissance pattern is the post-authentication kill chain here. Microsoft's report contains the full technical details and IOCs.

item.title: PHP2Shell: Two Critical PHP Vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619): Are Your…
item.description:
Two critical PHP flaws tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (PHP2Shell, CVSS v4.0 9.2) were disclosed ahead of their scheduled patch, leaving internet-facing PHP servers exposed while full technical details remain unconfirmed.
Key details:
- CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 carry a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 from the PHP security team. An emergency release was scheduled for October 21, 2026 at 14:00 UTC. At time of writing, affected version ranges are not officially confirmed, though initial reports suggest older PHP versions may also be impacted. Preliminary technical discussion mentions multipart requests and PHP session upload handling as possible vectors, but these remain unvalidated research leads, not confirmed exploitation indicators.
- Exploitation status: no confirmed in-the-wild exploitation has been attributed to PHP2Shell in this report. However, the Huntress report referenced in the report documented a separate PHP abuse case involving temporary PHP files created, executed, and then removed, a behavior directly relevant to web shell investigations regardless of which vulnerability is leveraged.
- The attack chain post-exploitation follows a recognizable pattern: PHP or web server processes (php-fpm, apache2, w3wp.exe) spawning shells or utilities (bash, cmd.exe, powershell.exe, curl, socat, nc), followed by reconnaissance commands (whoami, id, uname, hostname), then outbound connections to public IPs on unusual ports, and finally new PHP or phtml files written to /tmp/, /var/tmp/, /dev/shm/, or web root directories.
- The report provides six KQL hunting queries for Microsoft Defender XDR covering: PHP installation discovery via DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory, suspicious child process spawning via DeviceProcessEvents, reconnaissance command execution, PHP file creation in sensitive paths via DeviceFileEvents, outbound network connections by web processes via DeviceNetworkEvents, and a behavioral baseline comparison (28-day lookback vs. last 2 days) to surface new child processes spawned by PHP workers that have no historical precedent on that device.
- For Sentinel users, the report recommends correlating unusual HTTP POST requests, repeated 5xx responses, PHP worker crashes, and changes in request volume around the disclosure date with subsequent process execution or outbound connections on the same host. The exact KQL depends on the web server or WAF log schema ingested.
Practitioner takeaway: Start with DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory to identify PHP runtime installations and flag legacy or end-of-life versions (Major < 8, or 8.0/8.1). Prioritize internet-facing servers. Then run the behavioral baseline query against DeviceProcessEvents: any child process spawned by a PHP worker in the last 2 days that has no appearance in the prior 28-day window is your highest-priority lead. Cross-reference with DeviceFileEvents for .php or .phtml files written to /tmp/ or web directories, and DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound connections from those same processes. The KQL queries are published in the Detect FYI report and are ready to deploy in Defender XDR. Pin the patch date and re-run scope queries once affected version ranges are officially confirmed.

item.title: MythicRatatoskr: An Yggdrasil-enabled backdoor deployed in a UAC-0099-Sandworm collaboration
item.description:
UAC-0099 handed a Ukrainian 🇺🇦 grain logistics company to Sandworm, which wiped data 63 days later. The bridge: MythicRatatoskr, a new Go backdoor routing C2 through the Yggdrasil mesh network.
Key findings:
- UAC-0099 gained initial access on July 16, 2025 via spearphishing (T1566.001) with a malicious attachment, triggering the MATCHBOIL downloader, which pulled MATCHWOK from hxxps://egyptanimals[.]com/animals/photoalbum with C2 at hxxps://uztickets[.]com. MATCHWOK persists via HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\ as UpdateMonitor. One day later, MythicRatatoskr was delivered and installed as a Windows service named ieupdate (T1543.003). Lateral spread across the org used OpenSSH SFTP.
- MythicRatatoskr is a previously undocumented Go backdoor, detected as WinGo/Agent.ZO, that communicates exclusively over the Yggdrasil decentralized mesh network. Its C2 is an IPv6 address inside Yggdrasil: 201:b479:2771:8df4:b5eb:d007:63b0[:]2838, reached via HTTPS on port 443 (T1071.001, T1090.003, T1573). The malware embeds a hardcoded list of 32 public Yggdrasil peers, randomly picks three to join the mesh, and generates a fresh Ed25519 key pair on each run so its Yggdrasil IPv6 address rotates. Some samples include a 10-minute startup delay (T1678) to slow detection. The config file is AES-256-CFB encrypted, stored as a hidden-dot filename at paths including C:\Windows\Temp\.updatecache and C:\Windows\system32\.updatecache (T1027.013).
- The backdoor supports shell execution via cmd.exe (T1059.003), file upload and download (T1041, T1105), screenshot capture without touching disk (T1113), directory traversal (T1005), and a reverse SOCKS5 proxy command (T1090.001) that connects to 201:b479:2771:8df4:b5eb:d007:63b0[:]2838:8080. A separate standalone SOCKS5 server, internally named bindProxy and detected as WinGo/TrojanProxy.Agent.I, was also deployed, listening on 127.0.0.1:33690, with install paths including C:\Windows\system32\krbtman.exe and %localappdata%\SMBCache\nbtresolver.exe. Note that krbtman.exe is used as a filename for both MythicRatatoskr and the SOCKS5 server on different machines.
- Artifact flags suggesting a Linux variant: the config path %LocalAppData%/Temp/.crond uses Unix-style forward slashes and a dot-prefixed filename, and an unused path /tmp/.test_config was found in OneDriveLiveUpdater.exe. File paths, forward-slash usage, and dot-prefix naming conventions all point to a cross-platform codebase. Function naming inconsistency (CheckInAgent in mixed caps alongside agent_run in snake case) suggests code merged from another project, possibly the Mythic C2 framework given the name.
- On September 17, 2025, Sandworm executed a data-wiping attack using SDelete deployed via Active Directory Group Policy (T1485), consistent with documented Sandworm TTPs. This confirms UAC-0099 is operating as an initial access broker feeding Sandworm. ESET notes this mirrors the earlier Gamaredon-Turla collaboration, signaling a broader pattern of coordinated handoffs among Russian-aligned groups.
Hunt priority: look for a Windows service named ieupdate or new services spawning from paths like C:\Windows\system32\updater.exe or WindowsDefenderSvc.exe. Check Windows\Temp\ and system32\ for files named .updatecache (dot-prefixed, not hidden on Windows). Hunt outbound TLS connections to peers in the Yggdrasil public peer list on non-standard ports (993, 65534, 61995, 1337, and others embedded in the report). For the wipe, look for SDelete execution originating from Group Policy-driven processes. IOCs including 12 file hashes, the C2 Yggdrasil address, and the full 32-peer list are in the ESET GitHub repository linked from the report.

item.title: Parasitizing trust: How legitimate infrastructure becomes a delivery pipeline for attackers
item.description:
Attackers are parasitizing legitimate commerce, SaaS, and mail-delivery infrastructure to bypass sender authentication entirely, observed across more than 25 platforms in the past year by Cisco Talos.
Key findings:
- Talos documented two vishing-via-order-notification campaigns abusing Staples and Dell transactional email pipelines, totaling roughly 1,400 messages. Both passed DKIM and DMARC for their respective sending domains (orders[.]staples[.]com and order[.]dell[.]com), because the outer message was genuine. The malicious payload was not in the sender identity. It was injected into order fields like "Ship To" and "Bill To," embedding attacker-controlled phone numbers (806 283 7712 in the Staples campaign, 808 232 6397 in the Dell campaign) alongside fake high-value purchases. The goal was to drive the victim to call a fraudster, not click a link, bypassing URL-based security controls entirely.
- A parallel technique Talos calls "list bombing evolved" weaponizes registration and profile forms lacking input validation. Attackers submit a "hostile string," a cryptocurrency lure, for example, into a name or title field. The legitimate platform then reflects that string into an automated welcome or verification email sent to the victim. The outer message carries full platform authentication. The inner content is attacker-supplied. This is not yet widespread, Talos notes, but it represents deliberate exploitation of trust-boundary assumptions in SaaS notification pipelines, and it creates brand reputation damage and potential blocklisting for the abused platform.
- Bounce abuse, the third vector, forces delivery status notifications (DSNs) to carry attacker-controlled content. In one case Talos observed, a mail delivery failure notification contained a WeTransfer-themed file-sharing lure nested inside the DSN wrapper. This can occur through opportunistic backscatter (forging the victim as the envelope sender so a legitimate downstream bounce returns to them) or through intentional triggered failures. Users treat delivery failure messages as administrative and low-risk, making this an effective social engineering container.
- The root cause across all three vectors is the same: platforms implicitly trust data submitted from untrusted sources and render it into high-reputation automated notifications. SPF, DKIM, and DMARC confirm message origin, not content integrity. Authentication answered "did this come from Dell's infrastructure?" It could not answer "is this purchase real, and does this phone number belong to Dell?"
Practitioner takeaway: Treat sender trust and content trust as two separate signals during triage. For transactional email investigations, inspect every user-controlled field in the rendered message body, not just headers. Phone numbers, URLs, and urgency language appearing in shipping, billing, or order-note fields are red flags regardless of authentication pass status. For bounce-abuse cases, perform recursive MIME inspection: parse the DSN container, extract the returned message or fragments, and run full phishing and URL analysis on nested content. A delivery-failure wrapper is not a trust grant for the payload inside it. The report covers abuse observed across more than 25 platforms and details the specific field-reflection mechanism defenders should validate at input and again at render time.

item.title: Keep Calm, and Patch PHP2Shell
item.description:
PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) are two CVSS 9.2 critical RCE flaws in PHP disclosed October 20, 2026, affecting virtually every PHP deployment serving web requests. Patches are available and exploitation is expected within 24-48 hours of disclosure.
Key findings:
- Both CVEs carry a CVSS 9.2 (Critical) rating under CVSS v4.0 and achieve unauthenticated RCE before application code executes. The attack surface is multipart/form-data parsing at the PHP layer itself, meaning CMS security plugins, WAF rules scoped to application endpoints, and authentication layers offer no protection. CVE-2026-109618 triggers via out-of-memory corruption during a brief window where request-scoped memory is reachable but uninitialized: any OOM event in that window causes PHP's shutdown routine to branch on the half-built state, reliably producing RCE. CVE-2026-109619 is a use-after-free: a fatal error (OOM, execution timeout, failed compile) leaves global state pointing to freed request memory, and a second HTTP request handled by the same worker can read or act on that stale pointer to achieve RCE. mod_php is considered the highest-risk configuration, but PHP-FPM, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed are all affected.
- Patched versions are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. PHP 8.1 and earlier are end-of-life and receive no official patch, though PHP published minimal source-backports for PHP 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1. Unconfirmed reports suggest the flaw may reach back to PHP 5. After patching, restart is mandatory: PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php workers, queue workers, schedulers, and daemons all continue running the vulnerable binary until explicitly restarted. Container images must be rebuilt and redeployed, not just updated on the host. Confirm the fix via package changelogs, not version strings, because distributions backport fixes without changing the upstream version number.
- If you cannot patch immediately, PHP's interim measures reduce but do not eliminate exposure. Block multipart/form-data at the web server before requests reach PHP, covering all HTTP methods (PHP 8.4+ parses multipart bodies on methods beyond POST). For CVE-2026-109618: set memory_limit=-1 via php_admin_value in the FPM pool or Apache config (not overridable by the application), set a low post_max_size, and keep upload_max_filesize below post_max_size. For CVE-2026-109619: set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 in php.ini or the FPM pool config before request parsing begins; on PHP 8.5 also set fatal_error_backtraces=0. All of these require a worker restart to take effect. Systems on PHP older than 7.4 with no patch path should be isolated from public networks or taken offline.
- The forensic baseline starts at October 20, 2026, 15:00 UTC, when leaked details began circulating. Hunt for: PHP worker child processes (PHP-FPM, Apache) spawning shells or download utilities; unexplained worker crashes or segmentation faults in PHP-FPM and web server logs; anomalous multipart/form-data requests to endpoints that do not accept uploads; new or modified files in web roots, upload directories, plugin directories, and mu-plugins; changes to .user.ini files or the auto_prepend_file setting; and new persistence indicators including cron entries, systemd units, SSH authorized_keys additions, newly created application admin accounts, and unexpected outbound connections from PHP service accounts.
Preserve web server and PHP logs from October 20, 2026, 15:00 UTC onward before patching, redeploying, or rotating logs. Container rebuilds and redeployments will destroy the forensic baseline needed for a compromise assessment. Pull and archive those logs first, then patch. No vendor-published IOCs exist yet as of the report's writing, so behavioral hunting against the signals above is your primary detection mechanism. The GuidePoint GRIT team states updated IOCs will be published as the situation develops.

item.title: ARTEX in the Wild: Storm-0940 Expands Targeting of IT and Software Vendors
item.description:
Storm-0940 is deploying ARTEX, a Chinese-developed autonomous AI pentesting agent, against IT and software vendors throughout October 2026, targeting Okta, Entra ID, and AWS Cognito in what looks like staged supply chain compromise groundwork.
Key findings:
- ARTEX is an open-source agentic framework published to GitHub in July 2026 by a Chinese 🇨🇳 developer. An operator gives it a target and objective, a planner agent selects next steps, and worker agents execute tools including nmap, curl, and Impacket. Every result feeds a shared asset graph, enabling fully automated chaining: source maps downloaded, internal API routes called by name minutes later, disposable accounts registered, then cross-tenant data immediately probed.
- The attack sequence is consistent across victims: fetch JavaScript bundles, exposed source maps, runtime configs, and Swagger/OpenAPI docs first; then probe OAuth callbacks by injecting fabricated authorization codes and malformed state parameters; then test unsigned JWTs with alg:none payloads across more than 60 SSO route variations in under two minutes; then password-spray Entra and Okta in coordinated bursts at a strict one-second interval, targeting software engineer accounts specifically, with some individual users hit more than a dozen times per session.
- In AWS Cognito logs, look for clusters of InitiateAuth, ForgotPassword, ResendConfirmationCode, and SignUp API calls originating from rotating user agents including boto and python-urllib strings. In Okta and Entra sign-in logs, the spray pattern is distinctive: highly regular one-second cadence, unique user-agent string per burst, 20-60 minute burst durations, then a new source IP within minutes of a block. One session ran 24-30 hours continuously.
- Across victims, more than 15 user-agent strings were observed: Python clients, curl, truncated Chrome strings, headless browsers with randomized version numbers, and self-describing identifiers including ReconProbe/1.0. The combination of consistent attack pattern, ARTEX-related tooling, and shared infrastructure is what connected activity across multiple organizations. The reconnaissance footprint also includes requests to /zzz-nonexistent-xyz123-style paths as baseline fingerprinting before fuzzing runs.
- The targeting scope is broader than initial access: the Wiz report describes the same actor pivoting infrastructure and TTPs toward the broader software vendor sector, indicating supply chain positioning rather than opportunistic credential theft. Most individual attempts failed, but the agentic model means the agent iterates indefinitely until it finds a single weak point, a fundamentally different threat model than a time-constrained human operator.
Hunt tip: query your identity provider logs for authentication bursts with sub-two-second median inter-request timing across distinct user agents from the same source IP range, specifically against /sso, /forgot_password, /api/v1/Users/GeneratePasswordResetToken, and OAuth callback endpoints. In HTTP access logs, flag sequential hits to .js.map, config.json, env.js, and openapi spec files from a single client within a short window, that recon chain is ARTEX's opening move. IOC details are in the Wiz report.

item.title: PHP2Shell Attacks Started Four Days Before Public Disclosure, AWS Reports
item.description:
PHP2Shell RCE exploitation began 4 days before public disclosure of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, with AWS MadPot honeypots catching attempts from anonymized infrastructure as early as October 17, 2026.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are two critical unauthenticated remote code execution flaws in the PHP runtime itself, not in any specific CMS. Updating WordPress, Drupal, or similar applications does nothing if the underlying PHP runtime remains unpatched. Fixed versions are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35, released October 21. AWS confirms no configuration-only workaround fully addresses both flaws, though temporarily blocking multipart file uploads may reduce immediate exposure for systems that cannot be patched right away.
- The attack timeline is the critical forensic detail here. AWS MadPot recorded the first exploitation attempt on October 17, 2026, four days before the embargo lifted. By October 21 starting around 02:00 UTC, roughly 12 hours before the scheduled 14:00 UTC public release, multiple proof-of-concept exploits appeared from varied payloads and different anonymization services, pointing to multiple independent actors. Broad exploitation followed within hours of the official advisory.
- The exploit mechanism involves a specially crafted POST request containing the string PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS in multipart form data. That string in web server logs is the primary hunting pattern AWS calls out. Investigators should review POST requests with that string, look for unexpected processes spawned by PHP, and check for unexplained file changes on web application servers, because an attacker who progressed past probing may leave process and filesystem artifacts beyond the initial HTTP request.
- AWS published six IP addresses tied to observed activity: 103.216.220[.]92 (October 17), 31.223.184[.]166, 37.19.200[.]5, 134.209.159[.]64, 103.114.163[.]188, and 95.217.98[.]37 (all October 21). AWS explicitly cautions that several belong to shared commercial anonymization infrastructure and are not exclusive to PHP2Shell traffic. Treat matches as leads for investigation, not automatic block candidates, and correlate with other behavioral indicators before acting.
- The broader DFIR lesson AWS draws is blunt: the public advisory date is not a safe starting point for scoping an incident. With pre-disclosure exploitation confirmed, any PHP2Shell investigation must begin its log review on October 17, 2026, not October 21. Detection tooling that relies on signatures released at or after disclosure will miss this window entirely.
Takeaway: Pull web server logs from October 17 onward and search for POST requests containing PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS in multipart form data. Follow any hits with process tree analysis looking for unexpected command interpreters or shells launched as PHP children, and audit file system changes on web application servers in that same window. Patch to the fixed PHP runtime first; no WAF or upload restriction substitutes for it. IOCs and further technical analysis are in the AWS report.

item.title: Unboxing Phishing Kits: Huntress Examines 3 Real Kits
item.description:
Modern phishing kits hand low-skilled attackers authenticated session tokens and persistent footholds, bypassing MFA entirely. Three real kits targeting Microsoft 365 show how commoditized this capability has become.
Key findings:
- Huntress researchers analyzed three phishing kits, all targeting Microsoft 365 tokens. EvilTokens used device-code phishing and abused Railway as a PaaS token-harvesting and replay engine before a Microsoft Digital Crimes Unit and FBI collaboration led to an operator arrest. Kali365 goes further: it is described as a full criminal ecosystem with an admin dashboard, AI features, and infrastructure acquisition built in, not just a fake login page.
- The kits support three modern credential-bypass techniques: device-code phishing (victim authenticates to the real identity provider while the attacker captures the authorization), adversary-in-the-middle phishing (attacker relays the full auth flow and captures the session cookie after MFA completes), and token theft with replay (the captured session token is replayed into live cloud access). All three techniques mean a completed MFA prompt does not make the resulting session trustworthy.
- Scope and prevalence: Huntress' ITDR team found that roughly one in six investigated incidents involved a rogue device being registered, a direct downstream artifact of device-code phishing abuse. Conditional Access Policies blocking device-code flow are the cited prevention control, with the report noting the vast majority of Microsoft environments have no legitimate need for it.
- Detection follows the chain, not a single signal. The report frames it clearly: lure, authentication event, token issuance or theft, device registration, then mailbox activity. Successful sign-ins from unfamiliar cloud infrastructure, device-code authentication flows, automated token refresh, new authentication methods, and new device registrations are the correlated signals. Audience polling placed sign-in address and new device registration as the top two investigative starting points when token theft is suspected.
- Containment scope is wider than most runbooks account for. Revoking the session is not enough if the attacker registered a device or set Windows Hello credentials. Response must include revoking refresh tokens, removing unauthorized devices and Windows Hello credentials, auditing mailbox forwarding rules and outbound phishing activity, and restricting device-code authentication. Critically, hunting should continue after the original phishing domain disappears, since the token or registered device may still provide re-entry.
DFIR takeaway: when you see a suspicious sign-in, pivot immediately to the identity provider logs and check for device registrations and new authentication methods added in the same window. Do not close the incident when you pull the phishing page down. The session artifact and any registered device outlive the lure and will be used for re-entry if not explicitly revoked and removed.

item.title: China-Aligned Bronze Sandcastle Abuses Sandboxie DLL Sideloading to Deploy Backdoors
item.description:
China-aligned Bronze Sandcastle abuses Sandboxie DLL sideloading across eight application combinations to deploy an in-memory backdoor against targets in Asia and Africa, active from mid-2025 through at least August 2026.
Key findings:
- Bronze Sandcastle plants a malicious sbiedll.dll alongside the legitimate, signed SandboxieWUAU.exe, causing the trusted process to load attacker-controlled code at runtime. Beyond Sandboxie, the group uses seven additional sideloading pairs: javaw.exe/jli.dll, Krita.exe/Krita.dll, NvdaHelper.exe/NvdaHelperRemote.dll, Jcef_helper.exe/Libcef.dll, Vmmap.exe/version.dll, LineAppMgr.exe/msvcp140.dll, and bginfo64.exe/snmpapi.dll. Renamed legitimate executables are dropped to help the chain blend into victim environments.
- The sideloaded DLL reads and decrypts a config.ini file on disk, then executes the payload entirely in memory, leaving minimal disk artifacts. Two payload versions have been identified: 1.1.5 and 1.1.7. item.title: Where to Find Linux auditd Logs and How to Export Them
item.description:
Linux auditd log location, export commands, and collection gaps explained for incident responders handling Linux endpoints without a SIEM pipeline in place.
Key findings:
- The authoritative record lives at /var/log/audit/audit.log, root-only, rotated by auditd itself into audit.log.1, audit.log.2, and so on per the max_log_file and num_logs settings in /etc/audit/auditd.conf. For collection, oldest-first concatenation with "sudo cat $(ls -tr /var/log/audit/audit.log*) > web-03_audit_all.log" preserves the full timeline across rotated files. Use ausearch with the --raw flag to keep the original multi-line event structure (SYSCALL, EXECVE, CWD, PATH, PROCTITLE records sharing a common msg=audit epoch:serial stamp) since the interpreted view loses fidelity.
- auditd is not installed by default on Debian-adjacent systems including Ubuntu. On those hosts, kernel audit events route to journald instead and "sudo journalctl _TRANSPORT=audit --since yesterday -o json --no-pager" recovers what exists. Without rules loaded, that output covers logins, authentication events, and SELinux or AppArmor denials but nothing for command execution or file access: the kernel never received an instruction to record them.
- Even on Red Hat-family systems where auditd installs by default, "sudo auditctl -l" returning "No rules" means you have baseline authentication visibility only. Command execution (T1059.004), SSH key manipulation (T1098.004), and permission changes on sensitive files (T1222.002) will not appear in the log unless explicit rules were configured beforehand. A "backlog limit exceeded" message in kernel logs means the kernel dropped events under load: treat that log as having gaps, not as complete.
- The ausearch time keywords "today", "yesterday", "this-week", and "recent" (last ten minutes) avoid locale-driven date format mismatches that silently return zero results. Explicit dates follow locale format, 10/19/2026 00:00:00 in en_US, which is the most common cause of "no matches" surprises during live response when time pressure is highest.
Practitioner takeaway: before you need it, verify coverage. On any Linux endpoint under scope, run "systemctl is-active auditd" and "sudo auditctl -l" to confirm both that the daemon is running and that exec and file-access rules are actually loaded. If rules are absent, document the gap in your case notes: the absence of command execution records is not evidence nothing ran, it is evidence the host was not instrumented. For collection, --raw ausearch output is the artifact to preserve; the journal JSON route is the fallback, not the equivalent. Both should be hashed at collection time.
