item.title: Where to Find Sysmon Logs on Windows and How to Export Them
item.description:
Sysmon log location, export commands, and the event IDs that matter most when you pull a Windows host for investigation. A practical reference for any responder who needs to recover what Sysmon recorded before it overwrites.
Key findings:
- The Sysmon log lives at C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs\Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon%4Operational.evtx. In Event Viewer the path is Applications and Services Logs > Microsoft > Windows > Sysmon > Operational. Confirm the service is running with "sc query sysmon64" (or "sysmon" on 32-bit) and look for STATE: RUNNING. If the channel does not exist, Sysmon is not installed and you have no log to pull.
- Export from an elevated prompt with: wevtutil epl "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" C:\logs\sysmon.evtx. You can scope the export to the last 24 hours or to a single event ID during collection. On a busy server with a default channel size, that log can cover surprisingly little time, so run "wevtutil gl Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" and check maxSize before you assume you have full coverage.
- The event IDs that carry the most investigative weight: Event ID 1 (process creation with full command line, hashes, and parent) is the backbone of almost every investigation. ID 10 (process access) flags one process opening another, and access to lsass.exe is the classic credential-dumping signal. IDs 12, 13, and 14 cover registry changes including Run key persistence. ID 22 ties a DNS query to the process that made it. IDs 4 and 16 record Sysmon's own service state and config changes, which is where you look when events simply stop: an attacker turning Sysmon off or neutering its config leaves a trace right there.
- Sysmon only records what its configuration tells it to. A host with no config file gives you a limited default set built around process creation. No network events in the log does not mean no network activity occurred: it likely means event ID 3 was excluded in the config, which is common because of volume. Pull the running config with "sysmon64 -c" and send it alongside the EVTX export so the analyst understands the gaps, not just the events that are present.
- If events stop at a point in time, check for event IDs 4 and 16 immediately before the gap, then cross-reference the Windows System log for the Sysmon service being stopped or uninstalled. A gap with no service stop entry and no config change event suggests log rollover, in which case check maxSize and go to your SIEM for older data.
Takeaway: before you collect, run "wevtutil gl Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" to understand how far back the log actually goes, then "sysmon64 -c" to capture the active config. Export both together. The config output is what turns a confusing gap in coverage into an explainable artifact rather than a missing piece of the timeline.

item.title: How to Enable and Export PowerShell Script Block Logs
item.description:
PowerShell Script Block Logging (Event 4104) is one of the highest-value artifacts on a Windows host. Here is exactly how to verify it, export it, and avoid the gaps that trip up responders.
Key details:
- Script block logs live at Applications and Services Logs > Microsoft > Windows > PowerShell > Operational, as Event ID 4104. Verify the setting is actually on before you trust the log: query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging and confirm EnableScriptBlockLogging is 0x1. If the key is absent, logging is off. Windows PowerShell 5.1 still auto-logs blocks it deems suspicious as 4104 Warning-level events without the policy set, but those are partial captures, not the full picture. Do not treat a handful of Warning-level 4104s as evidence that full logging is active.
- Export the operational log with wevtutil epl "Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational" C:\logs\ps_4104.evtx. Add the query filter /q:"*[System[(EventID=4104)]]" if you want script blocks only. Do not stop there: also pull the classic "Windows PowerShell" log with wevtutil epl "Windows PowerShell" C:\logs\windows_powershell.evtx. Event 400 in that channel records every engine start with the host command line and the engine version. An EngineVersion of 2.0 on a modern system is a strong indicator of deliberate downgrading to evade script block logging, a technique responders need to catch at triage.
- PowerShell 7 is a separate product with a separate channel, PowerShellCore/Operational, and its own policy key at HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\PowerShellCore. If PowerShell 7 was installed from a zip rather than the MSI, its event channel may not be registered at all until RegisterManifest.ps1 is run from $PSHOME. Responders investigating a host with both versions installed need to check and export both channels independently.
- Script block logging records the code as compiled, after obfuscation layers are peeled away. When a malicious script builds and executes the next stage, that decoded stage gets its own 4104 event, often in readable plaintext. This is why it matters for T1059.001, T1027, and T1105 download cradle activity. The tradeoff: Protected Event Logging encrypts 4104 content as ciphertext. If you pull a log and the text is unreadable, the decryption certificate is required to recover it.
- Volume and secrets are the two operational hazards. Every script and module execution generates events, so the default channel size fills in hours on busy hosts. Raise the maximum log size before deployment or you will lose early-incident activity. Admin scripts frequently embed passwords and API keys in plaintext, and script block logging records them faithfully. Treat exported EVTX files from production systems with the same handling controls as credential material before sharing or uploading.
Takeaway: on any Windows incident, confirm 4104 logging status via the registry key before drawing conclusions from the log. Pull all three channels: PowerShell/Operational, Windows PowerShell, and PowerShellCore/Operational if PowerShell 7 is present. Hunt Event 400 for EngineVersion 2.0 as a downgrade indicator. The SOCPrime report notes 663 detection rules mapped to 417 MITRE ATT&CK techniques covering this log source, available in their platform.

item.title: LiteLLM release pipeline hacked to distribute info-stealer malware
item.description:
LiteLLM's PyPI release pipeline was compromised on Oct 21, pushing a credential-stealing payload to 92 million monthly download users via version 1.107.0 for roughly two hours.
Key details:
- The attacker modified only the installation package, placing three malicious files: cook.pth, cook[.]py, and sitecustomize[.]py into Python's library directory. Python processes .pth files and imports sitecustomize at startup, so the payload fires before the application on every Python launch, including when running pip or python to investigate the compromise. That means standard triage steps can re-trigger the malware.
- Affected artifacts have precise timestamps responders need for scoping: all seven PyPI wheels for litellm==1.107.0 were live from 11:39:51 to 13:23 UTC Oct 21. Docker Hub tags v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, and main-stable pointed to compromised image index sha256:1bbcb1443bc962e45f5aad53fe3d2c330600e0379715fb6c664cdd3ac126c339e from 11:46:56 to 14:20 UTC. GHCR tags for the same names pointed to three compromised image digests from 11:46:56 until ~13:51 UTC.
- The payload targeted an unusually wide credential surface: AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, Docker, and IaC secrets; AI provider credentials and LiteLLM model configs; Git, GitHub, npm, PyPI, and CI/CD tokens; .env files; SSH, GPG, and TLS private keys; browser login databases, cookies, and autofill data; environment variables, shell history, and system/network info. All exfiltrated data is AES-256-CBC encrypted under an RSA-4096 key and sent to litellm[.]dev/healthcheck.
- sitecustomize[.]py also drops a detached hourly loader that polls a GitHub-hosted pointer and pulls down arbitrary Python for execution, giving the attacker persistent RCE even after the malicious package is removed. Deleting the LiteLLM package directory alone does not eliminate this loader.
- This is the second supply-chain hit on LiteLLM in 2026. The March incident involved the TeamPCP group gaining access through Aqua Security's Trivy scanner in LiteLLM's CI/CD pipeline. Two compromises in seven months against one of the most widely deployed AI gateway libraries signals a sustained, targeted pattern against this project's release infrastructure.
DFIR takeaway: Do not run Python or pip on a potentially affected host; isolate it first. Check for the presence of cook.pth, cook[.]py, and sitecustomize[.]py in the Python library directory of any environment that pulled litellm==1.107.0 or ran the affected Docker tags during that UTC window. Look for outbound connections to litellm[.]dev and for any hourly scheduled or detached Python processes polling GitHub. Because the loader survives package removal, full host rebuild from a clean baseline is the only safe recovery path. Rotate every secret, token, and key accessible from affected environments immediately. The safe rollback version is litellm==1.106.2.

item.title: Detecting Compromised eMudhra Certificates with Zeek
item.description:
Indian 🇮🇳 CA eMudhra accidentally issued 8 intermediate certificates with weak private keys in April 2025, allowing anyone to mint valid TLS certs for any hostname on the internet.
Key details:
- eMudhra, an Indian 🇮🇳 Certificate Authority, issued 8 intermediate certificates with trivially guessable private keys, at least one of which is literally the integer 4. Six were valid for TLS; two for code signing. Because the private keys are public knowledge, any attacker can generate a trusted certificate for any domain, enabling transparent MitM, credential theft, or malware delivery against clients that still trust the compromised intermediates.
- Major browsers responded quickly: Chrome added the certificates to its CRLSet and Mozilla pushed them to OneCRL. But embedded devices, end-of-life Linux distributions, offline systems, and any software using the Mozilla root store without auto-update remain exposed. The eMudhra root was admitted to the Mozilla CA database in 2019, making the trust chain wide and the blast radius significant.
- Detection at the network layer is possible for TLS 1.2 and below because certificates appear in the clear during the handshake. TLS 1.3 encrypts the handshake, so passive inspection cannot see the certificate there, but any client that negotiates TLS 1.2 or lower will still reveal it. The Corelight Open Source team built a Zeek package that fires four notices in notice.log: Compromised_Intermediate_Cert, Compromised_Intermediate_Cert_Established, Compromised_Intermediate_Issuer, and Compromised_Intermediate_Issuer_Established.
- The detection logic matches on the SHA-256 hash of the Subject Public Key Info (SPKI) rather than a certificate fingerprint. This matters: ECDSA signatures used by these intermediates are malleable and can be encoded two valid ways, so fingerprint-only matching can be evaded. SPKI matching also catches cross-signed variants, which eMudhra used, and resists evasion through X.509 parser leniencies.
- The second notice pair covers a subtler evasion: a server can send only the end-entity certificate and omit the intermediate entirely. Some clients cache or pre-load intermediate CAs and will still validate and accept the connection. Zeek's Compromised_Intermediate_Issuer notices catch this by matching the issuer field even when the intermediate certificate itself never appears in the handshake.
For retroactive hunting in existing Zeek data, the report describes two paths: check the cert_chain_fps column in ssl.log or the fingerprint column in x509.log for SHA-256 certificate hashes, or match the issuer field in ssl.log against the affected CA names. The report points to a public JSON dataset at emudhra.we-have-a-problem[.]com/impacted-intermediates.json, queryable with jq, that provides the SHA-256 hashes and issuer names needed for both hunts. Note that Zeek does not log SPKI hashes by default, so historical searches must rely on those certificate-level hashes rather than the more evasion-resistant SPKI values the live detector uses.

Indian 🇮🇳 CA eMudhra accidentally issued 8 intermediate certificates with weak private keys in April 2025, allowing anyone to mint valid TLS certs for any hostname on the internet.

Key details:

- eMudhra, an Indian 🇮🇳 Certificate Authority, issued 8 intermediate certificates with trivially guessable private keys, at least one of which is literally the integer 4. Six were valid for TLS; two for code signing. Because the private keys are public knowledge, any attacker can generate a trusted certificate for any domain, enabling transparent MitM, credential theft, or malware delivery against clients that still trust the compromised intermediates.

- Major browsers responded quickly: Chrome added the certificates to its CRLSet and Mozilla pushed them to OneCRL. But embedded devices, end-of-life Linux distributions, offline systems, and any software using the Mozilla root store without auto-update remain exposed. The eMudhra root was admitted to the Mozilla CA database in 2019, making the trust chain wide and the blast radius significant.

- Detection at the network layer is possible for TLS 1.2 and below because certificates appear in the clear during the handshake. TLS 1.3 encrypts the handshake, so passive inspection cannot see the certificate there, but any client that negotiates TLS 1.2 or lower will still reveal it. The Corelight Open Source team built a Zeek package that fires four notices in notice.log: Compromised_Intermediate_Cert, Compromised_Intermediate_Cert_Established, Compromised_Intermediate_Issuer, and Compromised_Intermediate_Issuer_Established.

- The detection logic matches on the SHA-256 hash of the Subject Public Key Info (SPKI) rather than a certificate fingerprint. This matters: ECDSA signatures used by these intermediates are malleable and can be encoded two valid ways, so fingerprint-only matching can be evaded. SPKI matching also catches cross-signed variants, which eMudhra used, and resists evasion through X.509 parser leniencies.

- The second notice pair covers a subtler evasion: a server can send only the end-entity certificate and omit the intermediate entirely. Some clients cache or pre-load intermediate CAs and will still validate and accept the connection. Zeek's Compromised_Intermediate_Issuer notices catch this by matching the issuer field even when the intermediate certificate itself never appears in the handshake.

For retroactive hunting in existing Zeek data, the report describes two paths: check the cert_chain_fps column in ssl.log or the fingerprint column in x509.log for SHA-256 certificate hashes, or match the issuer field in ssl.log against the affected CA names. The report points to a public JSON dataset at emudhra.we-have-a-problem[.]com/impacted-intermediates.json, queryable with jq, that provides the SHA-256 hashes and issuer names needed for both hunts. Note that Zeek does not log SPKI hashes by default, so historical searches must rely on those certificate-level hashes rather than the more evasion-resistant SPKI values the live detector uses.

item.title: Beyond the Sandbox: Leveraging Android Intrusion Logs to Expose Advanced Threats
item.description:
Android's new Intrusion Logging feature exposes the full RatHat kill chain, from ADB self-pairing to C2 egress, giving BYOD defenders OS-generated forensic timelines that were previously only available to enterprise MDM deployments.
Key findings:
- Android Intrusion Logging, introduced in 2026 as part of Advanced Protection, captures SecurityLog-derived security events, DNS events, and connection events on supported Pixel devices running Android 16 or later. Logs are encrypted on-device using keys tied to the user's Google Account and screen lock, stored for 12 months, and decryptable only by the device owner. Critically, the user must opt in before an incident at Settings > Security & privacy > Advanced Protection > Intrusion Logging or evidence will not be preserved.
- RatHat (package com.wkfuhirj.lchmwg, UID 10023, SHA-256 bdfccc6ab3e592f6cfc47f6deb910950666fa47b5f87c6a08af7096d90e59d0f) breaks the Android application sandbox using Accessibility abuse and autonomous Wireless Debugging self-pairing. Within milliseconds of launch, the OS log records zygote forking two watchdog processes (com.wkfuhirj.lchmwg:guard1 and com.wkfuhirj.lchmwg:guard2) and a key_generated event for cipher_aes_key, the symmetric key used to encrypt harvested lock-screen PINs and stolen credentials before exfiltration. Static analysis alone would not surface whether this sequence actually ran.
- The loopback connection log is the pivot point of the chain. The malware probes 127.0.0.1:27042 for a live Frida server (anti-analysis check), then authenticates against the Wireless Debugging pairing port (41625) and connects to the ADB daemon port (35933) to obtain a UID 2000 shell. The subsequent adb_shell_cmd events in the security log record exact commands: the malware copies liblocal-service[.]so out of its APK native library path and stages it as /data/local/tmp/local-service, drops frpc_stage.tmp from /storage/emulated/0/Android/data/com.wkfuhirj.lchmwg/files/ to /data/local/tmp/frpc, applies chmod 777 to both, then adds itself to the device idle whitelist, sets its standby bucket to active, and whitelists UID 10023 from background network restrictions. These are verbatim log entries, not inferences.
- Once daemons are running, the Java layer communicates with the local Go agent over 127.0.0.1:7912 at short intervals (IPC outside normal Android framework APIs), while DNS events show resolution of fegrs.adidasabc[.]com resolving to 8.231.120[.]246:443 for external C2 heartbeats every 60-90 seconds. The malware simultaneously issues DNS queries to www.apps.disneyplus[.]com, disney.api.edge.bamgrid[.]com, and login.disney[.]com as a streaming lure rendered through embedded Chromium WebView to distract the user.
- Enterprise managed devices get equivalent telemetry through Android's Delegated Scope, which grants a security application access to OS-level Security and Network Logs without transferring MDM authority. Intrusion Logging extends a comparable capability to BYOD and personal devices via a consent-driven archive. The forensic value is the same: package-attributed DNS queries (no more orphan hostnames), exact ADB commands with timestamps, process start events with SHA-256 hashes, and loopback connection records that map the self-pairing sequence.
DFIR takeaway: If you receive a RatHat-suspected device, the Intrusion Log bundle will confirm or deny the pairing sequence via loopback connection events to high-range dynamic ports and adb_shell_cmd entries staging binaries into /data/local/tmp. Hunt the log for the cipher_aes_key key_generated event (confirms credential encryption initialized), the 27042 Frida probe (confirms anti-analysis ran), and package-attributed DNS queries to fegrs.adidasabc[.]com. Verify whether /data/local/tmp/local-service and /data/local/tmp/frpc are present. IOCs for RatHat are in the Zimperium report.

item.title: Cold Chain, Open Control: Exposed Refrigeration Systems Reveal Global Risk
item.description:
Refrigeration management systems across 700+ French 🇫🇷 supermarkets were compromised in October 2026, with attackers manipulating temperature and defrost controls to cause food losses at scale.
Key findings:
- The confirmed affected systems were Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC, Copeland and Dixell XWEB. This is not a new threat: pro-Russian hacktivist groups Z-Pentest Alliance and NoName057(16) claimed over 20 refrigeration attacks since January 2026, mostly targeting fruit storage, wineries, and food processors across Spain 🇪🇸, Italy 🇮🇹, and other European countries. On April 26 alone, Z-Pentest claimed 10 separate hits. The attack method in each case was the same: changing temperature and defrost settings via exposed HMIs, using legitimate supervisory functions.
- Forescout's global exposure scan found 12,976 service observations across 6,017 distinct public IPs in 99 countries. The two attack paths are weak or absent authentication (only 287 of 513 pCOWeb services returned HTTP 401 responses) and known unpatched vulnerabilities. Danfoss AK-SM 800 is end-of-life since May 2021 with no patch path. For AK-SM 800A, 80% of exposed StoreView services run firmware older than 4.3.1, leaving them exposed to CVE-2025-41451 and CVE-2025-41452. Copeland XWEB Pro has 23 known vulnerabilities below firmware 1.13. CAREL products carry 11 known vulnerabilities across boss, boss mini, and pCOWeb.
- Initial access methods and responsible actors in the French 🇫🇷 incidents remain unconfirmed. Manufacturer documentation for both Danfoss AK-SM and Copeland XWEB explicitly supported direct internet exposure, port forwarding, and HTTP access for remote maintenance, meaning many installations are intentionally reachable. This creates a fractured ownership model: contractors manage the refrigeration platform, facilities teams own hardware, IT manages the network path, and no single party sees the full picture.
- Beyond setpoints, devices like CAREL pCOWeb and XWEB Pro expose Modbus-readable and writable variables, widening the impact potential. Rapid successive configuration changes observed in France 🇫🇷 suggest automation, meaning attackers scripted supervisory API calls rather than making manual adjustments, and those changes can blend into routine contractor activity with no obvious alert.
For responders and operators: the audit gap here is the correlation problem. A supervisory session log may not record which setpoint changed; a controller alarm may not identify the account behind it. Hunting for this activity means correlating remote-access session timestamps against defrost schedule changes, temperature setpoint modifications, alarm suppressions, and user account changes in the controller audit log. Review NAT and port-forwarding rules for port 80 and 443 terminating at refrigeration management interfaces. Prioritize replacing Danfoss AK-SM 800 (no patch exists) and patching AK-SM 800A to firmware 4.3.1 or later. The Forescout report details the full vulnerability table by product family.

item.title: PHP2SHELL Detection Coverage in THOR
item.description:
PHP2SHELL (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) targets PHP memory corruption and stale global state. Nextron details existing and new Sigma and YARA coverage, and the forensic gaps that logging gaps create.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 cover out-of-memory corruption and stale global state in PHP respectively. As of 22 October 2026, trusted sources report that exploitation remains possible after the initial fixes, meaning patching alone does not close the window. The PHP advisory explicitly warns that affected paths may lack predictable log entries, so an absence of findings does not rule out compromise.
- Eight Sigma rules were already in place before PHP2SHELL was published, covering web-server processes spawning shells, download tools, and reconnaissance utilities on both Linux and Windows. The report estimates existing generic rules cover roughly 50 to 70 percent of early post-exploitation activity encountered, an experience-based figure drawn from past outbreaks including NetScaler compromises. New PHP2SHELL-specific additions are proposed in SigmaHQ PR #6506, which was open as of 22 October 2026. That PR updates six existing rules and adds one new rule: "PHP Memory Corruption Log: Potential Php2shell Indicators", targeting PHP fatal memory-exhaustion errors referencing rfc1867.c or Unknown on line 0, and session-open warnings containing /ndary=, sess_, and related terms.
- Four private YARA rules ship with the detection update: LOG_PHP2SHELL_Artifacts_Oct26_1, LOG_PHP2SHELL_Artifacts_Oct26, LOG_SUSP_PHP2SHELL_Artifacts_Oct26, and LOG_PHP_Exploitation_Indicators_Oct26. These target log artifacts and suspicious PHP activity rather than binary samples.
- The critical forensic gap is logging configuration. Apache's common and combined access-log formats do not capture Content-Type or Cookie headers, so multipart boundaries and session identifiers carried in those headers are invisible to request-level matching. PHP error logs are different and may contain upload-processing or session-path artifacts even when request headers are absent. Responders must verify log_errors, error_log, and Apache's LogLevel settings and confirm those logs are actually present and in scope for the scan. Process-event logs are equally essential: without parent-process and command-line fields, the Sigma rules covering apache2 spawning sh -c "id" or similar patterns cannot fire.
- Mitigation context matters for triage. The report details several configuration controls including setting memory_limit=-1 to remove the controllable memory-limit failure, disabling session.upload_progress.enabled, and on PHP 8.5 setting fatal_error_backtraces=0. None is described as complete protection against every variant, and the advisory specifically warns against RLIMIT_AS and RLIMIT_DATA because they can force the allocation failure that reaches the vulnerable path.
Practitioner takeaway: Before scanning, audit the effective PHP and Apache logging configuration for every serving pool and virtual host. Confirm error logs are routing to disk and are reachable. Preserve logs from before patching because remediation does not erase the need to investigate prior activity. Treat a memory-exhaustion error or Apache worker crash as a weak signal requiring correlation with child-process events, outbound connections, and persistence artifacts before drawing a conclusion. The new Sigma rule and the four YARA rules are in the report and in SigmaHQ PR #6506.

item.title: PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619): Detecting unauthenticated remote code execution in PHP core
item.description:
PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, CVSS v4.0 9.2 each) enables unauthenticated RCE in PHP core via memory-safety bugs dating to 2012. Exploitation was confirmed in the wild before the patch shipped, and working PoCs are circulating.
Key details:
- Four use-after-free and type-confusion bugs share a single root cause: when a PHP worker hits memory_limit and triggers a fatal out-of-memory error, it destroys the request heap but does not clear global pointers into it. The next request on the same worker inherits stale pointers into freed memory. CVE-2026-109618 abuses session upload progress (enabled by default, runs before any application code, requires no session_start() call) to trigger a use-after-free in the unserializer and to leak freed heap contents into the PHPSESSID response cookie, returning other users' credentials, session tokens, API keys, and potentially TLS private keys to an unauthenticated caller. CVE-2026-109619 covers a use-after-free in fatal-error backtraces and an OPcache type-confusion bug. Every web-facing SAPI is in scope: Apache mod_php, PHP-FPM, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. Default configuration is vulnerable. No application bug is needed.
- The timeline is the core DFIR pressure point. Amazon Threat Intelligence observed a PHP2Shell attempt against MadPot honeypots on October 17, four days before disclosure. Cloudflare logged attacks on October 21 at 07:43 UTC, more than six hours before the emergency release at 14:00 UTC. The CVE IDs and exploit details leaked to Hacker News on October 20, compressing the coordinated disclosure window by two days. Your investigation window opens October 17, not October 21.
- The bug lives in the PHP engine, not in application code. WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla sites with clean application logic are still fully exposed. Distribution vendors received patches before public release and often backport fixes without changing the upstream version number, so php -v is not a reliable exposure check. Verify against the vendor advisory and the installed package version.
- Post-exploitation follows the standard web-shell playbook: reverse shell, tool download and execution, credential theft from the container environment, and a path to the host via kernel LPE. The memory disclosure is independent of RCE and requires no code execution at all, so secrets should be rotated for any exposed server even if you see no shell activity. In a containerized environment, a compromised PHP worker exposes the container's service account, mounted secrets, and internal network position.
Practitioner takeaway: Patch to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35 and restart every PHP worker. Patching without a restart leaves old workers running vulnerable code in memory. If you cannot patch today, set memory_limit=-1 via php_admin_value, set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 in php.ini or the FPM pool config, and on PHP 8.5 also set fatal_error_backtraces=0, then restart every worker and verify values through a web request, not the CLI. For detection, Falco can observe what the exploit causes on the host rather than the HTTP request itself: look for shell processes spawned by PHP web worker processes as a post-exploitation signal. Investigate from October 17 forward. Hunt for web shells, new cron jobs, new accounts, and shells spawned by the web server process. Rotate secrets on any exposed server regardless of whether code execution is confirmed, because the memory disclosure path hands heap contents to unauthenticated callers silently.

item.title: SEO Poisoning Campaign Delivers New Armorsteal Malware
item.description:
Armorsteal, a new Python-based infostealer, is hitting users via SEO-poisoned results for Chocolatey and Microsoft Activation Scripts, deploying three modules: remote access, surveillance, and credential theft.
- SEO poisoning drove victims to typosquatted sites choclatey[.]org and massgravel[.]net, which displayed fake PowerShell install commands. Running the command silently downloaded install.ps1 (hashes f3846ec2 and fb11811 in the IOC table), which dropped a ZIP archive to C:\Windows\SystemHealth\Update\ containing a full Python 3.11 runtime and Pyarmor-obfuscated scripts. The legitimate target software also installed to avoid suspicion. Both lure sites went offline by early October 2026.
- Persistence lands via two scheduled tasks: SysCheck2 (user logon, highest privilege) and SysCheckX (system boot as SYSTEM, 45-second delay), both launching SysMon[.]py from C:\Windows\SystemHealth\Update\. item.title: PHP2Shell Exploit Tooling Found on Exposed Attacker Server
item.description:
PHP2Shell exploit tooling recovered from an exposed attacker staging server reveals a lab-tested RCE chain targeting PHP 8.4.26 under mod_php, with live screening traffic reaching roughly 20 sites across Europe, North America, and Asia.
Key findings:
- The central file, aslr_exploit.py, is a Python "one-click" exploit for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 that works over plain HTTP in three steps: recycling a PHP worker process, leaking memory addresses through the session cookie to bypass ASLR, then abusing PHP's session upload progress handler to execute a shell command. Two calibration profiles are included, one for the official PHP 8.4.26 Apache container image and one for a custom lab build, both targeting local containers, which confirms the operator tested this chain before pointing it at live infrastructure. The exploit requires display_errors on, session.upload_progress enabled, session.use_strict_mode off, a low memory limit, and a single Apache worker process. None of the 11 probed production sites met all those conditions, so no shell access was achieved.
- Three companion scripts extended the operation from the lab to the internet. php2shell_fp.py fingerprinted roughly 20 sites by reading PHP version from X-Powered-By and Server response headers and probing for session upload progress behavior with a small multipart request. deep_probe.py then drilled into 11 of those sites, requesting pages designed to trigger PHP warnings, querying six common phpinfo paths, testing 11 parameters for file inclusion, and uploading files named MARKER_ followed by eight hex characters to test session injection. A third script, wp_attack.py, pivoted to WordPress targets and enumerated users via the REST API, checked for roughly two dozen plugins, and probed XML-RPC and exposed debug logs. All screening traffic routed through a rotating proxy pool on the same server (T1090).
- Six of the 11 deeply probed sites ran PHP 8.4 releases older than the fixed version, four of them on 8.4.26 itself. The targets included a university, nonprofits, and small businesses. None exposed errors, a phpinfo page, a file inclusion flaw, or echoed the test session. Beyond PHP2Shell, other artifacts on the same server indicate the operator harvests API keys and backend URLs from client-side JavaScript, sweeps admin and API endpoints for unauthenticated access, uses automated CAPTCHA solving, and conducts web-archive reconnaissance. Attribution remains open, but the cryptocurrency and Web3 focus across the broader toolset suggests financial motivation.
- The attacker staging server is 206.188.197[.]105. The open directory listing was on port 9999, the rotating proxy pool on port 8899, and an out-of-band interaction listener on port 8888. IOCs including session ID prefixes (fprint, dp) and the MARKER_ upload filename pattern are in the report, mapped to MITRE techniques T1587.004, T1592.002, T1595.002, T1090, and T1190.
Practitioner takeaway: Block 206.188.197[.]105 at the perimeter now and search web server and proxy logs for past connections to any of its three active ports. In web logs, hunt for multipart POST requests carrying a PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS field, particularly uploads with filenames matching MARKER_ followed by eight hex characters, and requests with session ID prefixes fprint or dp from sources you do not recognize. On the server side, set display_errors off, session.use_strict_mode=1, session.upload_progress.enabled off, expose_php off, and remove any public phpinfo pages. Then patch: fixed releases are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. Hardened config slowed this operator; patching removes the underlying risk.

item.title: StealC Is Back, and This Time It's a RAT
item.description:
StealC's seller is back four months after Operation Endgame dismantled its infrastructure, rebranding as Stadia, a full RAT with HVNC, remote shell, and in-memory loading, with the StealC stealer still wired in as one of six modules.
- Operation Endgame (June 2026) seized 326 servers and 142 domains tied to StealC, recovered 25 million credentials from 385,000 machines, and effectively killed the operation. By October 16, the same seller was back under the name Stadia, offering former StealC customers a free month on the $900/mo Pro tier to migrate. The panel hit version 1.1.2, with the first beta logged September 10 and the StealC 3.5 stealer module merged in by September 29. The four-month rebuild shows how fast a seller with existing code and a customer base can reconstitute after infrastructure seizure.
- Stadia is a platform, not a stealer. The six modules cover HVNC (shared and hidden desktop with full input injection), Remote CMD, File Explorer, Process Manager, an in-memory Loader accepting EXE, PowerShell, BAT/CMD, and MSI, and the StealC-derived grabber harvesting 50+ browsers, 120+ crypto plugins, 50+ desktop wallets, Telegram, Discord, Steam, Outlook, Thunderbird, and VPN clients. The seller's own demo panel showed 596 hosts, with infections mapped across South and Southeast Asia, Africa, and Latin America.
- The binary (stadia_x32.exe, SHA-256 ea928494fd30d88b98141d39a502a4324889fb732e74b44bfee12c72137dd73e, 560,128 bytes, unsigned PE32, MSVC, no packer) decrypts to build marker STADIA_BETA. The code link to StealC is byte-exact: a 26,112-byte Chromium App-Bound Encryption helper blob at file offset 0x77D48 carries SHA-256 0e5337a4cc8ebc772bc50f6e79befd1e8efad3410022e050d08d5269733c4ea4, identical at the same offset in both StealC v3.5 x86 and x64 builds. Nearly all strings are RC4-encrypted using a per-build key at file offset 0x6B1A0, then Base64-encoded; the outer RC4 key in this build is eepkTOgSwdNCgrhITR. The locale gate exits on Russian 🇷🇺, Ukrainian 🇺🇦, Belarusian 🇧🇾, Kazakh 🇰🇿, and Uzbek language IDs (0x0419, 0x0422, 0x0423, 0x043F, 0x0443).
- C2 uses plain HTTP POST to the root path of three hard-coded bare IPs tried in fixed failover order: hxxp://93.152.213[.]215/, hxxp://91.92.43[.]45/, hxxp://193.148.56[.]97/. The body is RC4-encrypted JSON then Base64-encoded, but the Content-Type header still claims application/json. That mismatch is a detection signal independent of IP blocklists, which only cover one build. Persistence drops the agent to C:\ProgramData\<12-char-random>\<name>.exe using one of nine masquerade names (RuntimeBroker.exe, MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.exe, GoogleUpdate.exe, and six others), registers a COM-based hidden scheduled task running every 15 minutes for 3,650 days (schtasks.exe-based rules will miss it), and on elevated runs adds a Defender exclusion via powershell.exe Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath for the install directory. The single-instance mutex is Local\<username>.<computername>.
Practitioner takeaway: hunt three behavioral clusters together. First, an unsigned process under C:\ProgramData\ spawning Chrome, Edge, or Brave suspended and writing a ~26 KB code block into it, followed by a transient GUID-named .txt file in C:\ProgramData\ holding a 64-character hex string, which is the App-Bound key dump. Second, a COM-registered hidden scheduled task with a PT15M interval and P3650D duration, not created via schtasks.exe. Third, powershell.exe invoking Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath pointing into C:\ProgramData\. On the wire, flag HTTP POST to a bare IP on port 80 where Content-Type is application/json but the body is Base64 ciphertext. The Varonis report includes a Sigma rule for the scheduled task and the full IOC table.

item.title: M365 Token Spray and Replay Campaign Compromises Business Email Accounts
item.description:
A 10-week M365 token spray campaign hit 79 organizations across 497 successful sign-ins without ever needing a password, bypassing MFA entirely through AiTM relay capture and automated OAuth token replay.
Key findings:
- The attacker operated in two tiers: AiTM relays (including 185.238.2[.]195 and Evoxt host 2400:8d60:2::1:841d:5dd) captured post-MFA session tokens from victims on fake sign-in pages or through device-code phishing, then replay hosts in the 193.26.115[.]0/24 block (AS210558, 1337 Services GmbH) automated the OAuth2:Token exchanges within minutes. On July 21 the gap between MFA capture and session hijack was 12 minutes; by September 22 it was four. Two distinct toolsets ran in parallel: Build A used a node user agent with Microsoft Office and Microsoft Authentication Broker client IDs (d3590ed6-52b3-4102-aeff-aad2292ab01c and 29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e) targeting Microsoft Graph and Exchange via OAuth2:Token requests; Build B replayed browser sessions through OfficeHome (client ID 4765445b-32c6-49b0-83e6-1d93765276ca) using current Chrome/Edge user agents and Login:reprocess requests.
- Persistence was layered and durable. The attacker registered 48 rogue Entra-joined devices named DESKTOP- plus exactly eight uppercase hex characters (e.g., DESKTOP-54521F46), a pattern that differs from Windows' own default of seven alphanumeric characters. In 19 organizations, the victim's existing MFA methods were wiped and a new authenticator registered under a label like "iPhone 13" within three hours of first access. A rogue MFA method survives a password reset; a rogue device survives session revocation. Both require explicit auditing and removal.
- Post-compromise mailbox manipulation was designed to stay invisible. Hidden inbox rules with names like ".", "sss", "s", and "d" moved or deleted mail mentioning payroll, direct deposit, bank, or bonus, and hid responses from external CPAs in Conversation History or RSS Feeds. None of these rules were created from the 1337 Services range; every one came from a separate VPN or rented host (ExpressVPN, NordVPN, Interserver at 167.148.41[.]96, CrownCloud, and others), deliberately separating mailbox actions from the replay infrastructure. Four mailboxes had rules created through the Outlook REST API, not the Outlook client.
- The campaign rotated through six addresses in the /24 sequentially across four phases (July 14 to September 22), with each phase separated by quiet periods. Microsoft Entra ID Protection flagged individual addresses (193.26.115[.]221, 193.26.115[.]72, 193.26.115[.]16, 193.26.115[.]21) rather than the range, meaning single-IP blocks stopped at most one phase. Conditional Access blocked 1,052 attempts from 193.26.115[.]72 across only four organizations; the same address completed 303 successful sign-ins across 29 others with no overlap. AADSTS53003 (BlockedByConditionalAccess) means the credential was valid: treat it as a confirmed stolen token, not a near miss.
Practitioner takeaway: Start your hunt in Entra sign-in logs. Filter for OAuth2:Token and Cmsi:Cmsi request types from ASN 210558 or any hosting range using a node or bare Mozilla/5.0 user agent against the Microsoft Office, Authentication Broker, or OfficeHome client IDs listed above, and flag any touching the Device Registration Service resource (01cb2876-7ebd-4aa4-9cc9-d28bd4d359a9). For confirmed compromises: revoke sessions AND reset the password (a reset alone does not invalidate the current access token for up to 90 minutes), then audit Entra devices for the DESKTOP- plus eight hex character pattern, audit registered MFA methods for entries the user does not recognize, and search Exchange for inbox rules with one-to-three-character or punctuation-only names routing to RSS Feeds, RSS Subscriptions, or Conversation History. Block the full 193.26.115[.]0/24 at Conditional Access, not individual addresses. Full IOC tables, client app IDs, target resource GUIDs, and error codes are in the Huntress report.

item.title: Node2Shell: From Brotli Data to Remote Code Execution
item.description:
CVE-2026-111497 in Node.js's bundled Brotli decoder enables remote code execution via crafted compressed data. Imperva's red team confirmed exploitation on the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux arm64 image, with the fixed 24.22.1 rejecting the same inputs.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-111497 is a High severity out-of-bounds write in the native Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js. The flaw sits in shared decoder code reachable from two directions: a compressed HTTP response consumed by Node.js's built-in fetch(), and incoming Brotli request bodies decoded by configured middleware like Express 5.0.0-5.3.0 with body-parser 2.0.0-2.3.0. Both paths hit the same vulnerable decoder, so the runtime is the root cause, not the middleware.
- Imperva's proof of concept ran code carried inside the Brotli data against fresh containers running the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux arm64 image, with no debugger or instrumented binary required. The application had no logic to create a marker file; after receiving the crafted Brotli data, the file appeared, confirming code execution inside the target process. Execution required multiple attempts in the test setup.
- The root cause is a faulty state transition in the vulnerable decoder. When the stream reaches a block transition its own structure makes impossible, the decoder treats the condition as a request for more input rather than an error, continues with an invalid internal state, and can write beyond an intended buffer. The fix makes the decoder return a format error at that invalid transition. The patched Node.js 24.22.1 rejected the same inputs before code ran, and the server stayed running.
- Fixes are available in Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. The Node.js project disclosed the issue on October 21, 2026, crediting Matteo Collina with the report and Antoine du Hamel with the fix. The vulnerability is actively exploitable as demonstrated, and applications on unsupported Node.js lines need to move to a supported fixed release.
- Unexpected process exits during decompression and decoder errors are signals worth correlating during investigation, though neither is a reliable standalone indicator of exploitation. Correlate them with the Node.js runtime version in the affected container or host, application logs, and the origin of the compressed data. A package inventory can miss an older runtime bundled inside a container image: check the Node.js binary version directly in each deployed artifact.
Responder action: Map every service that decodes untrusted Brotli data, whether incoming request bodies through configured parsers or outbound fetch() calls consuming compressed responses. Verify the Node.js binary version inside each running container image directly; a dependency manifest will not catch a bundled older runtime. Unexpected decoder errors or process exits on decompression paths should be correlated with the runtime version and data source as a triage signal while updates roll out. Patch to 22.23.4, 24.22.1, or 26.12.1 as the definitive fix.

item.title: CA-26-041: Compromised eMudhra Intermediate Certificate Authority Certificates
item.description:
Eight eMudhra intermediate CA keys compromised via weak key-generation ceremony, enabling fraudulent TLS and code-signing certificates trusted by major browsers, OS platforms, and Microsoft's Authenticode chain.
Key details:
- The root cause is not a network breach but a wrap/unwrap flaw during a FIPS 140-2 Level 3 HSM key-generation ceremony that produced P-384 private values smaller than 256, making private key recovery from the public key effectively immediate. Six intermediates could issue browser-trusted TLS certificates; two (EM OV CS CA - G3B and G3C) could issue Microsoft-trusted code-signing certificates. Sectigo cross-signed the same key material, extending trust surface. No intrusion set has been attributed and no malicious use has been confirmed as of publication, but absence from Certificate Transparency logs does not exclude unlogged certificates against clients that do not enforce CT.
- The response timeline matters for scoping remediation: Chrome blocked TLS keys via CRLSet on October 17, 2026 and Mozilla completed a OneCRL block the same day. eMudhra revoked all eight certificates October 18, Firefox released out-of-band updates (158.0.1, ESR 115.43.1, ESR 153.5.1, Android 158.0.2). Go pushed deny-list releases 1.26.10 and 1.27.3 (tracked as CVE-2026-111943 / GO-2026-6809, no CVSS published). Google plans full removal of emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from the Chrome Root Store on October 27, 2026, which can break legitimate services that chain to the removed root even if they were never issued by a compromised intermediate.
- The MITRE-mapped threat scenarios are T1587.003 (Develop Capabilities: Digital Certificates, recovering weak CA keys to forge certificates), T1557 (Adversary-in-the-Middle, combining a forged TLS cert with DNS, routing, Wi-Fi, or proxy interception to impersonate services, decrypt traffic, or capture credentials), and T1553.002 (Subvert Trust Controls: Code Signing, making malicious software appear signed by a trusted chain where revocation or updated deny lists are not enforced).
- Risk is highest in environments where revocation checks fail open, CT is not enforced, or trust stores are bundled and rarely refreshed: TLS-inspection proxies, secure web gateways, EDR agents, VPNs, package managers, embedded devices, containers, and custom applications. These are also the environments least likely to have received browser-level CRLSet or OneCRL coverage automatically.
- For code signing, any executable, installer, driver, or script with an Authenticode chain through EM OV CS CA - G3B or G3C and a first-seen date on or after October 17, 2026 is a triage lead. Correlate against file prevalence, download source, parent process, and execution behavior before treating a chain match as proof of maliciousness.
Practitioner takeaway: Inventory all services chaining to emSign ECC Root CA - G3, emSign Root TLS CA - G3, or AAA Certificate Services and replace certificates before the October 27 root removal creates availability impact. For detection, alert when high-value domains present a new or unexpected issuer, when a chain includes eMudhra G3B/G3C intermediates, or when a client accepts a chain a patched Chrome or Firefox reference client rejects. Hunt for DNS poisoning, rogue proxy settings, unauthorized VPN gateways, ARP spoofing, or route changes coinciding with certificate anomalies. Audit Authenticode chains for files first seen on or after October 17, 2026 chaining through the two code-signing intermediates. After applying trust-store updates, watch for spikes in OCSP, CRL, or TLS handshake failures to surface devices still carrying stale bundles.

item.title: Dead Domains, Live Exploits: How Infected Ads and Expired Analytics Tags Deliver Coruna and DarkSword to iPhones
item.description:
Chinese-speaking exploit crew uses malvertising and hijacked analytics tags to mass-deliver Coruna and DarkSword iOS spyware, reaching an estimated 135 million monthly visitors across thousands of websites including major consumer brands.
Key findings:
- Two distinct delivery vectors feed the same operation. The DeadTag campaign works by buying up expired domains behind analytics and ad tags that thousands of websites never removed, then quietly routing iPhone visitors to Coruna and DarkSword. Separately, a P7 variant of DarkSword was confirmed delivered via a malicious Instagram ad themed around the World Cup, served from ad-track[.]live, infecting an employee device during routine feed scrolling. In both cases infection is automatic the moment the malicious asset loads. No click is required from the victim.
- The exploit crew targeting iPhones shows consistent Chinese-language fingerprints across the infrastructure. Code comments in Chinese 🇨🇳 were found inside both the DarkSword loader and worker, and inside the crew's own modified Coruna variant, indicating they were customizing the payload rather than running it as-is. Every server hosting the Coruna loader also contained hundreds of Chinese-language crypto exchanges, USDT and Tron payment sites, and lookalike sites for Chinese 🇨🇳 shopping and travel brands. The wallet targets lean toward Bitpie, TronLink, OKX, and Bitget, all popular with Chinese-speaking crypto users.
- Both kits steal keychain passwords, crypto wallet data from Binance, Coinbase Wallet, OKX, Bitget, Trust Wallet, Exodus, TronLink, and Bitpie, plus device information, location data, messages, and contacts, all sent to a shared backend server. A fake Polymarket page was observed serving both Coruna and P7 DarkSword simultaneously via browser exploitation. DeadTag's infrastructure already contains placeholders to route and deliver spyware built for iOS 26 and 27, signaling intent to scale forward as new exploit kits mature.
- DarkSword loaders were also found planted directly on hundreds of online shops running PrestaShop, hidden inside a folder named to mimic analytics code. A separate clothing retailer loaded both Coruna and DarkSword simultaneously from previously unseen servers, which were then traced to hundreds of additional sites. The same operator serving both kits was confirmed because stolen data was observed returning to the same command-and-control server.
- DeadTag currently reaches sites receiving 135 million visits per month and the investigation is still expanding. The campaign skews toward European domains rather than .com. Attribution for DeadTag itself is open: nothing in its code or infrastructure points to a specific country or group, and it operates like a commercial traffic brokerage that auctions qualified iPhone visitors to the highest bidder.
Practitioner takeaway: for website defenders, the immediate hunt is your own tag inventory. Audit every external script your site loads and identify any that resolve to domains that changed hands recently. A Content Security Policy with strict domain allowlisting and active script monitoring will surface new or altered domains the moment they appear, which is the earliest warning of a DeadTag-style takeover. For mobile incident responders, a confirmed or suspected hit on an iPhone means preserving on-device logs before restarting, then rotating every credential stored in the keychain and migrating crypto assets to wallets with fresh recovery phrases. The report does not publish a public IOC list, but Report URI's threat intelligence feed flags DeadTag domains, exploit hosts, and Coruna and DarkSword infrastructure.

item.title: LiteLLM Suspects GitHub Token Leak in AI Gateway Logs Behind Malicious Package Release
item.description:
LiteLLM's PyPI and Docker release pipeline was backdoored on October 21, 2026, delivering a credential stealer and hourly RAT to any environment that pulled an unpinned v1.107.0 between roughly 11:39 a.m. and 2:20 p.m. UTC.
- The initial access chain is the forensic story here. LiteLLM suspects a publicly exposed internal deployment was reached by an attacker, likely via a recently patched vulnerability, and that Claude Code had embedded GitHub CLI OAuth tokens into logged response bodies. Those tokens gave the attacker credentials for three developer accounts, one of which belonged to a GitHub org owner. That owner token was used to disable branch protections, force-push malicious changes, and redirect the signing workflow to a lookalike repo "Berri-AI/litellm" instead of the legitimate "BerriAI/litellm", so the poisoned artifacts were signed and published as if legitimate.
- The malware used a dual-persistence technique Wiz researchers describe as the first documented in-the-wild case combining both methods simultaneously. A path file "cook.pth" imports "cook[.]py" on interpreter startup, which deobfuscates itself and runs a stealer routine called "privcollect", harvesting system, browser, developer, cloud, and AI tool secrets and exfiltrating them via HTTP POST to litellm[.]dev/healthcheck. Separately, "sitecustomize[.]py" (Linux and macOS only) fetches a C2 domain from a GitHub dead drop at raw.githubusercontent[.]com/letters9813/pythonclient-test/main/domain[.]txt, downloads a second-stage payload from the path /codepy, and forks a background daemon that re-fetches and executes fresh payloads every hour, using /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock to prevent duplicate instances.
- Credential abuse began approximately 4.5 hours after exfiltration. Between 4:20 p.m. and 5:01 p.m. UTC, the attacker validated stolen AWS instance role credentials from CI runners and Kubernetes nodes using sts:GetCallerIdentity, then called bedrock:ListFoundationModels and ListModels, a pattern consistent with LLMjacking. In a subset of environments, IAM enumeration followed: ListRoles, ListUsers, ListAccessKeys, ListAccounts, and DescribeTrails. Attribution IPs observed by Wiz were 168.100.8[.]57 and 165.227.201[.]8.
- The .pth file delivery technique mirrors the March 2026 attack attributed to TeamPCP, but Socket has reviewed the public evidence and found no confirmed link: the embedded RSA public keys differ, as do the exfiltration implementation and backdoor behavior. Whether credentials stolen in March enabled this incident remains unverified. The supply-chain mechanic, compromised release permissions plus a lookalike org name, is the attack surface defenders should internalize regardless of attribution.
If LiteLLM 1.107.0 ran anywhere in your environment, your response priorities are: hunt for cook.pth, cook[.]py, and sitecustomize[.]py on all hosts that ran the package; check for /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock as an indicator of the daemon having started; investigate any outbound connections to litellm[.]dev and executions of /codepy; and rotate every credential reachable from those hosts, prioritizing AWS keys, GitHub tokens, and any AI service API keys. For your pipeline, audit who holds release permissions right now, verify that your package pins resolve to expected hashes, and treat response-body logging in AI gateway deployments as a token-exfiltration risk going forward.

item.title: New LiteLLM Supply Chain Attack Hits PyPI and Docker
item.description:
LiteLLM 1.107.0 trojanized via stolen developer tokens: all seven PyPI wheels and matching Docker images carried a credential stealer active for roughly two hours on October 21, 2026, with follow-on AWS credential abuse already confirmed.
Key details:
- The attack used stolen GitHub CLI OAuth tokens from three LiteLLM engineers to hijack the official release pipeline. One account overrode branch protection and altered the release workflow, a second approved the production gate, and a third deleted workflow records. Build code was pulled from the lookalike repo github[.]com/Berri-AI/litellm rather than the legitimate BerriAI repository. PyPI wheels were live from 11:39 to 13:23 UTC; Docker Hub tags (v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, main-stable) stayed affected until 14:20 UTC; GHCR variants including litellm-database and litellm-non_root were affected until 13:51 UTC.
- The payload uses Python Startup Hooks (T1546.018): cook.pth, cook[.]py, and sitecustomize[.]py drop into site-packages and fire on every interpreter start, no LiteLLM import required. A 16-module stealer targets cloud keys, Kubernetes, SSH, AI provider secrets, browser credentials, and LiteLLM proxy database tables, encrypts them, and exfiltrates to hxxp://www.litellm[.]dev/healthcheck. On Linux and macOS a second component polls raw.githubusercontent[.]com/letters9813/pythonclient-test/main/domain.txt hourly for remote code.
- Exploitation is active. Wiz observed the attacker validating stolen AWS instance role credentials approximately 4.5 hours post-exfiltration, then listing Amazon Bedrock models and enumerating IAM, a pattern consistent with LLMjacking. Attacker source IPs reported by Wiz: 168.100.8[.]57 and 165.227.201[.]8. This is a separate campaign from the March 2026 TeamPCP incident affecting versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8; no link between the two campaigns has been established.
- File hashes from the report: cook.pth SHA-256 7f191632e7320705d154b85204f1ae546b543acbd7e8861229b76f5042b92bdb, cook[.]py SHA-256 9dd0a3926f96a37eb86cf1ee2310d9be93139cc4ebef3ef9e2efe9531390be25, sitecustomize[.]py SHA-256 34bef04fe88ac9d0aae0475630b1738681d15b94f233ac8aa46eacf5968305fa, malicious image index digest sha256:1bbcb1443bc962e45f5aad53fe3d2c30600e0379715fb6c664cdd3ac126c339e. The official v1.107.0 source tag on GitHub does not contain the malicious files.
- Do not run pip to remove the package on an affected host: any Python process re-triggers the payload. Hunt site-packages for litellm-1.107.0.dist-info, cook.pth, cook[.]py, sitecustomize[.]py and their .pyc files; look for /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock and the /tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb marker. A missing marker does not confirm a clean host. Search egress logs for requests to the /healthcheck URL and the domain.txt dead drop. In CloudTrail, hunt GetCallerIdentity, Bedrock model listing, and IAM enumeration calls from unfamiliar IPs. Credential rotation (cloud roles, every provider key in the proxy database, master and virtual keys, DATABASE_URL password, SSH keys, registry tokens) must happen from a clean machine. Pin to litellm==1.106.2 or an earlier explicit version and use image digests rather than floating tags. Note a separate LiteLLM vulnerability is scheduled for disclosure October 27, 2026.

Hunt site-packages for litellm-1.107.0.dist-info, cook.pth, cook[.]py, sitecustomize[.]py and their .pyc files; look for /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock and the /tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb marker. A missing marker does not confirm a clean host. Search egress logs for requests to the /healthcheck URL and the domain.txt dead drop. In CloudTrail, hunt GetCallerIdentity, Bedrock model listing, and IAM enumeration calls from unfamiliar IPs. Credential rotation (cloud roles, every provider key in the proxy database, master and virtual keys, DATABASE_URL password, SSH keys, registry tokens) must happen from a clean machine. Pin to litellm==1.106.2 or an earlier explicit version and use image digests rather than floating tags. Note a separate LiteLLM vulnerability is scheduled for disclosure October 27, 2026.

item.title: Inside SiriusQT: A Seriously Skilled RAT
item.description:
SiriusQT is a capable Windows RAT-and-stealer combo sold as MaaS since April 2026, with at least 30 licensed buyers, 146 tracked license tokens, and campaigns hitting the UK 🇬🇧, Germany 🇩🇪, France 🇫🇷, Spain 🇪🇸, Italy 🇮🇹, and the Netherlands 🇳🇱.
Key findings:
- SiriusQT is sold by actor "GhostKernel" (author credited as "Amonus") on cracked[.]to and crax[.]pro at $500 for a lifetime license. A cracked version leaked in April 2026, spawning a parallel free distribution ecosystem including GitHub reposts. Group-IB extracted 146 unique license tokens from samples: 110 (75%) are leaked. License durations include non-standard tiers of 14, 28, 45, and 99 days alongside commercial 30-day and lifetime tiers, suggesting private operator agreements. The license field embedded in every client config (Caffee_Config resource, fallback marker: <<SIRIUS_STUB_CONFIG>>) is a direct clustering artifact. Samples sharing a COMM_KEY in the connection.key file on the server side can be tied to the same leaked builder instance.
- The client is an x64 C++ native binary or an optional .NET loader (x86/x64) that reads an XOR-encrypted overlay payload and executes it in memory via VirtualAlloc and CreateThread, never dropping the decoded payload to disk. The C++ client resolves APIs at runtime by walking the PEB and hashing export names with a custom 32-bit FNV-1 algorithm (seed 0x7158B20F). Persistence is configurable across six methods: HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, schtasks.exe with a logon trigger, a .lnk shortcut (default name WindowsUpdate.lnk) in the Startup folder, a logon.cmd batch script written to HKCU\Environment UserInitMprLogonScript, HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager BootExecute (admin required), and poisoning C:\Users\Default\NTUSER.DAT via RegLoadKeyA/RegUnLoadKeyA. Default install path masquerades as %APPDATA%\Microsoft\svchost.exe, with fallback to %TEMP%\msupdate\svchost.exe. Mutex name is a GUID embedded in config.
- HVNC is delivered at runtime via opcode 0x47 as an injected PE: HVNCInjection.x64.dll (SHA-256: c206fa613257110b0522b60b402ca0b35da2cb126113e47b67543ba3ff93c53c). The DLL uses MinHook to hook NtCreateFile, NtOpenFile, NtDeleteFile, NtSetInformationFile, NtQueryAttributesFile, and NtQueryFullAttributesFile, enabling transparent filesystem path redirection via RDI_SEARCH_PATH and RDI_REPLACE_PATH environment variables. The DLL uses a reflective loader with a ROR13-based PEB hash (0x6A4ABC5B identifies kernel32.dll). Browser cloning in the HVNC session steals full Chromium profiles. Process injection options include Process Hollowing (T1055.012), QueueUserAPC/Early-Bird (T1055.004), and Remote Thread Injection using NtCreateTreadEx or CreateRemoteThread (T1055.002).
- C2 uses custom TCP framing: a 4-byte little-endian length prefix in cleartext followed by an encrypted payload. The cipher is a custom stream cipher using the 32-byte COMM_KEY from config, a 64-bit packet counter, and MurmurHash3 fmix64 constants (0xFF51AFD7ED558CCD, 0xC4CEB9FE1A85EC53) to build 16-byte XOR keystream blocks. One observed C2 abuses Google Cloud infrastructure at 34.41.139[.]193, making traffic blend into trusted IP ranges. Other C2s in the dataset include server.activeworkshops[.]com:16614, 2.27.62[.]140:4449, serios.ydns[.]eu:4449, and 23.132.164[.]14:4449. SiriusQT infrastructure overlaps with Remcos, XWorm, AsyncRAT, QuasarRAT, NJRAT, and RedLine Stealer. It was delivered as a final-stage payload by the UpCrypter loader in May 2026.
- Credential theft covers 100+ targets via a 16-byte bitmask in opcode 0x38 (T1555.003, T1539), including Chromium AES-GCM secrets, Discord tokens (validated live against Discord endpoints), cryptocurrency wallets, password managers, VPN clients, and mail clients. Keylogging uses SetWindowsHookExA with WH_KEYBOARD_LL (0xD) and tracks the active foreground window title. Clipboard monitoring converts clipboard content to UTF-8 (code page 65001) and runs pattern matching, specifically relevant for cryptocurrency address interception. The server-side appdata.dat file (magic: SDB\x01, XOR-obfuscated JSON) stores offline victim records including license, COMM_KEY, and past connected clients, and is decryptable with four documented 64-bit constants from the report.
Hunt priority: pull any svchost.exe running from %APPDATA%\Microsoft\ or %TEMP%\msupdate\ and check parent process lineage. Hunt for schtasks.exe creating tasks named "Windows Update" via XML definition, .lnk files named WindowsUpdate.lnk in Startup folders, and HKCU\Environment UserInitMprLogonScript values pointing to logon.cmd. For C2 detection, look for TCP sessions to non-standard ports (4449, 7070, 16614, 31166) with a 4-byte little-endian length prefix pattern. Four YARA rules covering the server, native client, .NET loader, and HVNCInjection.x64.dll, plus the full IOC table and decryption scripts, are in the Group-IB report.

item.title: How APT41 revived the BlackLotus bootkit to attack diplomatic organizations in Central Asia
item.description:
APT41 revived the BlackLotus UEFI bootkit as "BlackX" to hit diplomatic targets in Central Asia, exploiting a patched-but-not-enforced vulnerability on fully updated machines.
Key findings:
- BlackX targets diplomatic agencies in Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan, deploying after attackers already hold admin privileges. The installer drops inst.exe and an RC4-encrypted blob (PVMDIJGKAX2) to C:\ProgramData\Intel\, launched as "inst.exe PVMDIJGKAX2 Q46F6MDLI3RX2KV1", with the RC4 key as the final argument. Payloads are entirely inside the encrypted file, leaving inst.exe clean on disk and complicating bootkit component recovery.
- The attack chain exploits CVE-2022-21894 (Baton Drop) to install custom Machine Owner Keys, enabling arbitrary EFI loading and Secure Boot bypass. The targeted machines were fully patched, but the patch requires manual activation: setting a registry flag under HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Secureboot and creating a scheduled task named Secure-Boot-Update. Without those manual steps, the certificate revocation never fires.
- The kernel driver is signed by "温江区明宇网络技术服务工作室" (certificate serial 0bcdf5e0da32d68900b8b7638459d072, now revoked). It disables process, thread, and registry callbacks, tampers with ETW providers to blind security tooling, and intercepts kernel file-open requests for bootkit files, returning a handle to calc.exe in place of the malicious file.
- Two user-mode espionage payloads follow. A RAT uses Google Drive, OneDrive, and Yandex.Disk for C2, polling files by suffix (0X01 through 0X06 plus SSSR for initial system info) to task and receive output. A second payload, OxiDLLRunner, is an OLLVM-obfuscated DLL sideloaded via a legitimate googleupdate.exe (MD5: AF8A983B9ADA07EAE1259BF2953ABD40). It decrypts v8_context_snapshot.bin in the same folder, executes embedded shellcode plus a Rust PE, and beacons to www.archivetj[.]com to receive plugin DLLs exporting a function named create_plugin.
- Attribution to APT41 is medium confidence. The identifier "xdd" appears in BlackX PDB paths, matching a kernel implant described in ESET's June 2026 FishMonger post. DLL sideloading with an encrypted payload blob and heavy OLLVM use are both patterns common among Chinese-speaking actors.
Takeaway: Check every Windows system for the Secure-Boot-Update scheduled task and the Secureboot registry flag under HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Secureboot. Absence of the task on a patched host means the Baton Drop revocation never activated and the machine remains exploitable. Hunt for inst.exe under C:\ProgramData\Intel\ and for googleupdate.exe (original filename jcef_helper.exe) loading unexpected DLLs alongside v8_context_snapshot.bin. Monitor cloud storage outbound connections from non-browser processes, and alert on ETW provider tampering and kernel callback removal. IOCs and full technical details are in the Kaspersky SecureList report.

item.title: PHP2Shell: AI uncovers critical RCE vulnerabilities affecting 70% of the Internet
item.description:
PHP2Shell: Critical RCE and memory disclosure flaws patched October 21, 2026, affect every PHP version back to 5.4, covering an estimated 70% of all websites. Two CVEs reach CVSS 9.2. Actively exploited in proof-of-concept by the discovering researchers; patch urgently.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-109618 is an upload-progress unserializer use-after-free. PHP's Session module can decode session data before full initialization; a fatal out-of-memory error destroys the request heap but leaves global unserializer state published. A later worker request can consume attacker-reclaimed memory as live bookkeeping, enabling controlled corruption. Separately, a stale PS(id) pointer left after OOM abort causes PHP to URL-encode raw heap contents into a PHPSESSID response cookie, disclosing an attacker-sized window of live worker memory, including passwords, tokens, API keys, and certificates from other requests. This memory disclosure is application-agnostic: it fires even when the application never calls session_start().
- CVE-2026-109619 covers two additional primitives. The fatal-error backtrace use-after-free leaves EG(last_fatal_error_backtrace) pointing to freed memory after a fatal OOM; an early diagnostic on the next request follows the dangling pointer before the executor reinitializes, yielding cross-request memory corruption. The OPcache type confusion arises during zend_accel_script_persist() when an allocation failure leaves the process-local CG(map_ptr_last) frontier advanced but the shared frontier unpublished; a second worker reuses those slots for a different runtime object, producing a cross-worker type confusion in shared OPcache memory. Wiz chained these into unauthenticated pre-authentication RCE demonstrated against WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla latest container images.
- The bugs live below the application layer. Application logs may be sparse, but defenders should look for unusual multipart requests followed by memory-limit errors or repeated HTTP 500 responses, unexpectedly large or malformed PHPSESSID response cookies, and unexplained PHP worker churn. These are the signals the report identifies as investigation starting points for unpatched systems.
- The AI angle is operationally significant for DFIR threat modeling. Wiz used Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol alongside Wiz Atlas; the models reduced exploit development and cross-version adaptation from an estimated months-long effort for a world-class team to roughly one week for a single researcher. The report frames this as a shift in exploitability economics: complexity no longer provides the barrier it once did, and defenders should reassess how they prioritize "difficult to exploit" memory-safety flaws in critical runtimes going forward.
- Coordinated disclosure involved the PHP team, OpenAI, Calif, Automattic, Akamai, AWS, Cloudflare, Fastly, Google, Imperva, Microsoft, and Vercel. The PHP patch released October 21, 2026, fixes the root cause and eliminates known variants. The report notes additional untracked variants exist in the PHP codebase; all should be covered by the same patch.
Practitioner takeaway: Patch to the October 21, 2026 PHP release immediately. While awaiting patching, instrument your PHP-FPM or mod_php environment to alert on multipart POST requests that trigger memory-limit errors (HTTP 500 bursts from the same worker), and monitor outbound PHPSESSID cookie sizes for anomalously large values. The Wiz report includes remediation and threat hunting guidance; CDN and WAF-level mitigations were pre-deployed by several providers for customers who cannot patch immediately. If you observe the worker churn or cookie anomalies the report describes on a system that has not yet been patched, treat it as a potential active exploitation event and begin memory and process forensics on the affected PHP workers.

item.title: [remote] Synametrics Syncrify 6.2 - command execution
item.description:
Synametrics Syncrify 6.2 path traversal in its chunked-upload handler chains to root command execution via cron injection, no admin session required, only a valid backup-user credential.
Key findings:
- The vulnerable sink is the PublicLink handler's chunked-upload branch, reached at /app?operation=pb&st=u. That branch reads a raw binary frame from the socket including a client-supplied filename and passes it directly to new File(base, filename) with no separator rejection, no basename extraction, and no canonical containment check. Three sibling handlers in the same codebase do filter this exact field; the chunk-upload branch calls none of them. The result is an arbitrary file write to any path the service identity can reach, with attacker-controlled bytes, in append mode, with parent directories created automatically via mkdirs().
- The demonstrated escalation path writes a cron fragment to /etc/cron.d/ using a traversal depth of five components above the user's own PublicLinks folder. On the verified deployment the service runs as uid 0, so the fragment lands as root-owned at mode 0644 and the host scheduler treats it as a trusted root job. Execution was confirmed: uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root). The execution happens entirely outside the application; argument hygiene inside Syncrify would not have prevented it.
- The authentication gate is the backup-user store at config/UserMappings.xml, a completely separate credential store from the web-admin store at config/umap.dat. The handler is registered at secLevel=0 meaning no admin session is needed, only a valid backup-user pair. The report notes passwords in that store are compared in plaintext or under a reversible transform, so a successful file read of UserMappings.xml delivers credentials directly. The factory admin password of letmein belongs to the separate admin store, does not gate this sink, and is documented only as a contributing context note.
- CVSS 3.1 published score is 7.5 High (AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H). AC:H reflects two conditions outside the attacker's control: the /app?operation= listener must be reachable and a cron daemon must be active. The conditional reading where that listener is normally reachable (the expected operating mode for a backup server) scores 8.8 High (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N). CVE is listed as pending. Only build 1178 was decompiled and exercised; no version-range claim is made. The report also flags the same sradef framework underpins sibling product SynaMan, identified by the web.xml display-name on this very build.
- Beyond the identity capture, the report argues root on a backup server means read access to the entire repository tree across all tenants, plaintext or reversible credentials from UserMappings.xml, integrity control over the replication path including the server's own binaries, and structural persistence: a cron fragment survives both service and host restarts until explicitly removed. The backup set itself becomes a tampered distribution channel whose corruption remains invisible until restore time.
Responder takeaway: if Syncrify 6.2 is in your environment, examine /etc/cron.d/ for unexpected fragment files owned by root with recent creation timestamps, and check the Syncrify application log for POST requests to /app?operation=pb&st=u from unexpected source addresses or unexpected backup-user accounts. The user's PublicLinks folder at /opt/Syncrify/PublicLinks/ should contain no entries with path separator characters in the folder or file names. The full analysis, proof-of-concept Python script, and PoC repository are at the 0day-rubbish[.]com blog post and github[.]com/Exploit-Garbage/0day-Rubbish linked in the Exploit-DB entry.

Three sibling handlers in the same codebase do filter this exact field; the chunk-upload branch calls none of them. The result is an arbitrary file write to any path the service identity can reach, with attacker-controlled bytes, in append mode, with parent directories created automatically via mkdirs().

- The demonstrated escalation path writes a cron fragment to /etc/cron.d/ using a traversal depth of five components above the user's own PublicLinks folder. On the verified deployment the service runs as uid 0, so the fragment lands as root-owned at mode 0644 and the host scheduler treats it as a trusted root job. Execution was confirmed: uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root). The execution happens entirely outside the application; argument hygiene inside Syncrify would not have prevented it.

- The authentication gate is the backup-user store at config/UserMappings.xml, a completely separate credential store from the web-admin store at config/umap.dat. The handler is registered at secLevel=0 meaning no admin session is needed, only a valid backup-user pair. The report notes passwords in that store are compared in plaintext or under a reversible transform, so a successful file read of UserMappings.xml delivers credentials directly. The factory admin password of letmein belongs to the separate admin store, does not gate this sink, and is documented only as a contributing context note.

- CVSS 3.1 published score is 7.5 High (AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H). AC:H reflects two conditions outside the attacker's control: the /app?operation= listener must be reachable and a cron daemon must be active. The conditional reading where that listener is normally reachable (the expected operating mode for a backup server) scores 8.8 High (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N). CVE is listed as pending. Only build 1178 was decompiled and exercised; no version-range claim is made. The report also flags the same sradef framework underpins sibling product SynaMan, identified by the web.xml display-name on this very build.

- Beyond the identity capture, the report argues root on a backup server means read access to the entire repository tree across all tenants, plaintext or reversible credentials from UserMappings.xml, integrity control over the replication path including the server's own binaries, and structural persistence: a cron fragment survives both service and host restarts until explicitly removed. The backup set itself becomes a tampered distribution channel whose corruption remains invisible until restore time.

Responder takeaway: if Syncrify 6.2 is in your environment, examine /etc/cron.d/ for unexpected fragment files owned by root with recent creation timestamps, and check the Syncrify application log for POST requests to /app?operation=pb&st=u from unexpected source addresses or unexpected backup-user accounts. The user's PublicLinks folder at /opt/Syncrify/PublicLinks/ should contain no entries with path separator characters in the folder or file names. The full analysis, proof-of-concept Python script, and PoC repository are at the 0day-rubbish[.]com blog post and github[.]com/Exploit-Garbage/0day-Rubbish linked in the Exploit-DB entry.
