item.title: Traces for Deleted photo/video Under Apple Photos app
item.description:
Deleted photos and videos on iPhone leave behind multiple forensic traces in the Photos.sqlite database and surrounding artifacts, even when the media itself is permanently unrecoverable due to file-based encryption.
Key findings:
- The Photos.sqlite database is the primary target. Even when acquisition is limited to an iTunes backup, this database retains metadata about permanently deleted media, including evidence of the deletion event itself, historical creation timestamps, the original filename, camera information, and recovered deleted ZASSET records. The media file is gone, but the database entry describing it may not be.
- File-based encryption (FBE) on modern iPhones makes recovering the underlying photo or video extremely difficult or impossible with current forensic techniques, but it does not necessarily wipe the database records that referenced that media. This is the critical gap investigators can exploit: the capture event may be provable even when the image is not recoverable.
- A full file system extraction opens additional corroborating sources beyond Photos.sqlite: File System Events, Biome data, and the Unified Logs. Cross-referencing these with ZASSET records from the database can build a more complete timeline of when media was created, managed, and deleted, which matters enormously in cases like upskirting where the timing of capture is the central question.
- These artifacts are transient. They can be automatically purged, overwritten, or become unavailable as the device continues to operate. The report is explicit: the longer the gap between the relevant activity and device acquisition, the higher the probability that valuable traces are lost for good.
Practitioner takeaway: In cases involving suspected deleted media on an iPhone, prioritize early acquisition. Parse Photos.sqlite for ZASSET table records, including deleted rows, and extract creation timestamps, filenames, and camera metadata even where no image is recoverable. If full file system access is available, correlate with File System Events, Biome, and Unified Logs to corroborate and timestamp the capture event. An iTunes backup is a viable fallback, but a full file system pull gives you the broader picture. Time is the enemy here: secure the device and acquire it before those transient records are gone.

item.title: eMudhra CA Key Compromise: Weak Keys, Risks and Fixes
item.description:
Eight eMudhra intermediate CA private keys were trivially recoverable for 17 months, with one key literally being the integer 4. Browsers blocked within hours of disclosure, but non-browser clients remain the open wound.
Key findings:
- The root cause was a flawed key ceremony script run on April 30, 2025. A bug on the HSM caused a second, weak key pair to be generated and then used for certificate signing requests due to similar key labels and human errors at multiple steps. Every affected P-384 private key was an integer below 256, roughly 8 bits of strength instead of 384. The EM OV TLS CA G3C key was the integer 4. Recovery requires testing at most 256 candidates against the public key, a task a laptop finishes in milliseconds. A missed signal: in June 2025, Mozilla bug 1970728 recorded invalid CRL signatures from the same six TLS intermediates. eMudhra blamed a manual process error, published corrected CRLs, and the bug was closed. That key mismatch was the same weak-key problem, unrecognized for another 16 months.
- Six of the eight intermediates are TLS issuing CAs covering DV, OV and EV tiers in G3B and G3C variants. Two are code-signing CAs under emSign Root CS CA G3, a root Microsoft trusts. The TLS keys allow issuance of valid-looking certificates for any domain trusted by clients in that chain. The code-signing keys could make malware appear to carry a verified-publisher signature on Windows systems that skip revocation checks. Sectigo cross-signed all eight under AAA Certificate Services, so each compromised key also appears in a Sectigo-issued certificate: blocking eMudhra's root alone is not sufficient.
- No confirmed malicious use exists as of October 21, 2026, and Google reports no CT-logged TLS certificates chaining to the affected intermediates before the block. That clears CT-enforcing clients. Clients that skip CT have no equivalent assurance, and the keys were publicly accessible for approximately 17 months beginning April 30, 2025. All eight key values are now public and must be treated as attacker-known. Code-signing certificates are not logged to CT, so no public record exists of what the two code-signing CAs may have signed.
- The browser response was rapid. Chrome shipped a CRLSet update at 19:45 UTC on October 17, 2026, under two hours after Wayne's report. Mozilla's OneCRL block reached standard Firefox installs by 22:59 UTC the same night. Apple blocked on October 19, Microsoft on October 20. Mozilla went further and removed the emSign ECC Root CA G3 root entirely in NSS 3.131.1 on October 20, 2026. Chrome's root removal is expected to reach all devices by October 27, 2026. The downstream CVEs are CVE-2026-111943 for the Go crypto/x509 block (fixed in Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10, rebuild required) and CVE-2026-113470 for the Firefox OneCRL update (Mozilla rates it High, CISA ADP scores it 5.4 CVSS v3.1), addressed in Firefox 158.0.1, ESR 153.5.1, ESR 115.43.1, and NSS 3.131.1. Node.js fixed in 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. Python certifi 2026.10.19, Ubuntu and Debian ca-certificates packages, and Alpine ca-certificates 20261020-r0 also carry fixes. Bun and FreeBSD ca_root_nss remain pending as of October 21, 2026.
- Non-browser clients are the unresolved exposure. API clients, containers, CI/CD pipelines, and IoT devices that bundle their own CA store and skip revocation and CT checks can still be presented with a forged certificate and accept it. Scott Helme's tests confirmed that curl, Python, and Node.js on Linux and macOS accepted a forged certificate under EM DV TLS CA G3B before patching. The built-in /usr/bin/curl on macOS reads an unupdated /etc/ssl/cert.pem and does not check revocation. Go binaries only gain the block after recompilation with a patched toolchain: deployed binaries retain the old trust behavior regardless of OS-level updates.
Practitioner takeaway: the hunt window is April 30, 2025 through October 17, 2026. Review TLS inspection, proxy, and endpoint logs for certificates chaining to any of the eight named intermediates (EM DV/OV/EV TLS CA G3B and G3C, EM OV CS CA G3B and G3C). On Windows, examine Authenticode verification events for binaries with publisher chains touching emSign Root CS CA G3. Test non-browser clients directly using the disclosure site's test hosts: a successful connection to dv-g3b-emudhra.we-have-a-problem[.]com or dv-g3b-aaa-emudhra.we-have-a-problem[.]com is an open finding requiring immediate trust store remediation. Rebuild Go binaries and container images from patched base layers; do not assume a running container inherited the OS fix. The disclosure site documents manual distrust steps for macOS curl, major Linux distributions, NetBSD, and FreeBSD for frozen devices that cannot receive updates.

item.title: “Next Exploit Opportunities”: How a Threat Actor Used AI to Help Plan and Execute Multiple Types of Cybercrime Activities
item.description:
Low-skill actor BUGSTER used jailbroken AI to attack Indian 🇮🇳 universities, exfiltrate 5,200+ PII records, and plan VoIP fraud, credential theft, Wi-Fi cracking, and crypto targeting from a single US-based server.
Key findings:
- BUGSTER ran the Hermes Agent framework with DeepSeek V4 as its reasoning engine, controlled via Telegram, across three specialized bot profiles: make-good (general criminal assistant), alice (VoIP fraud advisor covering STIR/SHAKEN bypass, LLC formation, and carrier evasion), and pandarouter (carrier research). Cursor IDE was configured through a proxy script named cipher-proxy[.]sh that forced full agent mode and bypassed sandbox and permission controls. All safety controls were defeated via a system-prompt override, evidenced in the actor's own test scripts such as test_batch1.py. The entire operation ran from a single US 🇺🇸 server at 162.243.3[.]92.
- The university attack chain ran four stages: subdomain enumeration of 12 subdomains including a WordPress site, LMS, student portal, and admin dashboard; WordPress REST API enumeration that extracted 13 active user IDs by abusing post author fields and author sitemaps to bypass Cloudflare WAF; AI-generated brute force against 117 usernames and 28 common passwords; and one confirmed valid credential. A second Indian 🇮🇳 university suffered a confirmed MongoDB exfiltration of more than 5,200 student and faculty PII records after the actor obtained an admin account protected by a weak password. The exfiltration manifest also exposed cloud load balancing, edge routing, database services, and a third-party cloud storage account.
- The Wi-Fi cracking pipeline used a Kali Linux device labeled Pi placed physically near target networks to capture WPA PMKID or EAPOL handshakes, tunneled them over SSH to the actor's server, then dispatched them to Vast[.]ai cloud GPU instances for cracking, with results returned via Discord webhooks. Physical proximity to the targets is a confirmed requirement and an investigative anchor. A Go-based credential-scanning toolkit also scraped exposed .env values, S3 signed URLs, Google Cloud service account keys, CDN API keys, and private keys in log files.
- The C2 infrastructure at 162.243.3[.]92 hosted a Python-based listener accepting Windows reverse shell connections. Payloads included a Base64-encoded PowerShell reverse shell delivered via VBScript, a QubesOS VM setup script using SSH and ncat, and multiple Windows shell variants. The actor also scraped the top 500 ETH holders via the DeBank API, producing intelligence files documenting 45 cryptocurrency whales with net worth figures, assessed as pre-targeting for future campaigns.
- Attribution indicators in the report: handle BUGSTER, email bugstergap@gmail[.]com, Cursor IDE user ID 158034011, Telegram user ID 7593151260. Unit 42 notes multiple unrelated actors independently adopting the Hermes + DeepSeek combination, pointing to an emerging low-cost, low-friction criminal toolchain. DeepSeek V4 is inexpensive, easily accessed, and jailbroken with a simple system-prompt override, making it the path of least resistance for actors who would have lacked these capabilities before AI lowered the skill floor.
Practitioner takeaway: If you are investigating a compromised university or e-commerce platform in India 🇮🇳, look for AI-structured recon output with sections like "NEXT EXPLOIT OPPORTUNITIES" as a post-compromise artifact. Hunt for outbound connections from 162.243.3[.]92, VBScript dropping Base64-encoded PowerShell that spawns a reverse shell, and ncat or SSH tunneling activity on non-standard ports. For the Wi-Fi cracking angle, Discord webhook traffic carrying hash-cracking results and Vast[.]ai API calls from internal hosts are the pivot. IOCs are in the Unit 42 report.

item.title: LiteLLM Compromised, Steals Credentials
item.description:
LiteLLM 1.107.0 on PyPI and Docker was trojanized with a 16-module credential stealer and dormant C2, active for roughly 101 minutes before quarantine. AI developer pipelines were the primary target, with post-exploitation LLMjacking confirmed within hours.
Key findings:
- The malicious package dropped three files into the Python site-packages root on install: cook.pth, cook[.]py, and sitecustomize[.]py. cook.pth forces cook[.]py to execute on every Python interpreter start. The credential stealer, internally named privcollect, harvests browser credentials and cookies (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari), AWS credentials from ~/.aws/ and EC2/ECS IMDS, GCP service account keys, Azure CLI tokens, SSH and GPG private keys, shell history, and API keys for OpenAI, Anthropic, Cohere, and other LLM providers. It also runs a direct PostgreSQL query, SELECT * FROM "LiteLLM_CredentialsTable" LIMIT 500, to drain all configured upstream provider credentials from LiteLLM Proxy deployments. Harvested data is AES-256-CBC encrypted with an RSA-4096 wrapped key and exfiltrated via HTTP POST to www.litellm[.]dev/healthcheck using a hardcoded X-Token header and an Internet Explorer 7 user-agent string. That domain impersonates legitimate LiteLLM infrastructure.
- sitecustomize[.]py (Linux and macOS only) attempts a GitHub dead drop fetch from letters9813/pythonclient-test/main/domain.txt to retrieve a C2 domain, then downloads a second-stage Python script from hxxp://<domain>/codepy. The domain.txt file was never populated beyond test values, so the C2 remained dormant. The dual technique of using both .pth files and sitecustomize[.]py simultaneously is reported as the first documented case in the wild. The malware shows strong indicators of LLM-aided development: verbose variable names, silent failure on Windows (the /tmp/ path is hardcoded), fcntl and fork calls that crash on untested platforms, and a dead code module, exec_py, that was defined but never called.
- The attacker gained initial access to an internal LiteLLM deployment exposed to the public internet, suspected to be through a recently patched vulnerability. Claude Code was found to embed GitHub CLI OAuth tokens into response bodies in certain conditions, and those tokens appeared in LiteLLM logs. The attacker harvested at least two engineers' GitHub CLI OAuth tokens from those logs, used one compromised account to trigger the project-releaser workflow, and a second to approve it. Ten commits were pushed between 08:56 and 10:46 UTC on October 21 from ckdi82fkoos@proton[.]me via the spoofed Berri-AI/litellm repository (note the hyphen, distinct from the legitimate BerriAI org). All involved OAuth tokens have been revoked.
- Post-exploitation began approximately 4.5 hours after exfiltration. Between 16:20 and 17:01 UTC, the attacker validated stolen AWS instance role credentials harvested from CI runners and Kubernetes nodes, calling sts:GetCallerIdentity, bedrock:ListFoundationModels, and ListModels from 168.100.8[.]57 and 165.227.201[.]8. In a subset of environments, IAM enumeration followed: ListRoles, ListUsers, ListAccessKeys, ListAccounts, and DescribeTrails. This pattern is consistent with LLMjacking, using compromised cloud credentials to abuse AI inference APIs at victim expense. Affected Docker tags were v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, and main-stable. The last confirmed safe version is v1.106.2.
Practitioner takeaway: If any environment installed LiteLLM between 11:39 and 13:20 UTC on October 21, treat it as compromised. Hunt for cook.pth, cook[.]py, and sitecustomize[.]py in Python site-packages directories. Check outbound HTTP POST connections to www.litellm[.]dev and any User-Agent strings matching Internet Explorer 7. Review CloudTrail and AWS Config for sts:GetCallerIdentity followed by bedrock:ListFoundationModels from the attacker IPs above. Rotate all credentials in scope: AWS keys, GCP service accounts, Azure CLI tokens, LiteLLM Proxy database credentials, and any LLM provider API keys stored in environment variables or the LiteLLM_CredentialsTable. Audit any internal LLM deployment logs for embedded OAuth tokens, particularly from Claude Code sessions. IOC table and attacker commit details are in the Wiz report.

Ten commits were pushed between 08:56 and 10:46 UTC on October 21 from ckdi82fkoos@proton[.]me via the spoofed Berri-AI/litellm repository (note the hyphen, distinct from the legitimate BerriAI org). All involved OAuth tokens have been revoked.

- Post-exploitation began approximately 4.5 hours after exfiltration. Between 16:20 and 17:01 UTC, the attacker validated stolen AWS instance role credentials harvested from CI runners and Kubernetes nodes, calling sts:GetCallerIdentity, bedrock:ListFoundationModels, and ListModels from 168.100.8[.]57 and 165.227.201[.]8. In a subset of environments, IAM enumeration followed: ListRoles, ListUsers, ListAccessKeys, ListAccounts, and DescribeTrails. This pattern is consistent with LLMjacking, using compromised cloud credentials to abuse AI inference APIs at victim expense. Affected Docker tags were v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, and main-stable. The last confirmed safe version is v1.106.2.

Practitioner takeaway: If any environment installed LiteLLM between 11:39 and 13:20 UTC on October 21, treat it as compromised. Hunt for cook.pth, cook[.]py, and sitecustomize[.]py in Python site-packages directories. Check outbound HTTP POST connections to www.litellm[.]dev and any User-Agent strings matching Internet Explorer 7. Review CloudTrail and AWS Config for sts:GetCallerIdentity followed by bedrock:ListFoundationModels from the attacker IPs above. Rotate all credentials in scope: AWS keys, GCP service accounts, Azure CLI tokens, LiteLLM Proxy database credentials, and any LLM provider API keys stored in environment variables or the LiteLLM_CredentialsTable. Audit any internal LLM deployment logs for embedded OAuth tokens, particularly from Claude Code sessions. IOC table and attacker commit details are in the Wiz report.

item.title: SleeperWidget: How Ad-Driven Installs Activate Hidden Browser Extension Behavior
item.description:
SleeperWidget: 250+ browser extensions across Edge, Chrome, and Firefox used ad-funnel activation to hide browsing surveillance and affiliate fraud from store reviewers, impacting over one million users.
Key findings:
- The core evasion mechanic is ad-gated activation. Installing directly from the store delivers only the advertised widget. Installing via a paid search ad (tracked with msclkid and campaign SID parameters from landing pages like viewpoint3dearth[.]com and earthview360[.]net) stores an activation ticket in the landing page's localStorage. The extension's content script reads that ticket on first run and copies it into extension storage, creating a handoff that leaves no trace in the reviewed package. A server-side flag kept malicious behavior disabled in shipping builds, so a static reviewer or automated scanner sees an inert extension until the operator flips the switch.
- Once activated, page.js (matching hxxps://*/* and hxxp://*/* at document_start) reads document.title and window.location.href on every navigation and posts them to campaign infrastructure like etailers.viewpoint3dearth[.]com/blase. The report documents the full POST body with obfuscated field names: page title in hallo.crick.hierarch, full URL in ozonic.qualm, tab ID in ruc.outside.lodge. The server returns destination URLs the extension opens without user interaction, injecting affiliate tags on shopping pages (confirmed on Amazon). Critically, the server fully controls destinations and the extension does not validate them. The same channel could deliver phishing or malware without any extension update.
- Cross-extension identity sharing expands the surveillance surface. A shared UID is negotiated between family members via a window.postMessage exchange using the message type get-ext-uid. The report confirms this behavior between View Point 3D Earth (mfmgmgocbldnnanccchdmngckohenkmg) and Free Digital Books Online (lokabladohpkccobnhbehkopcjphgehg), two extensions from separate campaigns that stored the same UID. Removing one extension does not clear the UID held by remaining family members, so partial remediation still allows cross-extension activity correlation.
- Evasion evolves with detection. Older builds padded source files with dead code copied from open-source libraries to appear benign to scanners. Newer builds ship clean webpack bundles, indicating the operator actively re-tools in response to detection approaches. Shadow DOM overlays render injected content inside a shadow root at high stacking order, hiding ads from the page's own scripts and many content blockers. The server's injection-exclusion list deliberately avoids AI assistants, healthcare portals, tax software, and high-trust consumer brands where an unexpected overlay would more likely trigger a user report.
- Scope and response: Microsoft Edge protections placed more than one million client identifiers in a malware-blocked state. The investigation identified at least 250 related listings across Microsoft Edge Add-ons, Chrome Web Store, and Mozilla Add-ons. Microsoft began taking action against Edge listings in April 2026 and shared extension identifiers and indicators with Google and Mozilla security teams.
Takeaway for responders: the activation, reporting, and UID-sharing behavior is more durable than any individual domain or build, so hunt on behavior rather than IOCs alone. In an enterprise context, baseline installed extensions against approved lists and flag any extension with broad host_permissions or content_scripts matching hxxps://*/* that does not operationally require it. For affected users, disabling "Sponsored content" in the extension UI stopped visible ad injection but did not stop URL and page-title exfiltration, so toggle state is not a reliable remediation signal. Full removal is required. The complete extension ID set across all three stores and the infrastructure domain list are in the SleeperWidget IOC PDF linked in the report.

item.title: [remote] Parasoft Continuous Testing Platform 10.7.5 - JSP command execution
item.description:
Parasoft CTP 10.7.5 scores CVSS 9.8 Critical for unauthenticated RCE in two plain HTTP requests, combining a filter bypass, a fail-open auth gate, and unfiltered Java deserialization with no credential, no callback, and no setup required.
Key findings:
- Three composing defects chain to RCE. EMLicenseFilter reads the raw un-normalized request URI and exempts any path ending with "about", "welcome", "forgot", etc. Because the servlet container strips semicolon-delimited path parameters before routing, a POST to /em/database/restore;welcome clears the license gate entirely while still reaching the restore handler. With no external security provider configured, EMRememberMeServices hands the anonymous request a fully authenticated ROLE_ADMIN Spring Security principal it manufactures itself rather than a container anonymous principal, and /database is mapped to authenticated() not hasRole("ADMIN"), so any valid account suffices when a provider is present (Conditional A: CVSS 8.8). CsrfSecurityRequestMatcher explicitly exempts /database, so the state-changing POST needs no CSRF token.
- The sink is unfiltered Java deserialization. AbstractDatabaseBackup wraps the uploaded database.ser zip member with new ObjectInputStream(in) and calls readObject() at line 117, nine lines before getConnection() at line 126. The gadget executes before the ClassCastException lands. A corpus-wide search found ObjectInputStream in 68 files with 149 occurrences and readObject in 81 files; ObjectInputFilter, jdk.serialFilter, and serialFilter each appear zero times. The write primitive is a HashSet forcing hashCode() on a TiedMapEntry wrapping a LazyMap backed by an aspectjweaver SimpleCache$StoreableCachingMap, writing arbitrary bytes to an attacker-controlled path with no extension forced, no traversal check, and no content validation. The only content restriction is that bytes must not equal the 4-byte IDEM sentinel.
- Execution lands inside the deployed web application. The default landing directory is webapps/em/images/, which is writable by uid 1000 and already exempt from the license filter via the contains("/images/") clause. Tomcat's Jasper engine compiles the dropped JSP into work/Catalina/localhost/em/org/apache/jsp/images/ and serves it on a plain anonymous GET. A second independent sink was confirmed: WEB-INF/classes/com/parasoft/rest/api/core/docs/templates/ is the FreeMarker root and freemarker.template.utility.Execute is unrestricted, demonstrated with 7x119 returning 833 and an id call returning the full identity string. Success on hop 1 is an HTTP 500 carrying the product's own 119-byte "An error occurred while applying changes to the database configuration" message, not a failure. The product log pairs AbstractDatabaseBackup.restore(AbstractDatabaseBackup[.]java:114) with a ClassCastException naming a JDK collection class, distinguishable from a malformed payload which produces ClassNotFoundException instead.
- Persistence survives naive cleanup. After the dropped JSP and both Jasper compilation artefacts were deleted, the same URL still returned HTTP 200 with a body two bytes shorter than the original, because the compiled servlet instance remained loaded in the JVM. Only a context reload or full container restart removes it. Overwriting deployed application pages or class files to survive a restart is a structurally reachable but unexercised consequence of the proven write primitive. The fail-open auth branch, the license filter bypass, and the deserialization sink are all unconditional and stateless: the chain was fired repeatedly against one instance with no state consumed between runs.
- The CVE is pending and only CTP 10.7.5-SNAPSHOT on the vendor's parasoft/ctp:latest image (id prefix f99f7210fc67, md5 47946c7d1e7d99a00d6c90f4ae675f90) was executed. No patch is available as of disclosure. The published PoC is Python 3 standard-library only, takes target URL and command as arguments, and is available in the public repository at github[.]com/Exploit-Garbage/0day-Rubbish. Full analysis is at 0day-rubbish[.]com/blog/parasoft-ctp-unfiltered-deserialization-license-gate-fail-open-jsp-rce.
Practitioner takeaway: if Parasoft CTP is in your environment, hunt now. On the network side, look for POST requests whose URI contains a semicolon targeting the /em/database/restore path. On disk, check webapps/em/images/ for any non-image file and compare the file count against a known baseline, then inspect work/Catalina/localhost/em/org/apache/jsp/images/ for compiled JSP stems the product did not ship. In the product log, correlate AbstractDatabaseBackup.restore() stack frames carrying ClassCastException against JDK collection class names as the success signature for hop 1. Note that license refusals from the filter flush before calling setStatus(403), so they surface as HTTP 200 with a JSON body carrying status 403: any WAF or SIEM rule keyed on HTTP 403 for license failures will not fire. Until a patch ships, network-segment the CTP management ports (8080/8443) and confirm no external security provider is left unconfigured, which moves the base score to Conditional A (CVSS 8.8) and requires a valid account rather than zero credentials, though the deserialization sink and the license filter bypass remain fully open.

item.title: LiteLLM supply chain compromise: What you need to know
item.description:
LiteLLM's second PyPI supply chain compromise in 2026 drops a credential stealer and RAT backdoor into any Python environment that installed version 1.107.0, targeting cloud, developer, and AI-tool secrets at scale.
Key findings:
- Attackers stole GitHub CLI OAuth tokens from three LiteLLM engineers and used them to launch, approve, and then delete evidence of an unauthorized run of the legitimate release pipeline against a malicious fork named Berri-AI/litellm (note the hyphen vs. the real BerriAI/litellm). The resulting wheels and Docker images published to PyPI, GHCR, and Docker Hub carried valid build provenance pointing to the malicious fork. Tags affected beyond the versioned release include latest, main-latest, and main-stable, meaning any environment pulling those tags was exposed. The window was approximately two hours: 11:39 UTC (publish) to 13:53 UTC (Docker images removed).
- Three files are dropped into the Python installation's site-packages directory: cook.pth, cook[.]py, and sitecustomize[.]py. Because Python automatically executes .pth files and sitecustomize[.]py at interpreter startup, every Python process in the environment runs the malware regardless of whether litellm is ever imported. Critically, uninstalling the litellm package does not remove these files, and running python or pip in the affected environment re-triggers execution.
- The infostealer (cook[.]py) collects a wide credential surface: AWS, GCP, and Azure secrets including instance metadata endpoints, Kubernetes, Docker, Vault and Terraform secrets, SSH, GPG and TLS keys, Git, npm and PyPI tokens, .env files, shell history, LLM provider API keys, sessions for Claude, Codex, Gemini, Cursor, and Copilot, saved browser passwords and cookies, and if a LiteLLM proxy database is configured, it queries the upstream provider credential tables directly. Exfiltration goes to www.litellm[.]dev/healthcheck, encrypted with AES-256 and RSA-4096, and includes the HTTP header X-Token: XWiA8gZNa7NcX2XRoAEb as a beacon fingerprint.
- The RAT backdoor (sitecustomize[.]py) polls raw.githubusercontent[.]com/letters9813/pythonclient-test/main/domain.txt hourly for a C2 domain, then downloads and executes arbitrary Python. That file held only test values and no second-stage payload was observed in the wild, but the mechanism was fully functional. Two runtime artifacts mark execution: /tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb (run-once flag after successful infostealer execution) and /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock (ensures a single infostealer instance runs at a time). Hashes for all platform-specific malicious wheels are in the Datadog Security Labs report.
- This is the second LiteLLM supply chain compromise in 2026. Datadog's earlier report linked the first (versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8) to TeamPCP activity. No connection between the two incidents has been established at time of writing.
DFIR takeaway: If litellm 1.107.0 or any of the affected Docker tags touched your environment during the exposure window, do not simply uninstall the package. Manually locate and delete cook.pth, cook[.]py, and sitecustomize[.]py from every affected site-packages directory. From a clean machine, immediately rotate all credentials in scope: cloud provider keys and IAM roles, SSH and GPG keys, Git, npm and PyPI tokens, LLM API keys, and any secrets reachable via .env files or shell history. Audit CloudTrail, GCP Audit Logs, and equivalent logs for use of exposed credentials between 11:39 and 13:53 UTC on October 21, 2026. Hunt for /tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb and /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock as host-level indicators of execution. IOCs including all platform wheel hashes are in the Datadog Security Labs report.

item.title: Inside a Global AI-Assisted Hacking Campaign
item.description:
A Chinese-speaking operator ran a globe-spanning data-theft campaign from August through October 2026, combining the ARTEX pen-testing framework with Claude Code, Codex, and Grok workspaces to orchestrate autonomous hacking across dozens of targets worldwide.
Key findings:
- The operator ran two servers: a work server (23.248.226[.]250 through 23.248.226[.]254) hosting a custom ARTEX Docker container tagged artex-local:perf2-20261003, and a jump server at 38.244.50[.]120 used as the default outbound route to targets. ARTEX was extended with nmap, sqlmap, nuclei, httpx, jadx, apktool, and frida-tools, and backed by a PostgreSQL 16 database. Upstream SOCKS proxies at 205.214.59[.]31:443 and 161.8.161[.]140:11005, plus a proxy pool API at 154.201.79[.]246:443, provided per-project outbound IPs to reduce direct exposure.
- AI models were assigned structured roles rather than used interchangeably. ARTEX routed to deepseek-v4.1-flash via xcai[.]pro/v1. GLM (glm-5.3) was explicitly instructed to audit DeepSeek's completed work for missed attack surfaces (AML.T0051). Grok (grok-4.7-xhigh) ran research tasks on the jump server via a grok2api bridge, with separate sessions reviewing its output. Three sync scripts, sync-all[.]sh, sync-memory[.]sh, and tools/sync-cc-users.sh, kept instructions and memory files consistent across accounts (AML.T0052).
- Persistent project state was maintained per target using scope[.]md, surface[.]md, notes[.]md, a findings/ folder, and an evidence/ folder. A hook script, tools/project_context_hook.py, injected a status summary into every new prompt so AI sessions could resume prior work without operator recap. System prompts told agents to treat all supplied targets as pre-authorized and to act autonomously without per-step approval (AML.T0054). Investigation assets were archived to Backblaze B2.
- Targeting spanned dating apps, SMS providers, crypto and NFT platforms, retail, education, legal settlement systems, and more across Canada 🇨🇦, China 🇨🇳, Cuba, India 🇮🇳, Japan 🇯🇵, Kenya, Nigeria 🇳🇬, South Korea 🇰🇷, the United States 🇺🇸, the United Kingdom 🇬🇧, and at least a dozen other countries. Prompts explicitly sought bulk PII including mobile phone numbers, demographic query results, and payment gateway API keys. One prompt asked where Korean stolen data is typically sold; another noted that database dumps without phone number fields were worthless.
- The operator deliberately avoided direct financial withdrawals to prevent triggering fraud alerts, indicating operational awareness of detection mechanisms. The MITRE ATLAS techniques recorded include AML.T0040, AML.T0043, AML.T0048, AML.T0051, AML.T0052, and AML.T0054. Zscaler detects campaign indicators under the threat name AI.HackTool.ARTEX.
Responder takeaway: Hunt for the jump server and work server IPs in proxy, firewall, and web application logs, especially connections to APIs and admin panels. If ARTEX or sqlmap traffic is present, look for project-structured output directories and context-injection scripts. The IOC table is in the report. Review any AI coding assistant logs in your environment for prompts referencing pre-authorized scope or autonomous tool execution, those are your guardrail-bypass signals.

Upstream SOCKS proxies at 205.214.59[.]31:443 and 161.8.161[.]140:11005, plus a proxy pool API at 154.201.79[.]246:443, provided per-project outbound IPs to reduce direct exposure.

- AI models were assigned structured roles rather than used interchangeably. ARTEX routed to deepseek-v4.1-flash via xcai[.]pro/v1. GLM (glm-5.3) was explicitly instructed to audit DeepSeek's completed work for missed attack surfaces (AML.T0051). Grok (grok-4.7-xhigh) ran research tasks on the jump server via a grok2api bridge, with separate sessions reviewing its output. Three sync scripts, sync-all[.]sh, sync-memory[.]sh, and tools/sync-cc-users.sh, kept instructions and memory files consistent across accounts (AML.T0052).

- Persistent project state was maintained per target using scope[.]md, surface[.]md, notes[.]md, a findings/ folder, and an evidence/ folder. A hook script, tools/project_context_hook.py, injected a status summary into every new prompt so AI sessions could resume prior work without operator recap. System prompts told agents to treat all supplied targets as pre-authorized and to act autonomously without per-step approval (AML.T0054). Investigation assets were archived to Backblaze B2.

- Targeting spanned dating apps, SMS providers, crypto and NFT platforms, retail, education, legal settlement systems, and more across Canada 🇨🇦, China 🇨🇳, Cuba, India 🇮🇳, Japan 🇯🇵, Kenya, Nigeria 🇳🇬, South Korea 🇰🇷, the United States 🇺🇸, the United Kingdom 🇬🇧, and at least a dozen other countries. Prompts explicitly sought bulk PII including mobile phone numbers, demographic query results, and payment gateway API keys. One prompt asked where Korean stolen data is typically sold; another noted that database dumps without phone number fields were worthless.

- The operator deliberately avoided direct financial withdrawals to prevent triggering fraud alerts, indicating operational awareness of detection mechanisms. The MITRE ATLAS techniques recorded include AML.T0040, AML.T0043, AML.T0048, AML.T0051, AML.T0052, and AML.T0054. Zscaler detects campaign indicators under the threat name AI.HackTool.ARTEX.

Responder takeaway: Hunt for the jump server and work server IPs in proxy, firewall, and web application logs, especially connections to APIs and admin panels. If ARTEX or sqlmap traffic is present, look for project-structured output directories and context-injection scripts. The IOC table is in the report. Review any AI coding assistant logs in your environment for prompts referencing pre-authorized scope or autonomous tool execution, those are your guardrail-bypass signals.

item.title: AI-driven, large-scale nation-state campaign using ARTEX enables supply chain compromise
item.description:
Chinese 🇨🇳 Storm-0940 weaponized the ARTEX agentic AI framework to compromise ConnectWise's supply chain, hitting 2,250+ tenants at machine speed and achieving privileged cloud access in under 3 hours.
Key findings:
- Storm-0940, a Chinese 🇨🇳 state-aligned actor active since 2021, exploited the ConnectWise supply chain compromise beginning October 15, 2026, using ARTEX, an open-source multi-agent LLM penetration testing framework written in Go with a Next.js frontend. ARTEX automates the full kill chain from reconnaissance through data exfiltration with minimal human interaction and can operate against 2,250 tenants at 2,900 sign-in attempts per minute. Four application IDs were abused: ConnectWise Cloud Backup (506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae), ConnectWise MS Teams (24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640), ConnectWise MS Graph (0de14c77-b9b0-4137-9360-34878a929827), and SkyKick Partner Portal (c921256f-04a7-44e8-9b2a-69c33929ba19).
- The pre-compromise password spray (October 10-14) originated from 144.172.64[.]99, generating 151,000+ failed logon events across 327 accounts at eight organizations, peaking at 2,900 failures per minute on October 11. The same 144.172.64.x range then appeared in ConnectWise's own published IOCs, directly linking the spray infrastructure to the supply chain pivot. Additional IPs used for Graph API access include 144.172.64[.]128, 144.172.64[.]60, 187.15.88[.]186, 187.15.90[.]217, and 187.15.89[.]186. User agents observed: Python-urllib/3.12, python-requests/2.31.0, python-requests/2.34.2, curl/7.88.1, and azure-toolkit/1.0.
- Once inside via stolen OAuth app credentials (T1528, T1078.004), AI agents authenticated to Microsoft 365 without interactive user sign-in, then moved through Microsoft Graph performing cloud account discovery (T1087.004, T1580), adding credentials to existing service principals (T1098.001), and self-assigning Global Administrator roles (T1098.003). These backdoor credentials survive remediation of the original compromised application and can persist as independent access paths. The report confirms multiple environments with evidence of this follow-on activity. MITRE techniques also include T1595, T1195.
- Microsoft's report stresses that successful authentication alone does not confirm data exfiltration, but application credential modifications and role assignments made during the intrusion may remain active even after the original ConnectWise application is disabled. The report explicitly warns: do not delete enterprise applications as a first response, preserve Entra sign-in and audit logs, Microsoft Purview Audit records, SIEM data, and Graph telemetry before making any irreversible changes. Review activity from at least October 15, 2026, and extend service-principal sign-in review back to October 1 where logs allow.
Practitioner takeaway: Hunt using OAuthAppInfo to confirm app presence and permissions, then pivot to EntraIdSpnSignInEvents and GraphAPIAuditEvents (Defender XDR) or SigninLogs and MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs (Sentinel) against the four ConnectWise app IDs and the 144.172.64.x range from October 13 onward. Look specifically for credential additions to service principals and self-assigned privileged roles in Entra audit logs, as those changes outlast the initial compromise. The report includes full KQL hunting queries, IOC tables, Defender XDR and Defender for Cloud Apps alert names, and named MITRE ATT&CK technique IDs.

item.title: php2shell: Zeek and Suricata Detections for PHP RCE
item.description:
Two critical PHP RCE vulnerabilities (CVSS 4.0: 9.2 each) affect the majority of public web servers globally. Corelight releases open-source Zeek and Suricata detections under coordinated disclosure.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 both exploit memory-handling issues in PHP, enabling remote code execution via two distinct attack strategies. Both carry a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. Credited researchers include teams from Wiz, OpenAI, Quarkslab, and Calif. Given how deeply PHP is embedded in CMS platforms, e-commerce, and business applications, the exposure surface is enormous across managed and unmanaged hosts alike.
- The Zeek detection package ships nine distinct behavioral notice types, not signature or pattern matching. Notices cover PHP_Crash_Sequence (correlated suspicious HTTP transactions in a bounded session window), Multipart_Header_Flood, Large_Form_Key, Serialized_Integer_Overflow, Serialized_Integer_Collisions, Serialized_String_Collisions, Serialized_Duplicate_Array, and Serialized_Object_Repetition. Each notice includes a sub field containing a sample of the triggering network event, giving responders a concrete evidentiary anchor rather than an opaque alert.
- The Potentially_Affected_PHP_Version notice passively inventories PHP versions from Server and X-Powered-By HTTP response headers. This is especially valuable for finding unmanaged or shadow IT hosts running vulnerable PHP that may not appear in a CMDB. Suricata rules add three complementary detections in two classes, including a phpinfo() trigger, with alerts rate-limited to one per server IP per hour to reduce noise.
- Both Zeek and Suricata detections require HTTP visibility, meaning either plaintext HTTP traffic or an architecture that decrypts HTTPS for inspection. The report notes that attackers, automated scanners, and bots frequently operate over plain HTTP, so network-layer visibility catches a meaningful share of exploitation attempts even without TLS inspection.
Practitioner takeaway: The detection code, configuration guidance, and a public HTTP regression test are published at github[.]com/corelight/php2shell-detect. Start by deploying the Potentially_Affected_PHP_Version notice to build a real-time inventory of vulnerable PHP hosts across your environment, including assets you do not know about, before hunting behavioral notices for active exploitation attempts. Prioritize patching any host advertising a PHP version in the affected range.

item.title: The Science of Exploitability: Decoding BlueHammer
item.description:
CVE-2026-33825 "BlueHammer" chains eight Windows Defender subsystems to reach NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, then pivots to full domain compromise via LSASS credential theft and pass-the-hash. Patch threshold is Defender Antimalware Platform 4.18.26030.3011.
Key findings:
- BlueHammer is a local privilege escalation only: the attacker needs standard-user code execution first (phishing, malicious content, or valid-account abuse), then the eight-stage chain fires. The stages chain CloudFilter callbacks, batch oplocks on RstrtMgr.dll, object-manager symlinks, Defender's MpAmDefinitionUpdateAPI RPC over ncalrpc, offline SAM parsing via offreg.dll's OROpenHiveByHandle, and SAMR's SamiChangePasswordUser. Stage 0 gates everything on a pending Defender signature update (category GUID E0789628-CE08-4437-BE74-2495B842F43B): no pending update, no exploit. The PoC binary is FunnyApp.exe, SHA-256 f4ffef4204880031a6a532ff5c1b5686e6a301c365f492071c1d462fa5b6b4a0.
- The core timing primitive (Stages 2-3) places MsMpEng.exe in a controlled kernel-mode wait by registering a CloudFilter sync root named IHATEMICROSOFT, dropping a decoy foo.exe in it, and holding the cldflt.sys callback open with a SetEvent pivot. MsMpEng shows "Running" in Task Manager throughout because PPL hides per-thread wait states from unprivileged observers. Stage 6 then uses a batch oplock (FSCTL 0x90008) on mpasbase.vdm with FILE_DELETE_ON_CLOSE to open a microsecond race window, swaps the WDUpdateDirectory symlink under NT object path \Sessions\N\BaseNamedObjects\GUID\WDUpdateDirectory to redirect Defender's SYSTEM-token file open at the SAM hive on a VSS shadow copy, and leaks a usable SAM handle without touching the live registry.
- Stage 7 parses the offline SAM hive, reconstructs the 16-byte LSA bootkey from four hidden subkey class names under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa, decrypts NT hashes via AES-CBC, then calls SamiChangePasswordUser with the recovered old hash to reset the local admin to the hardcoded password $PWNed666!!!WDFAIL. It unwraps the UAC-elevated linked token (T1134.001), creates a GUID-named service under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\ as LocalSystem (T1543.003), and pivots the SYSTEM token into the interactive session via DuplicateTokenEx plus SetTokenInformation(TokenSessionId) to spawn conhost.exe. If the process is killed between reset and restore, the admin account is left with the residual password $PWNed666!!!WDFAIL: a persistent forensic marker.
- MITRE ATT&CK technique IDs from the report: T1518.001 (Stage 0, IUpdateSession Defender version query), T1211 (Stage 3, CloudFilter freeze for defense evasion), T1559 (Stage 5, MpAmDefinitionUpdateAPI IPC), T1068 (Stage 6, oplock-symlink race for privilege escalation), T1003.002 (Stage 7, offline SAM parsing), T1098 (Stage 7, SAMR hash swap), T1134.001 (Stage 7, token manipulation), T1543.003 (Stage 7, GUID service creation). In the lab, the SYSTEM shell exposed cached CITRIX\administrator credentials in LSASS; pass-the-hash via PsExec to domain controller dc60 then yielded NTDS.dit extraction, demonstrating domain compromise from a single workstation foothold when privileged credentials are present.
- Version-based scanning is insufficient: runtime conditions (pending update, WinDefend state, cldflt.sys presence, VSS availability, CloudFilter reachability) determine whether the chain executes. Affected does not equal exploitable. The report's highest-signal behavioral correlation: a single process requesting batch oplocks (FSCTL 0x90008) on unrelated files within 60 seconds, registering a CloudFilter sync root, binding to MpAmDefinitionUpdateAPI (RPC UUID c503f532-443a-4c69-8300-ccd1fbdb3839), and issuing a SAMR password change, all within one process tree. Static strings IHATEMICROSOFT and $PWNed666!!!WDFAIL are present in the analyzed PoC but can be stripped from modified builds.
Practitioner takeaway: Update Defender Antimalware Platform to 4.18.26030.3011 or later to close the Stage 3-4 boundary. For hunting, correlate: unexpected CloudFilter sync-root registration, two FSCTL 0x90008 oplock requests from the same process, outbound ncalrpc binding to UUID c503f532-443a-4c69-8300-ccd1fbdb3839 from a non-Windows-Update process, SAMR password-change events, and GUID-named orphan service entries in HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\. On any host where the exploit may have run and been interrupted, check whether the local administrator account's NT hash decrypts to MD4(UTF-16LE("$PWNed666!!!WDFAIL")) and whether an orphan GUID-named service with a user-writable ImagePath remains. IOCs and MITRE mappings are in the Qualys report.

item.title: php2shell: Assessing Elastic detection coverage relevant to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619
item.description:
Two critical unauthenticated PHP core RCE flaws (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, CVSS v4.0 9.2) leaked before coordinated disclosure. No public PoC exists yet, but patched versions shipped October 21, 2026.
Key details:
- CVE-2026-109618 (GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w) is an RCE via out-of-memory corruption: OOM handling can interrupt PHP while request data is only partially initialized, and cleanup then treats invalid data as valid. CVE-2026-109619 (GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp) is an RCE via stale global state: request-owned internal state can survive after its backing memory is freed, and a later worker request may use that stale pointer before initialization resets it. Both are reachable by an unauthenticated web request. The PHP security team flags mod_php as highest risk because the trigger fires before any application code runs. Fixed versions are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35, patched via commit 31c0ea7d7ff1d1fccb6492e52dab544011628065. PHP 8.1 and older receive no upstream fixes, though minimal source backports exist for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1. Exploitation maps to T1190, with post-exploitation expected to follow T1059 and T1505.003.
- The PHP security team is explicit: there are no complete mitigations, only partial exposure reduction. For the OOM path, set memory_limit=-1 via php_admin_value in FPM pool or Apache config (not ini_set), keep post_max_size low, and enforce container or cgroup limits. For the stale-state path, set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart workers; on PHP 8.5 also set fatal_error_backtraces=0. These block specific attack paths, not the vulnerability itself. Treat any social-media advice presenting a single config toggle as a complete fix with skepticism.
- The detection opportunity is not the trigger, it is the outcome. A PHP worker spawning a shell is abnormal regardless of which vulnerability opened the door. The post-exploitation convergent flow is consistent: discovery commands (id, whoami, uname -a), interpreter pivots (python3 -c, perl -e, php -r), payload staging via curl or wget piped to bash, reverse shells via /dev/tcp or mkfifo, credential harvesting from .env or ~/.aws/credentials or mounted Kubernetes service account tokens, webshell writes into the web root (.php, .phtml, polyglots), and persistence via cron, systemd, or ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. Elastic's report references a prior wp2shell incident where apache2 spawning dash to run id; whoami; hostname was caught by the same behavioral rules, a completely different initial access vector, identical detection surface.
- Named Elastic detection rules covering this convergent flow across process and file telemetry: Payload Execution by Web Server (EDR, preventive), Payload Downloaded via Curl or Wget by Web Server (EDR, preventive), Suspicious Web Server Child Process (EDR, preventive), Suspicious Command Execution via Web Server, Unusual Command Execution via Web Server (new_terms baseline), Suspicious Child Execution via Web Server, Unusual Child Execution via Web Server (new_terms baseline), Unusual File Creation via Web Server (new_terms baseline), Unusual File Creation by Web Server, and File with High Entropy Created by Web Server. The high-entropy file rule requires Elastic Stack 9.3.0 or later and the linux.advanced[.]events.populate_file_data advanced setting set to true so that file events include file.Ext.entropy.
- To inventory affected PHP installs before a PoC lands, the report provides Osquery queries covering Linux paths across /usr/bin, /usr/local/bin, cPanel (ea-php), Plesk, Remi, LiteSpeed (lsphp), Snap, and Nix store locations, plus mod_php Apache modules (libphp%.so). Windows queries cover C:\PHP, Program Files, wamp, and Laragon paths for php.exe, php-cgi.exe, and php-win.exe. Package-manager queries for deb_packages and rpm_packages cover php, libapache2-mod-php, lsphp, ea-php, plesk-php, and sw-engine. Process telemetry queries against logs-endpoint[.]events.process-* using process[.]name matching php*, lsphp*, frankenphp, and sw-engine-fpm round out the inventory picture.
Prioritize internet-facing PHP hosts for immediate patching. Run the Osquery inventory queries to surface bundled runtimes in vendor appliances, control panels, and CMS installs (WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, Magento) that may not appear in your primary asset register. Enable all ten named SIEM and EDR rules on PHP hosts now, before public exploit code exists. If you find evidence of compromise, isolate the host, preserve web server and PHP logs, and look for new files in the web root, new cron jobs, new services, and new accounts. IOCs and detection rule queries are in the Elastic report.

Key details:

- CVE-2026-109618 (GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w) is an RCE via out-of-memory corruption: OOM handling can interrupt PHP while request data is only partially initialized, and cleanup then treats invalid data as valid. CVE-2026-109619 (GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp) is an RCE via stale global state: request-owned internal state can survive after its backing memory is freed, and a later worker request may use that stale pointer before initialization resets it. Both are reachable by an unauthenticated web request. The PHP security team flags mod_php as highest risk because the trigger fires before any application code runs. Fixed versions are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35, patched via commit 31c0ea7d7ff1d1fccb6492e52dab544011628065. PHP 8.1 and older receive no upstream fixes, though minimal source backports exist for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1. Exploitation maps to T1190, with post-exploitation expected to follow T1059 and T1505.003.

- The PHP security team is explicit: there are no complete mitigations, only partial exposure reduction. For the OOM path, set memory_limit=-1 via php_admin_value in FPM pool or Apache config (not ini_set), keep post_max_size low, and enforce container or cgroup limits. For the stale-state path, set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart workers; on PHP 8.5 also set fatal_error_backtraces=0. These block specific attack paths, not the vulnerability itself. Treat any social-media advice presenting a single config toggle as a complete fix with skepticism.

- The detection opportunity is not the trigger, it is the outcome. A PHP worker spawning a shell is abnormal regardless of which vulnerability opened the door. The post-exploitation convergent flow is consistent: discovery commands (id, whoami, uname -a), interpreter pivots (python3 -c, perl -e, php -r), payload staging via curl or wget piped to bash, reverse shells via /dev/tcp or mkfifo, credential harvesting from .env or ~/.aws/credentials or mounted Kubernetes service account tokens, webshell writes into the web root (.php, .phtml, polyglots), and persistence via cron, systemd, or ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. Elastic's report references a prior wp2shell incident where apache2 spawning dash to run id; whoami; hostname was caught by the same behavioral rules, a completely different initial access vector, identical detection surface.

- Named Elastic detection rules covering this convergent flow across process and file telemetry: Payload Execution by Web Server (EDR, preventive), Payload Downloaded via Curl or Wget by Web Server (EDR, preventive), Suspicious Web Server Child Process (EDR, preventive), Suspicious Command Execution via Web Server, Unusual Command Execution via Web Server (new_terms baseline), Suspicious Child Execution via Web Server, Unusual Child Execution via Web Server (new_terms baseline), Unusual File Creation via Web Server (new_terms baseline), Unusual File Creation by Web Server, and File with High Entropy Created by Web Server. The high-entropy file rule requires Elastic Stack 9.3.0 or later and the linux.advanced[.]events.populate_file_data advanced setting set to true so that file events include file.Ext.entropy.

- To inventory affected PHP installs before a PoC lands, the report provides Osquery queries covering Linux paths across /usr/bin, /usr/local/bin, cPanel (ea-php), Plesk, Remi, LiteSpeed (lsphp), Snap, and Nix store locations, plus mod_php Apache modules (libphp%.so). Windows queries cover C:\PHP, Program Files, wamp, and Laragon paths for php.exe, php-cgi.exe, and php-win.exe. Package-manager queries for deb_packages and rpm_packages cover php, libapache2-mod-php, lsphp, ea-php, plesk-php, and sw-engine. Process telemetry queries against logs-endpoint[.]events.process-* using process[.]name matching php*, lsphp*, frankenphp, and sw-engine-fpm round out the inventory picture.

Prioritize internet-facing PHP hosts for immediate patching. Run the Osquery inventory queries to surface bundled runtimes in vendor appliances, control panels, and CMS installs (WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, Magento) that may not appear in your primary asset register. Enable all ten named SIEM and EDR rules on PHP hosts now, before public exploit code exists. If you find evidence of compromise, isolate the host, preserve web server and PHP logs, and look for new files in the web root, new cron jobs, new services, and new accounts. IOCs and detection rule queries are in the Elastic report.

item.title: AOMEI Backupper supply chain attack
item.description:
UNC7017 poisoned AOMEI's update infrastructure for minutes at a time across April-July 2026, delivering the CROSSROAD downloader and SHINYROAD backdoor to IT, telecom, and education orgs across 11 countries.
Key details:
- UNC7017 modified configuration files on AOMEI's ABMarket update infrastructure during windows lasting five to ten minutes on May 28, July 16, and July 20, 2026. Only systems that checked for updates during those windows received malicious content, which means exposure is determined by connection timing, not software version. Affected sectors span IT services, telecommunications, and higher education across Australia 🇦🇺, Brazil 🇧🇷, India 🇮🇳, Pakistan 🇵🇰, Portugal 🇵🇹, Singapore 🇸🇬, South Africa 🇿🇦, Spain 🇪🇸, Switzerland 🇨🇭, Türkiye, and the United States 🇺🇸.
- The modified configs redirected AOMEI clients to download a malicious ZIP from adversary infrastructure, executed automatically through the application's notification workflow via Backupper.exe and ABNotify.exe. The archive dropped CROSSROAD, a downloader that performs environment checks, pulls additional payloads, creates a scheduled task for persistence, then deletes itself from disk.
- CROSSROAD's scheduled task launches SHINYROAD, a modular backdoor operating through a legitimate signed Radmin component. Later campaign stages deployed the Adaptix C2 framework disguised as Nitro PDF-related software. Hunt for scheduled tasks named RadminComponentRuntime and NitroRuntime, unexpected executables in AOMEI application directories, and EDR telemetry involving Backupper.exe, ABNotify.exe, upgrade-now.exe, and Radmin-related components.
- On July 20, 2026, UNC7017 added a second technique: a one-pixel invisible popup in the notification config directed affected systems to a WebDAV resource, causing them to transmit NTLM authentication hashes to attacker-controlled infrastructure. Any system that connected to AOMEI update services on that date should have its authentication logs reviewed for accounts potentially exposed through this credential harvesting path.
- Unlike SolarWinds or 3CX, no software code was modified, so file integrity checks and version audits return clean results. Vendor-side remediation does not clean already-infected endpoints. Backup servers and admin workstations running AOMEI Backupper carry elevated risk given their privileged access and broad network visibility.
Practitioner takeaway: Start with historical endpoint, proxy, and network telemetry to identify which hosts contacted AOMEI update infrastructure during April-July 2026. Exposure is a timing question first. Then hunt the scheduled tasks RadminComponentRuntime and NitroRuntime, review AOMEI application directories for unexpected binaries, and pull NTLM authentication events for any system active on July 20. IOCs, detection guidance, and hunting artifacts are published by GTIG, Mandiant, and ManageEngine METAL.

item.title: Amazon-Themed ClickFix Campaign Serves Up Finger-Licking Malware
item.description:
A ClickFix campaign spoofing Amazon used the ancient finger utility, a Veil-derived loader chain, Doina RAT, Lumma Stealer, and a pirated NetSupport RMM to hit at least three victims with a layered, heavily obfuscated infection chain.
Key details:
- The attack began with a malvertising link, orders-amazon[.]com.advancedfences[.]com, appearing as a paid Google search result for "amazon business." It redirected to a fake Amazon login page at sites[.]google[.]com/view/ch-pc/sign-in, then served a fake CAPTCHA that pastejacked a ClickFix command into the user's clipboard. The visible portion of the Run dialog was padded with spaces and hyphens to show only "Push the Enter key," concealing the real payload. Google ad-click parameters (aclk, gclid, gadsource, gadcampaignid, gbraid) are preserved in browser history and proxy logs and can tie a victim session to the malvertising chain.
- Stage 1 used finger.exe, a legitimate Windows LOLbin transmitting plaintext over port 79/tcp, to retrieve a weaponized .plan file from grillrecipespro[.]com. The command was character-obfuscated with commas, carets, hyphens, and underscores that the Windows command interpreter silently ignores. The .plan file hid its payload behind 68 blank lines. It then downloaded a legitimate IronPython 3.4.2 ZIP to the Temp directory disguised with a .pdf extension, unpacked it with the built-in tar command, and passed a Base64/zlib-compressed Python blob directly to ipyw32.exe, ultimately fetching timer6 from grillmasterchef[.]com.
- Timer6 (SHA256: d864b28c302db9ed10baf8def0fb26bac0b97d27349d22c4e9390d30fce54649) is a Python script encoded in Base64 with select ASCII letters substituted by visually similar Cyrillic characters to break naive decoders. After reversing the substitution, it decodes to another Python layer protected by a 19-byte XOR key (hex: 84 0d ff da 80 29 b6 1b 52 9b 42 40 5d 55 aa 80 a5 7e 7c) embedded as a separate Base64 blob. The decoded output is a PE loader using a Veil-derived shellcode inject pattern (HeapCreate, HeapAlloc, native API sequence) that searches disk for an .ini file containing a URL, fetches the target using a standard Chrome User-Agent string, and RC4-decrypts it using the first 64 bytes of the downloaded file as the key. The decrypted v6 payload (SHA256: 891cc3ca2d29e9b185a8913e93810f48859d2be1f23ddd977a15cdbeed509e0e) is Doina, a modular RAT previously linked to ransomware precursor activity, injected directly into memory.
- Doina immediately beaconed to grillmasterchef[.]com and retrieved a 52MB ZIP from kiriosyka[.]com containing a portable Node.js runtime and a heavily obfuscated index.js (SHA256: 87a047160eb1a9b92e6ede511252dfc624b0f5a7185ac2cec1c7ebde8cdf4eea), unpacked to C:\ProgramData\NodeView. The index.js component decrypts two GUID-named .tmp files using AES-256-GCM (first 12 bytes: nonce; next 16 bytes: key). The smaller file is a shellcode reflective DLL injector (sRDI); the larger is Lumma Stealer (multiple decrypted SHA256 hashes in the report), injected via process hollowing. Lumma beaconed to perfectgrillrecipes[.]com for initial check-in, then switched to websocket for continuous C2 with thegrilljournal[.]com and homelygrill[.]com handling exfil. Targets included Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Opera, Ledger, Electrum, Atomic Wallet, LastPass, Dashlane, 1Password, NordPass, and RoboForm. A pirated NetSupport RMM client (Client32.exe, signed eight years ago) was also dropped to C:\ProgramData\Prodclear, beaconing to 167.148.201[.]106:725 and calling /fakeurl.htm.
Practitioner takeaway: Hunt for finger.exe execution (any child process or network connection over port 79/tcp is anomalous on modern enterprise endpoints), ipyw32.exe spawned from a Temp-resident file with a .pdf extension, tar.exe extracting content from a non-archive-named file in Temp, and node.exe running from C:\ProgramData\NodeView. Check for GUID-named .tmp files with high entropy and no PE header in ProgramData. Flag HTTPS connections on port 725/tcp for unauthorized NetSupport. In browser history and proxy logs, correlate aclk and gclid parameters to reconstruct the malvertising click chain. Full IOC list and hashes are published to Huntress's GitHub.

item.title: LiteLLM Hijacked Again: Malicious 1.107.0 Wheels Steal Credentials and Load Remote Code
item.description:
LiteLLM 1.107.0 wheels on PyPI contain three injected files that steal credentials on Python startup and open an hourly remote-code execution channel, with the payload absent from the source distribution entirely.
Key findings:
- The malicious wheel adds cook.pth, cook[.]py, and sitecustomize[.]py into the site-packages root via the purelib data directory. cook.pth is processed by Python's site module at interpreter startup, importing cook[.]py before any application code runs, including when pip itself is invoked. cook[.]py base64-decodes and exec()s roughly 61 KB of compressed Python identifying itself as privcollect, a credential stealer targeting SSH keys, GPG keys, TLS private keys, shell and DB client histories, browser credential stores, AWS/Azure/GCP credentials, Kubernetes configs, Docker secrets, CI/CD secrets from Jenkins, GitLab Runner, Vault, Terraform, GitHub CLI, package manager tokens (.npmrc, .pypirc, .git-credentials), AI tooling configs for Cursor, Claude, Copilot, Hugging Face, and more, plus every readable /proc/*/environ on Linux. It also connects through Prisma to dump LiteLLM_CredentialsTable and LiteLLM_ProxyModelTable, potentially exposing every upstream LLM provider credential stored in a proxy deployment at once.
- Exfiltration goes to hxxp[:]//www.litellm[.]dev/healthcheck over plaintext HTTP with a static token (X-Token: XWiA8gZNa7NcX2XRoAEb) in the header. Content is AES-256-CBC encrypted under a session key wrapped with an embedded RSA-4096 public key, so network captures do not recover stolen data without the attacker's private key. The exfiltration domain is distinct from the legitimate litellm[.]ai and from the earlier TeamPCP incident's models.litellm[.]cloud domain.
- sitecustomize[.]py forks a daemonized process holding /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock, changes working directory to /, and loops hourly. Each cycle reads a C2 domain from the dead-drop at hxxps[:]//raw.githubusercontent[.]com/letters9813/pythonclient-test/main/domain.txt, runs a second privcollect pass synchronously (no run-once guard), then fetches and exec()s arbitrary Python from hxxp://{domain}/codepy with no authentication or integrity check. The dead-drop returned zero bytes at time of analysis, making the loader dormant but re-armable instantly. The os.fork() path fails silently on Windows, but cook.pth still fires the credential stealer there.
- The critical forensic gap: the sdist and the Git tag contain none of the three payload files. The sdist's pyproject.toml carries an added data = "cook" setting absent from the corresponding tag, and wheel metadata timestamps match legitimate files, consistent with injection during normal wheel construction. All seven platform wheels (macOS, Linux, musl Linux, Windows) are affected. This is a supply-chain injection at the artifact layer, and source review or sdist inspection will not surface it.
Practitioner takeaway: do not run pip inside an affected environment to remediate, that invocation will re-trigger cook.pth. First, without invoking the affected Python interpreter, remove cook.pth, cook[.]py, sitecustomize[.]py, their __pycache__ compiled counterparts, /tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb, and /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock. Hunt for detached Python processes using setsid, running with / as working directory, or holding the lock file. Check /tmp/.pc_sq_* and /tmp/.pc_e_* for staging artifacts. Block and preserve logs for www.litellm[.]dev and the letters9813/pythonclient-test dead-drop. Rotate every credential class the report enumerates, treating LiteLLM_CredentialsTable as fully compromised. For artifact verification going forward, diff wheel RECORD manifests against sdist contents and inspect .pth files and sitecustomize[.]py in site-packages as standard post-install hygiene. IOCs are listed in the JFrog report; JFrog Xray tracks this as XRAY-955589.

item.title: How to Export Windows Event Logs (EVTX)
item.description:
Exporting Windows EVTX logs correctly preserves every field, record ID, and UTC timestamp that text exports silently destroy. Here is the method, the caveats, and what responders miss when they get it wrong.
Key details:
- Never copy live .evtx files directly from C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs using Explorer or a file manager. The Event Log service holds them open, which produces errors or unusable output. The single exception: a disk mounted offline, such as a drive pulled from a non-booting machine, where nothing holds the files open and a straight copy is exactly the right move. For live systems, use Event Viewer (right-click the log, Save All Events As, keep .evtx format) or wevtutil epl from an elevated prompt. Text exports drop structure; EVTX keeps every field intact and is what parsers like EvtxECmd expect.
- wevtutil gives responders surgical control during collection. Export with time filters using XPath queries: a 24-hour window uses timediff([@]SystemTime) <= 86400000 (milliseconds), and an exact UTC range uses [@]SystemTime >= and < operators. Filter by event ID on the fly, for example EventID=4624 or EventID=4625 for all logon events. On a busy domain controller, an unfiltered Security export can run to gigabytes; filter first. Build complex queries in Event Viewer's XML tab and copy the XPath rather than writing it by hand.
- The logs that carry the story in most investigations: Security (event IDs 4624, 4625, 4688, 4720, 4728, 1102), System (7045 new services, 7036 service state, 104 log cleared), Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational if Sysmon is deployed, Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational for script block logging (4104), Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler/Operational for scheduled task creation (event 106), and Microsoft-Windows-TerminalServices-LocalSessionManager/Operational for RDP sessions (21, 24, 25). Event 4688 process creation and PowerShell script block logging are off by default; check auditpol /get /category:* before hunting for events that were never written.
- Remote collection with wevtutil /r:<computer> has a trap that wastes responder time: the export file lands on the remote machine's disk, not yours. Retrieve it afterward via the admin share (\\srv-01\C$\logs) or use PowerShell remoting with Invoke-Command plus Copy-Item -FromSession to pull files back in one step. Either path requires admin rights on the target and Remote Event Log Management firewall rules enabled. Log retention is the other silent killer: wevtutil gl Security shows maxSize and retention settings. If the attack predates the oldest event in the log, the evidence is not there, and the SIEM or a Windows Event Forwarding collector is the only fallback.
Practitioner takeaway: before you collect, run wevtutil gl Security on each target and check maxSize and the timestamp of the oldest event. If retention has rolled past the incident window, pivot to forwarded event logs or your SIEM immediately rather than collecting a log that cannot answer the question. For triage at scale, the PowerShell loop in the report exports Security, System, Sysmon, PowerShell, Defender, and TaskScheduler logs from any host into a named folder and skips missing channels cleanly, making it reusable across an environment without modification.

Exporting Windows EVTX logs correctly preserves every field, record ID, and UTC timestamp that text exports silently destroy. Here is the method, the caveats, and what responders miss when they get it wrong.

Key details:

- Never copy live .evtx files directly from C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs using Explorer or a file manager. The Event Log service holds them open, which produces errors or unusable output. The single exception: a disk mounted offline, such as a drive pulled from a non-booting machine, where nothing holds the files open and a straight copy is exactly the right move. For live systems, use Event Viewer (right-click the log, Save All Events As, keep .evtx format) or wevtutil epl from an elevated prompt. Text exports drop structure; EVTX keeps every field intact and is what parsers like EvtxECmd expect.

- wevtutil gives responders surgical control during collection. Export with time filters using XPath queries: a 24-hour window uses timediff([@]SystemTime) <= 86400000 (milliseconds), and an exact UTC range uses [@]SystemTime >= and < operators. Filter by event ID on the fly, for example EventID=4624 or EventID=4625 for all logon events. On a busy domain controller, an unfiltered Security export can run to gigabytes; filter first. Build complex queries in Event Viewer's XML tab and copy the XPath rather than writing it by hand.

- The logs that carry the story in most investigations: Security (event IDs 4624, 4625, 4688, 4720, 4728, 1102), System (7045 new services, 7036 service state, 104 log cleared), Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational if Sysmon is deployed, Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational for script block logging (4104), Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler/Operational for scheduled task creation (event 106), and Microsoft-Windows-TerminalServices-LocalSessionManager/Operational for RDP sessions (21, 24, 25). Event 4688 process creation and PowerShell script block logging are off by default; check auditpol /get /category:* before hunting for events that were never written.

- Remote collection with wevtutil /r:<computer> has a trap that wastes responder time: the export file lands on the remote machine's disk, not yours. Retrieve it afterward via the admin share (\\srv-01\C$\logs) or use PowerShell remoting with Invoke-Command plus Copy-Item -FromSession to pull files back in one step. Either path requires admin rights on the target and Remote Event Log Management firewall rules enabled. Log retention is the other silent killer: wevtutil gl Security shows maxSize and retention settings. If the attack predates the oldest event in the log, the evidence is not there, and the SIEM or a Windows Event Forwarding collector is the only fallback.

Practitioner takeaway: before you collect, run wevtutil gl Security on each target and check maxSize and the timestamp of the oldest event. If retention has rolled past the incident window, pivot to forwarded event logs or your SIEM immediately rather than collecting a log that cannot answer the question. For triage at scale, the PowerShell loop in the report exports Security, System, Sysmon, PowerShell, Defender, and TaskScheduler logs from any host into a named folder and skips missing channels cleanly, making it reusable across an environment without modification.
